chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: A language model never sees a letter. Before any of the machinery people talk about, attention, layers, billions of parameters, the text is cut into pieces and each piece is replaced by a list of numbers: its embedding. Everything the model knows about a word has to be reachable from that list, or built up from it. This is the first of two posts on embeddings. This one is about the vectors inside the model: how text is cut into tokens, how the table of token vectors is learned, what the geometry of those vectors means and does not mean, and how a model is told where in the sentence each token

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Part 2 is about the separate embedding models that turn a whole sentence or document into one vector, and how they are used to search and to feed language models the right documents. Nothing here is illustrative. The tokeniser is trained on text8, the first 100 million characters of an English Wikipedia dump; word2vec is trained on the same text; the analogy tests use the 6-billion-token GloVe vectors; and the transformer section uses GPT-2's own embedding table.

chunks.heading: The embedding table
chunks.text: Fix a vocabulary of V tokens and a dimension d. The embedding is a matrix E R^{V d}, one row per token. Token t becomes row t: where xt \{0,1\}^V is the one-hot vector with a single 1 in position t. The matrix product is how it is written; in practice it is an array lookup. The point of writing it as a product is that the lookup is linear, so the gradient of anything with respect to E is easy to find, which is how the table gets learned.

chunks.heading: The embedding table
chunks.text: The table is large. GPT-2's smallest model has V = 50{,}257 tokens and d = 768, so E holds 38.6 million numbers: almost a third of that model's 124 million parameters. Recent models have bigger vocabularies and wider vectors: Llama 3 uses 128,256 tokens of dimension 4,096 in its 8-billion-parameter version, over half a billion numbers for the input table alone. Two choices sit behind that table: what the V tokens are, and how the rows get their values. The next sections take them in turn.

chunks.heading: Cutting text into tokens
chunks.text: The obvious unit is the word, and it fails twice. English has an unbounded supply of words (names, numbers, misspellings, "tokenisation"), so any fixed list leaves some out, and those become an unknown-word symbol the model can learn nothing about. And a list long enough to cover most text would make E enormous, with most rows seen too rarely to learn. Characters fix both problems and create a third: sequences become five or six times longer, and the cost of attention grows with the square of the sequence length.

chunks.heading: Cutting text into tokens
chunks.text: Subword tokenisation sits between them. Frequent words get one token; rare words are spelled out from common pieces. The method used by the GPT family is byte-pair encoding (BPE). Philip Gage published it in 1994 as a data compression algorithm: repeatedly find the most frequent pair of adjacent bytes and replace it with a new byte that does not occur in the data. Rico Sennrich, Barry Haddow and Alexandra Birch adapted it for machine translation in 2016. As a tokeniser it is learned once, from a corpus:

chunks.heading: Cutting text into tokens
chunks.text: 1. Start with every word spelled as characters, plus an end-of-word marker (written here). 2. Count every adjacent pair of symbols, weighted by how often each word occurs. 3. Merge the most frequent pair into a single new symbol, everywhere. Record the merge. 4. Repeat until the vocabulary is the size you want. To tokenise new text, apply the recorded merges in the order they were learned. I ran this on text8: 17,005,207 words, 253,854 of them distinct. The first merges are the most common pairs in English: e + (a word ending in e), s, th, in, er, then th + e to make the word the by the tenth

chunks.heading: Cutting text into tokens
chunks.text: By a hundred merges the common short words are whole tokens: for, was, that, with, and the number words that text8 spells out. By a thousand, frequent suffixes such as ation and ings have their own tokens. The cost of the text falls fast and then slowly:

chunks.heading: Cutting text into tokens
chunks.text: Sixteen thousand merges bring the average to 1.16 tokens a word, against 5.88 symbols a word with characters alone. That is the trade the vocabulary size controls. GPT-2 made two changes. It works on bytes rather than characters, so the 256 possible bytes are the starting alphabet and no input can ever be unrepresentable: an emoji or a Chinese character is just a few bytes. And before merging, the text is split by a regular expression into words, numbers and punctuation, with a leading space kept attached to the word that follows it.

chunks.heading: Cutting text into tokens
chunks.text: GPT-2's 50,257 tokens are the 256 bytes, 50,000 merges and one end-of-text marker. Its vocabulary therefore has " token" (with the space) and "token" (without) as different tokens with different embeddings. Here is GPT-2's tokeniser next to the one used by GPT-4o, which has about four times the vocabulary:

chunks.heading: Cutting text into tokens
chunks.text: The spaces are shown as ␣. Numbers are a well-known weak point: GPT-2 cuts digit strings wherever its merges happen to fall, so the same number can be split differently in different contexts, which is one reason early models were poor at arithmetic. Later tokenisers split numbers into fixed groups of digits. Other subword schemes work on the same principle with a different rule for choosing what to merge or keep. WordPiece, used by BERT, merges the pair that most increases the likelihood of the training data under a unigram model; the Unigram method in SentencePiece starts from a large vocabul

chunks.heading: Meaning from company
chunks.text: Where do the vectors come from? The idea that makes it possible is old. Zellig Harris proposed in 1954 that words occurring in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings, the distributional hypothesis; J. R. Firth put it as "You shall know a word by the company it keeps" in 1957. If that is right, meaning can be measured by counting. Count, over a corpus, how often word w appears within a few positions of context word c: call it \#(w,c), with \#(w) = \#(w,c), \#(c) likewise and |D| the total number of pairs.

chunks.heading: Meaning from company
chunks.text: Raw counts are dominated by frequent words (everything co-occurs with the), so the useful measure is how much more often the pair occurs than chance: This is pointwise mutual information. A word's row of PMI values against every context is already a vector that captures meaning: coffee and tea have high PMI with cup, drink and hot. But the rows are as long as the vocabulary and mostly empty (unobserved pairs have PMI -, usually clipped to zero). The classical fix is to compress the matrix: take the singular value decomposition M = U V^ and keep the top d singular values. By the Eckart–Young th

chunks.heading: word2vec
chunks.text: In 2013 Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google published word2vec, which learned word vectors with a shallow neural network instead of by counting and factorising. It was fast, it scaled to billions of words, and its vectors did something that made it famous: the analogies of the next section. Its most successful form is the skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS). Every word w gets two vectors: w when it is the centre word and c when it is a context word. Slide a window along the text. Each (centre, context) pair seen in the window is a positive example, and the model should say "yes, these o

chunks.heading: word2vec
chunks.text: Using '(x) = (x)\,(1-(x)), so that {d}{dx}(x) = 1-(x) = (-x), the gradients are Read as an update, gradient descent pulls w towards the true context by an amount proportional to how wrong the model was ((- w c) is the probability it gave to "no"), and pushes it away from each noise word in proportion to how much it wrongly believed in it. Only k+2 vectors change per pair, which is what made it cheap. The original paper uses k between 5 and 20, a noise distribution of unigram frequencies raised to the power 34 (which samples rare words more often than their frequency would), and randomly discar

chunks.heading: What word2vec actually learns
chunks.text: For a few years word2vec looked like a different kind of thing from counting and SVD. Omer Levy and Yoav Goldberg showed in 2014 that it is not. Collect the loss over the whole corpus and group the terms by the pair (w,c). The pair appears as a positive \#(w,c) times, and as a negative k\,\#(w)\,Pn(c) times on average. Writing x = w c, the part of the total loss that depends on x is Suppose the dimension is large enough that each dot product can be chosen freely.

chunks.heading: What word2vec actually learns
chunks.text: Setting L'(x) = 0: with Pn standing in for P(c). Skip-gram with negative sampling is factorising the matrix of pointwise mutual information, shifted down by k, as W C^. It is a weighted, implicit version of the counting method it replaced. The difference in practice comes from the weighting, the smoothed noise distribution and the subsampling, not from a different principle.

chunks.heading: What word2vec actually learns
chunks.text: The theorem assumes unlimited dimension and full convergence. To see how close a real model comes, I trained word2vec with gensim on all of text8 (100 dimensions, window 5, k = 5, 5 epochs; 71,290 words kept) and counted the co-occurrences of the 3,000 most frequent words with the same window weighting and subsampling the training used. For the 247,000 pairs seen at least 20 times: GloVe (Jeffrey Pennington, Richard Socher and Christopher Manning, 2014) makes the factorisation explicit. It fits the log of the co-occurrence counts X{ij} directly, by weighted least squares: with biases bi, bj ab

chunks.heading: The geometry of meaning
chunks.text: Similarity between two embeddings is measured by the cosine of the angle between them, = u v / (\| u\|\,\| v\|). Length mostly reflects how often a word occurs and how consistently it is used; direction carries the meaning. Here are the nearest neighbours in the GloVe space (100 dimensions, the 20,000 most frequent words, stored here to 8 bits): Try bank, whose neighbours are all financial: a single vector per word has to average over every sense of it, and the commonest sense wins. That is the main limitation of static embeddings, and the reason transformers exist, as the next section explain

chunks.heading: Analogies, and a caveat
chunks.text: The result that made word2vec famous was that relationships appear as directions. If king is to man as queen is to woman, then {king} - {man} + {woman} should land near {queen}. The test set Mikolov's group released has 19,544 such questions in fourteen categories, from capital cities to plural verbs. The method, called 3CosAdd, answers a : b :: c : ? with The last condition matters more than its size suggests. For GloVe on the 19,230 questions whose words are all in its top 100,000: Allow the input words as answers and accuracy falls from 64% to 34%.

chunks.heading: Analogies, and a caveat
chunks.text: Of the 12,717 answers then wrong, 10,392 are c itself, the word the offset b - a was added to, and another 1,308 are b. The nearest vector to {king} - {man} + {woman} in GloVe is king itself, at a cosine of 0.84; queen is second, at 0.77. Offsets between related words are small compared with the distance between unrelated ones, so the sum stays close to its starting point, and the test only works because the starting point is ruled out. Tal Linzen (2016) and Malvina Nissim and colleagues (2020) made this point at length.

chunks.heading: Analogies, and a caveat
chunks.text: The parallelogram is real, the categories where it works best (capitals, nationalities, comparatives) are real, but the famous example is weaker than its reputation. The same geometry carries the corpus's biases. Tolga Bolukbasi and colleagues showed in 2016 that {programmer} - {man} + {woman} in a widely used word2vec model landed near homemaker. Embeddings record how words are used, not how they should be.

chunks.heading: Inside a transformer
chunks.text: A transformer language model does not train its embeddings separately. The table E is just the first layer, initialised at random and learned with everything else, from one task: predict the next token. Write h R^d for the model's final hidden state at some position, after all the layers have mixed in context from earlier tokens. The output layer scores every token in the vocabulary with a matrix W R^{V d}, z = W h, and turns the scores into probabilities with the softmax, pv = e^{zv}/ e^{zu}.

chunks.heading: Inside a transformer
chunks.text: If the true next token is y, the loss is the cross-entropy L = - py. Its gradient with respect to the scores is the standard result The row for the correct token is pulled towards h; every other row is pushed away from it, in proportion to the probability the model wrongly gave it. Compare the input table: its gradient reaches only the rows of tokens that actually appeared in the input. The two tables are trained very differently.

chunks.heading: Inside a transformer
chunks.text: Many models, GPT-2 among them, use the same matrix for both, W = E. Ofir Press and Lior Wolf (2017) and Hakan Inan and colleagues (2017) showed this tying works as well or better while saving V d parameters, and it has a clean reading: the model predicts the next token by producing a hidden state that points in the direction of that token's embedding. Tying also has a side effect. Every update pushes all the rows that were not the answer away from h, and rare tokens are almost never the answer, so they receive nothing but these pushes. Jun Gao and colleagues (2019) showed this drives rare toke

chunks.heading: Inside a transformer
chunks.text: The embedding is only the starting point. The vector for bank is the same whether the sentence is about rivers or money; the attention layers that follow combine it with the vectors around it, and by the middle layers the representation of bank in "river bank" and in "bank account" have moved apart. Kawin Ethayarajh (2019) measured this, and also found that these contextual vectors occupy a narrow cone of the space, the same anisotropy as the static table. Part 2 is about what to do with those contextual vectors.

chunks.heading: GPT-2's table
chunks.text: The neighbours mix meaning with form: case and spacing variants of the same word sit next to each other, because the model has to learn that " King", " king" and "King" are related from use alone.

chunks.heading: Where am I in the sentence?
chunks.text: Attention, the operation at the heart of a transformer, compares every token's vector with every other token's and mixes them according to the comparison. It has no notion of order. If X is the matrix of input vectors and P any permutation matrix, self-attention satisfies {Attn}(PX) = P{Attn}(X): shuffle the words and the outputs are shuffled in the same way and otherwise unchanged. "Dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would be the same input. Position has to be added. Learned positions. The simplest answer is a second table, one vector per position, added to the token embedding. GPT-2 does thi

chunks.heading: Where am I in the sentence?
chunks.text: Each pair of coordinates is a point going round a circle at frequency = 10000^{-2i/d}, from one radian per position down to one cycle in about 63,000 positions. The reason for sines and cosines is that a shift is linear. By the angle-addition formulas, so {PE}(p+k) is a fixed rotation of {PE}(p), the same for every p. A layer can learn to attend "three tokens back" with one linear map. Rotary positions. Most current models use a refinement, rotary position embedding, or RoPE (Jianlin Su and colleagues, 2021).

chunks.heading: Where am I in the sentence?
chunks.text: Instead of adding a position vector to the input, it rotates the query and key vectors inside each attention layer. Split a d-dimensional vector into d/2 pairs and treat each pair as a complex number; at position m, multiply pair i by e^{ i m}, with = 10000^{-2i/d} as before. Attention compares a query q at position m with a key k at position n through their dot product, which for one pair is the real part of q\, k:

chunks.heading: Where am I in the sentence?
chunks.text: The absolute positions cancel; only the offset m-n remains. Summing over pairs, the attention score depends on the content of the two tokens and on how far apart they are, and nothing else, without adding anything to the token's embedding. RoPE also builds in a decay with distance. The panel takes a random query, sets the key equal to it, so that without rotation they would match perfectly, and plots their rotary score against the distance between them. Each pair contributes |qi|^2((m-n)), so the score is a sum of cosines at d/2 frequencies: The fast pairs fall out of phase within a few tokens

chunks.heading: Where am I in the sentence?
chunks.text: The base sets that balance: lower it to 100 and almost every pair turns fast, so the score falls to noise around zero; raise it and more of the score survives at long range. Llama 3 raised the base from 10,000 to 500,000 to stretch the useful range to longer documents, and later methods for extending context work mostly by rescaling these frequencies.

chunks.heading: Method and sources
chunks.text: Tokeniser. Classic BPE (Sennrich and colleagues' variant, with an end-of-word marker) on the 253,854 distinct words of text8, weighted by count, with incremental pair-count updates; ties broken by the pair's characters. The page holds the first 8,000 merges and applies them by rank, as the learned tokeniser would. The GPT-2 and GPT-4o tokenisers are the r50kbase and o200kbase encodings, loaded in your browser from the gpt-tokenizer package. word2vec. gensim 4.4, skip-gram, 100 dimensions, window 5, 5 negative samples, subsampling threshold 10^{-3}, minimum count 5, 5 epochs, seed 1.

chunks.text: For the PMI comparison, co-occurrences among the 3,000 most frequent words were counted with gensim's effective weighting: a context at distance in a window of 5 counts with weight (6-)/5 (its dynamic window), multiplied by the probability that subsampling keeps each word. \#(w) is the weighted count of all pairs with centre w, Pn is the unigram distribution to the 34 power, and the dot products use the input vectors and gensim's output (syn1neg) vectors. Analogy accuracy uses gensim's evaluatewordanalogies with the 30,000 most frequent words.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: The Meade LX90 8-inch is a Schmidt–Cassegrain telescope (SCT): a Cassegrain reflector with a thin aspheric glass corrector plate across the front. That is a slight correction to calling it a "Cassegrain": a plain Cassegrain has no corrector, and the plate is what lets this design use cheap spherical mirrors. This post builds a ray-trace model of such a telescope in Python, follows the light from a star to the eye, and then uses the model to look at the qualities that make a telescope good or bad: diffraction, off-axis aberrations, field curvature, and chromatic focus (including how an SCT comp

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: What this model is, and is not. Meade does not publish the lens and mirror prescription, so I have not reproduced the real instrument. Instead I built a representative 8-inch f/10 SCT from the published specifications (203 mm aperture, f/10, a central obstruction of roughly a third of the aperture) and designed the corrector plate myself by optimisation. The behaviour is therefore realistic, but individual numbers (for example the exact field curvature) will differ from a particular telescope. The LX90 also comes in an "ACF" version, whose optics Meade describes as having a hyperbolic secondar

chunks.heading: The telescope at a glance
chunks.text: Two of these numbers set the tone for everything that follows. The Airy disk is about 13 µm across: even a perfect telescope cannot image a star to a point, only to a diffraction pattern that size. And the plate scale of about 100″ per millimetre means that 13 µm is about 1.4″ on the sky. The model below is judged against that diffraction limit.

chunks.heading: How a Schmidt–Cassegrain works
chunks.text: Light enters through the corrector plate (nearly flat glass with a subtle aspheric figure on its inner face), travels down the tube to a concave primary mirror, returns to a convex secondary mirror mounted on the back of the corrector, and then passes back through a hole in the primary to a focus behind the telescope. The light crosses the tube three times, which is how a 2032 mm focal length fits into a tube about half a metre long. Geometry. Let the primary have focal length f1 (for these telescopes it is about f/2, so f1 = 406.4 mm) and let the secondary magnify the primary's image by a fac

chunks.heading: How a Schmidt–Cassegrain works
chunks.text: and the mirror equation for the convex secondary, with virtual object distance s = f1 - d and image distance s' = d + b, gives its radius of curvature The folded path packs a 2.0 m focal length into a tube about 0.31 m long between the corrector and the primary mirror, a "compression" of more than six. The price is the secondary mirror's shadow, the central obstruction.

chunks.heading: Building the optical model in Python
chunks.text: I'll use Optiland, an open-source Python package for sequential ray tracing, aberration analysis, wavefront and MTF calculation, and optimisation. A sequential model lists surfaces in the order the light meets them, including the reflections: corrector front, corrector back, primary, secondary, image. Mirrors use material="mirror", and after each reflection the thickness changes sign. The paraxial focal length comes out at exactly 2032 mm and f/10, which confirms the geometry and the sign conventions.

chunks.heading: Designing the corrector plate
chunks.text: Two spherical mirrors in this configuration have enormous spherical aberration: rays from the edge of the primary focus much closer than rays near the centre. Bernhard Schmidt's 1930 insight was that a weak aspheric plate at the entrance can pre-compensate. Here I let a least-squares optimiser choose the plate's figure. The variables are the coefficients of the r^2, r^4 and r^6 terms on the plate's back face, plus the focus position and the curvature of the image surface. The objective is the RMS spot radius at field angles of 0°, 0.1° and 0.2°.

chunks.heading: Designing the corrector plate
chunks.text: The optimiser turns an uncorrected blur of more than a millimetre into a few microns, using a plate whose sag at the edge is only about 70 µm (roughly a tenth of the thickness of a sheet of paper). That the correction needs so little glass is why the corrector can be a thin, cheap plate. The optimiser also chose a curved image surface, with a radius of about 0.33 m, which reflects a real SCT trait that we meet again below.

chunks.heading: Following the light: the ray trace
chunks.text: With the model built, we can draw it. The figure shows three star directions (on axis and 0.25° and 0.5° off axis) entering from the left as parallel beams. Look for the three-pass path: through the corrector plate, back off the primary, forward to the small secondary on the back of the plate, and then back through the hole in the primary to the focus.

chunks.heading: The eyepiece and the eye
chunks.text: The model so far stops at the focal plane, where a camera sensor would sit. For visual use we add an eyepiece. I designed a 26 mm Plössl, the classic eyepiece that comes with many telescopes: two identical cemented crown/flint doublets, mounted with their flint faces toward each other. The radii were found by optimising, from the eye side, for small spots at field angles up to 26° (a 52° apparent field), with the focal length held at 26 mm. To see the whole chain at once I join the telescope to the eyepiece, then to a simple reduced-eye model (one refracting surface of radius 5.73 mm and index

chunks.heading: The eyepiece and the eye
chunks.text: What the eyepiece does to the numbers. The magnification is the ratio of the focal lengths, M = f{scope}/f{eyepiece}, the true field is the apparent field divided by M, and the exit pupil (the beam diameter at the eye) is D/M. A table for typical eyepieces assuming a 50° apparent field: The 26 mm eyepiece gives 78×, a field of about two-thirds of a degree (a bit larger than the full Moon), and a 2.6 mm exit pupil, well matched to the eye in daytime and comfortable at night. The highest useful magnification for an 8-inch aperture is about 2D in millimetres, near 400×, which corresponds to the 4

chunks.heading: Diffraction: what perfection looks like
chunks.text: Even with no aberrations at all, a circular aperture produces an Airy pattern. The central obstruction changes it: it transfers a little energy from the central disk into the rings. To quantify that, I compute the point-spread function by Fourier transform of the pupil, for the clear 8-inch aperture and for the aperture with a 34% obstruction. The dashed line is the radius of the first dark ring, 6.7 µm. A clear aperture puts about {python} f"{100eeclearfirst:.0f}"% of the light inside it, close to the textbook 84%. With the obstruction the figure falls to about {python} f"{100eeobsfirst:.0f}"

chunks.heading: The MTF
chunks.text: The modulation transfer function (MTF) says how much contrast the telescope preserves at each spatial frequency. For a perfect circular aperture it falls steadily to zero at the diffraction cutoff = 1/( N), about 182 cycles/mm here. A central obstruction cuts contrast at low and mid frequencies, and gives a slight boost near the cutoff. I compute the ideal curves from the autocorrelation of the pupil, and then the actual model with its aberrations from Optiland's FFT-based MTF. On axis the model follows the ideal obstructed curve closely: the corrector and mirrors work as designed. Moving off

chunks.heading: Off-axis performance and field curvature
chunks.text: Off axis, three things degrade the image: coma (stars become comet-shaped), astigmatism, and field curvature, where the sharpest focus lies on a curved surface instead of a flat sensor. To separate them I trace the model with a flat image plane and find, for each field angle, the focus position that minimises the RMS spot. The shift of that best focus from the axial focus measures the curvature of the focal surface. The best-focus surface is close to a sphere with radius of about {python} f"{abs(Rfit):.0f}" mm, about a tenth of the focal length.

chunks.heading: Off-axis performance and field curvature

A mirror reflects every wavelength identically, so the mirrors add no chromatic aberration at all. The RMS spot radius is {python} f"{rmsbywl[0.45]:.1f}" µm at 450 nm, {python} f"{rmsbywl[0.55]:.1f}" µm at 550 nm and {python} f"{rmsbywl[0.65]:.1f}" µm at 650 nm, because the plate's spherical-aberration correction is exact only at the design wavelength (a residual called spherochromatism). Real throughput depends on mirror coatings and on the plate's anti-reflection coatings. - The eyep

chunks.heading: Takeaways
chunks.text: - An SCT folds a 2032 mm focal length into a tube a third as long, using two spherical mirrors and a thin aspheric corrector plate. chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: When people say "the multiverse" they can mean two quite different things. One is cosmological: the idea, which Martin Rees takes seriously in the six-numbers post, that there may be many regions or universes with different values of constants such as N, and Q. The other comes from quantum mechanics: the many-worlds interpretation (MWI), which holds that the equations of quantum theory describe reality exactly as written, with no collapse, so that every possible outcome of a quantum measurement really occurs, each in its own branch of one enormous wave function. This post is about the second.

chunks.heading: The problem Everett was trying to solve
chunks.text: Quantum mechanics has two rules for how a state changes. Between measurements, the state evolves smoothly and deterministically under the Schrödinger equation, i\,| = H|. At a measurement, the textbook (Copenhagen) account adds a second rule: the state collapses at random to one of the possible outcomes, with probability given by the Born rule, pi = | i||^2. The trouble is that the second rule never says what counts as a "measurement". A measuring device is made of atoms that themselves obey quantum mechanics, so why should a detector, a physicist, or a cat be exempt from the smooth evolution?

chunks.heading: The problem Everett was trying to solve
chunks.text: Schrödinger's cat (1935) and Wigner's friend (1961) were designed to expose exactly this tension. Everett's answer was radical in its simplicity: drop the second rule. Keep only the Schrödinger equation, apply it to everything including the observer, and see what it predicts.

chunks.heading: Hugh Everett III
chunks.text: Hugh Everett III (1930–1982) was born in Washington, D.C., and studied chemical engineering at the Catholic University of America before moving to Princeton in 1953, where he turned to mathematics and physics. At Princeton he studied under John Archibald Wheeler, who had earlier supervised Richard Feynman and later coined the terms "black hole" and "wormhole". Everett's 1957 PhD thesis, originally titled "Wave Mechanics Without Probability" and later shortened to "On the Foundations of Quantum Mechanics", is the founding document of the interpretation. A condensed version appeared the same yea

chunks.heading: Hugh Everett III
chunks.text: The reception was cool. In 1959 Everett travelled to Copenhagen to present the idea to Niels Bohr and his circle. The meeting went badly: Bohr's school saw the idea as missing the point, and Everett came away discouraged. By then he had already begun a second career. He worked from 1956 for the Pentagon's Weapons Systems Evaluation Group on nuclear-war modelling, and later at defence-analysis firms he co-founded, where he did influential work on optimisation (a generalised Lagrange-multiplier method) and on military operations research. He never held a physics professorship, and published almo

chunks.heading: Hugh Everett III
chunks.text: Everett did not use the phrase "many worlds". It was Bryce DeWitt, who admired the idea and championed it, who popularised the name in a 1970 Physics Today article, and who with Neill Graham edited the 1973 collection The Many-Worlds Interpretation of Quantum Mechanics, which finally printed Everett's long thesis. Everett died of a heart attack in 1982, aged 51, after years of heavy smoking and drinking. His son, the musician Mark Oliver Everett of the band Eels, made a 2007 BBC documentary about his father, Parallel Worlds, Parallel Lives. The idea gained wide attention only after his death.

chunks.heading: Measurement as entanglement
chunks.text: Take a system qubit in the state | = c0|0 + c1|1 and a measuring device that starts in a "ready" state |R. A good measurement is just an interaction that correlates the device with the system: The result is an entangled state. There's no collapse here, just linear evolution. If the device is an observer, the right-hand side contains one term where the observer saw 0 and one where they saw 1. Each term is a self-consistent "world" in which the observer remembers a definite result. Everett called each term's observer state relative to the system state, hence "relative-state formulation".

chunks.heading: Measurement as entanglement
chunks.text: We can check numerically that this entangled state is genuinely not a product state. Its entanglement entropy vanishes only for a product state: The two Schmidt weights are 0.9 and 0.1, and the entropy is about bits. A product state would have a single weight of 1 and zero entropy.

chunks.heading: Why branches don't interfere: decoherence
chunks.text: If the post-measurement state is just a quantum superposition, why can't we see interference between the two terms, as we do in the double-slit experiment? The answer, developed from the 1970s by H. Dieter Zeh, Wojciech Zurek and others, is decoherence: the branches become entangled with the enormous number of microscopic degrees of freedom in their surroundings, and this makes interference between them unobservable in practice. Here is a minimal model. Our system qubit interacts with N environment qubits, each initially |0. If the system is |0, the environment is untouched. If it is |1, each

chunks.heading: Why branches don't interfere: decoherence
chunks.text: Each extra environment qubit multiplies the coherence by < 1, so it decays exponentially with environment size. I'll verify this formula by building the full 2^{N+1}-dimensional state vector explicitly and tracing out the environment numerically: The brute-force trace and the closed form agree to machine precision (maximum difference ). Even with only 10 environment qubits, the coherence has dropped to % of its initial value. Real environments contain something like 10^{20} or more degrees of freedom, so the suppression is for practical purposes total. This is the mechanism that makes the bran

chunks.heading: Why branches don't interfere: decoherence
chunks.text: Once the off-diagonal terms are negligible, nothing that happens in one branch can be detected from another, and each branch evolves as though the others did not exist. This is what Everettians mean by saying the "worlds" are real but emergent: they are not added to the theory, they are patterns in the wave function that decoherence makes robust. One common objection is that branching must violate energy conservation. It does not: the total state remains normalised, |ci|^2 = 1, and each branch carries only its share. Branching does not copy the universe; it describes how a single wave function

chunks.heading: The hard part: where do the probabilities come from?
chunks.text: If every outcome occurs, what does it mean to say that outcome 0 has probability 0.9? A tempting answer is to count branches. After a single measurement there are two branches, so each has "probability 1/2" regardless of the amplitudes. That gives the wrong answer. The problem is sharper with repeated measurements. Prepare n copies of {0.9}|0+{0.1}|1 and measure them all. There are 2^n branches, one for each sequence of results. Counting branches treats all sequences as equally likely, so the number of zeros would follow a Binomial(n, 1/2) distribution.

chunks.heading: The hard part: where do the probabilities come from?
chunks.text: The Born rule instead gives each sequence with k zeros a weight 0.9^k\,0.1^{n-k}, so the total weight of branches with k zeros is Binomial(n, 0.9). Experiments see frequencies near 90% zeros, so the amplitude-squared weighting is the one that matches experience. The question is why that weighting, rather than branch-counting, should govern what an observer expects.

chunks.heading: The hard part: where do the probabilities come from?
chunks.text: Everett's own argument was a law-of-large-numbers result. Measure the weight (squared norm) of the branches whose relative frequency of zeros deviates from 0.9 by more than 0.05. That weight goes to zero as n grows, so the branches that carry almost all the weight are those in which the observed frequencies match the Born rule: By n = 1000 the atypical branches carry a negligible weight. But critics, notably Adrian Kent, point out that this is circular: it assumes the squared-amplitude weighting is the right measure of "how much a branch matters" and then derives that observers will see Born f

chunks.heading: The hard part: where do the probabilities come from?
chunks.text: It does not independently justify the weighting. - Decision theory (Deutsch 1999, Wallace 2012). Show that a rational agent who accepts Everettian quantum mechanics and some plausible rationality axioms must bet as if branch probabilities equal |ci|^2. - Self-locating uncertainty (Sebens and Carroll 2018). Before learning which branch you are in, you have uncertainty about where you are, and symmetry arguments fix that uncertainty to the Born weights. This links to ordinary Bayesian reasoning, like the posterior calculations in the prosecutor's fallacy post: the question is not "what will happ

chunks.heading: The hard part: where do the probabilities come from?
chunks.text: - Objective-weights or "measure" proposals. Treat |ci|^2 as a basic feature of the world, akin to a mass, not a probability to be derived. Whether any of these succeeds is a matter of live disagreement. It remains the main technical objection to the interpretation.

chunks.heading: Who defends it today?
chunks.text: The interpretation was a fringe position for decades, but has found serious advocates: - David Deutsch (Oxford) is the most committed champion. He argues that the interpretation is demanded by quantum computing, since the computation seems to need explaining by many parallel computational histories, and made the case in The Fabric of Reality (1997). His 1999 decision-theoretic derivation of the Born rule started the modern probability debate. - David Wallace (philosopher of physics, now at the University of Pittsburgh) gave the most careful defence in The Emergent Multiverse (2012), which trea

chunks.heading: Who defends it today?
chunks.text: - Sean Carroll (Johns Hopkins and the Santa Fe Institute) brought the view to a wide readership in Something Deeply Hidden (2019) and, with Charles Sebens, developed the self-locating-uncertainty approach. - Simon Saunders (Oxford) has contributed foundational work on branching and probability, and Lev Vaidman (Tel Aviv) is another long-standing advocate, and the author of the standard encyclopedia entry on the topic. - Max Tegmark (MIT) treats many-worlds as one level of a hierarchy of multiverses (below), and has argued that the interpretation follows naturally from taking the Schrödinger eq

chunks.heading: Who defends it today?
chunks.text: It remains a minority view. A 2013 survey of conference participants by Schlosshauer, Kofler and Zeilinger found roughly 42% favouring Copenhagen-style views and about 18% favouring Everett, with the rest split among other approaches. The main rivals each have prominent supporters and each has costs: - Collapse theories (GRW, Penrose) modify the dynamics, adding a physical collapse mechanism, with testable differences. - Pilot-wave (Bohmian) mechanics adds definite particle positions guided by the wave function, at the cost of non-locality. - QBism and relational views treat the quantum state

chunks.heading: How it connects to cosmology
chunks.text: It is not the same as Rees's multiverse. Tegmark organises the possibilities into levels: The multiverse that bears on the six numbers is Level II: different regions can have different N, , Q and , so an anthropic selection effect can explain why we see values that permit observers. That is the argument Carr and Rees made in 1979, and it is the cosmological version of the carbon-resonance reasoning behind the Hoyle state. Level III does not do that job. Every Everettian branch obeys the same Schrödinger equation with the same constants.

chunks.heading: How it connects to cosmology
chunks.text: Many-worlds therefore gives no anthropic explanation for why N 10^{36} or why 0.007. The two ideas are logically independent: one can accept either, both or neither. Aguirre and Tegmark (2011) have argued that Level I and Level III are closely related: in an infinite universe, quantum mechanics and spatial copies make similar predictions.

chunks.heading: How it connects to cosmology
chunks.text: A place where they meet: the origin of structure. The amplitude Q10^{-5} of primordial density fluctuations is, in the inflationary picture, set by quantum fluctuations that were stretched to cosmic size. On the Everettian reading, the specific pattern of hot and cold spots in the microwave background is one of an enormous number of branches, each with a different realisation of the same statistics. The galaxies in our branch sit where they do because of one such history; our measured Q describes the statistics that all branches share. Probability again. Questions like "which observers am I?"

chunks.heading: Takeaways
chunks.text: - Everett (1957) removed the collapse postulate and kept only unitary evolution; measurement becomes entanglement, and each outcome corresponds to a branch. - Decoherence explains why branches don't interfere: coherence falls as ()^N with environment size, as the numerical check shows. - The unresolved issue is probability. Counting branches gives the wrong answer; the Born weights come from decision theory, self-locating arguments or a postulate, and critics contest each. - Many-worlds is not the cosmological multiverse. It does not explain fine-tuned constants, which belong to Level II argum

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: In 1999 the astrophysicist Martin Rees published a short book, Just Six Numbers, built around a claim that is easy to state and hard to dismiss: the large-scale structure of the universe, and its ability to contain anything as intricate as life, depends on six dimensionless numbers. None of them is predicted by any current theory. Change any one by a modest amount and the universe would look utterly different. This post introduces Rees himself, then goes through the six numbers one at a time, with the physics behind each and a short calculation in R.

chunks.heading: Who is Martin Rees?
chunks.text: Martin Rees was born in York in 1942 and studied mathematics at Trinity College, Cambridge. He completed his PhD in 1967 under Dennis Sciama, whose students over the years included Stephen Hawking, George Ellis and Brandon Carter. That group worked on general relativity and cosmology at a time when the subject was moving from speculation to observation. He has spent most of his career in Cambridge, as Plumian Professor of Astronomy and Experimental Philosophy from 1973, Astronomer Royal since 1995, Master of Trinity College from 2004 to 2012, and President of the Royal Society from 2005 to 201

chunks.heading: Who is Martin Rees?
chunks.text: His research output is unusually broad. A few landmarks, all from my memory of the literature and worth checking against the references: - Superluminal motion (1966). Rees showed that jets from quasars moving close to the speed of light at a small angle to our line of sight can appear to move faster than light. No physics is violated; it is a light-travel-time effect. - Evolving radio sources. In the 1960s, with Sciama, he worked on how the numbers of distant radio sources and quasars change with cosmic time, evidence that the universe evolves, as the Big Bang picture says and the steady-state

chunks.heading: Who is Martin Rees?
chunks.text: - The Rees–Sciama effect (1968). Light crossing a changing gravitational potential, such as a collapsing cluster, picks up a small net energy shift. This is a tiny signature on the cosmic microwave background. - Radio galaxies and black holes (1970s–80s). With Roger Blandford he developed the "twin-exhaust" model in which jets carry energy from a galactic nucleus to giant radio lobes. His wider reviews established the picture of supermassive black holes powering active galactic nuclei. - Galaxy formation. With Jeremiah Ostriker (1977) he studied how gas cools and collapses to form galaxies, an

chunks.heading: Who is Martin Rees?
chunks.text: He is also a prolific author for general readers: Before the Beginning (1997), Just Six Numbers (1999), Our Cosmic Habitat (2001), Our Final Hour (2003, published in the UK as Our Final Century) and On the Future (2018). He gave the BBC Reith Lectures in 2010 and co-founded Cambridge's Centre for the Study of Existential Risk in 2012. The theme running through the later work is that the cosmos is far larger and older than we usually keep in mind, and that humanity's own future is much less settled than the cosmos's.

chunks.heading: The anthropic thread
chunks.text: The six-numbers argument has a lineage. In 1961 Robert Dicke observed that the age of the universe cannot be arbitrary if observers like us are to exist. In 1974 Brandon Carter, Rees's Cambridge contemporary, gave the idea a name, the anthropic principle. In 1979 Rees and Bernard Carr wrote a long Nature review, "The anthropic principle and the structure of the physical world", which assembled the evidence that many features of physics seem tuned to allow complex structure. The Hoyle carbon resonance (covered in the stellar nucleosynthesis post) is one of its classic examples. Just Six Numbers

chunks.heading: The six numbers
chunks.text: Rees groups them: N and govern small-scale physics (atoms, stars), , and Q govern the large-scale cosmos, and D sets the framework in which everything operates.

chunks.heading: 1. $N \approx 10^{36}$: the weakness of gravity
chunks.text: Two protons repel each other electrically and attract each other gravitationally. The ratio of the two forces does not depend on distance, since both fall off as 1/r^2: So N = . Gravity is feeble compared with electromagnetism, and that is why large objects are needed for it to matter. A characteristic stellar mass comes out of dimensional analysis alone, where = G mp^2/ c = /N: That is a stellar mass, so N is why stars are about the size they are. Since M N^{3/2}, a universe with gravity 10^6 times stronger (N 10^{30}) would have stars about a billion times lighter.

chunks.heading: 1. $N \approx 10^{36}$: the weakness of gravity
chunks.text: Lifetimes. The standard result for radiative stars is L G^4 M^3, so a star's lifetime goes as t M/L G^{-4}M^{-2}. Combined with M G^{-3/2} this gives t G^{-1} N. A million-fold stronger gravity therefore shortens stellar lifetimes about a million-fold, from roughly 10^{10} years to roughly 10^4. That's Rees's "Lilliputian universe": there would be no time for evolution to do anything. Going the other way, a much larger N (weaker gravity) gives huge, cool, slowly evolving stars, and galaxies would struggle to form from gas that is so slow to collapse. Rees's point is that life needs something l

chunks.heading: 2. $\varepsilon \approx 0.007$: the efficiency of fusion
chunks.text: When four hydrogen nuclei fuse into one helium-4 nucleus, a fraction of their mass is converted to energy: That gives = . It is set by the strong nuclear force, and it fixes how long stars shine: a star's nuclear fuel supply is roughly M c^2, so lifetime is proportional to at fixed luminosity. Beyond that, it determines what the hydrogen-burning chain can do at all. The chain starts with deuterium, and its stability depends on the strength of the nuclear force. Rees's examples are qualitative: - With around 0.006, the first step toward helium would not proceed, so the universe would stay hydro

chunks.heading: 2. $\varepsilon \approx 0.007$: the efficiency of fusion
chunks.text: - With around 0.008, nearly all hydrogen would have been fused in the early universe, leaving no hydrogen for water or long-lived stars. These are Rees's illustrations of sensitivity, and I haven't derived them here. Detailed nuclear calculations in the literature find that the range of habitable values is somewhat wider than such sharp statements suggest, but still narrow.

chunks.heading: 3. $\Omega \approx 0.3$: how much matter
chunks.text: The expansion of a homogeneous universe obeys the Friedmann equation The critical density is the value of for which a universe with =0 is spatially flat, = 3H0^2/8 G, and = /. The critical density is about kg m^{-3}, equivalent to roughly protons per cubic metre. The measured density of ordinary matter plus dark matter is about 0.3 of that, so . The flatness problem. If is not exactly 1 at the start, it runs away from 1 as the universe expands. Writing the deviation as |^{-1}-1| = |k|c^2/(a^2H^2), one can compute how finely the early universe had to be balanced to leave of order unity today: A

chunks.heading: 3. $\Omega \approx 0.3$: how much matter
chunks.text: Too much matter and the universe would have collapsed in a fraction of a second; too little and it would have expanded too quickly for galaxies to form. Inflation, proposed in the early 1980s, offers a mechanism that drives the universe toward flatness automatically, and it is one reason Rees treats as less mysterious than the other numbers.

chunks.heading: 4. $\lambda \approx 0.7$: the cosmological constant
chunks.text: Until the late 1990s most cosmologists assumed that = 0. Then supernova surveys (Riess et al. 1998; Perlmutter et al. 1999) showed that the expansion is accelerating, which requires a repulsive component, the cosmological constant or dark energy. It is parametrised as = c^2/(3H0^2) 0.7, Rees's . With + = 1 the Friedmann equation can be integrated for the age and the history of the scale factor: The flat ΛCDM age is Gyr, which is comfortably older than the oldest stars. A matter-only universe with the same H0 would be only Gyr old, an awkward conflict that was one of the early hints for . Accel

chunks.heading: 4. $\lambda \approx 0.7$: the cosmological constant
chunks.text: Why is interesting? Two reasons. First, it is absurdly small compared with what particle physics naively suggests. Vacuum energy computed with a Planck-scale cutoff is about = c^5/( G^2): The observed dark-energy density is smaller than the Planck density by a factor of about : roughly 120 orders of magnitude, a famous failure of naive estimates. Second, Steven Weinberg noted in 1987 that if were much larger than observed, repulsion would have stopped structure forming before galaxies could assemble. That anthropic bound is what pointed toward a small, non-zero value before the supernova resul

chunks.heading: 5. $Q \approx 10^{-5}$: how lumpy was the early universe?
chunks.text: The cosmic microwave background is uniform to about one part in 10^5. Those tiny temperature ripples correspond to density fluctuations of a similar relative size, and Rees calls their amplitude Q. Gravity amplifies them: in a matter-dominated universe, small perturbations grow in proportion to the scale factor. In a universe with dark energy the growth factor D(a) obeys normalised so that D = a at early times. Today D(1) = : dark energy has already throttled structure growth by about % relative to a matter-only universe. In this picture a region collapses into a bound structure once its linea

chunks.heading: 5. $Q \approx 10^{-5}$: how lumpy was the early universe?
chunks.text: - If Q were much smaller (around 10^{-6}), gas clouds would take far longer to contract. Galaxies would form late, if at all, and their stars would be diffuse, so supernova ejecta could escape and no second generation of enriched stars would form. - If Q were much larger (around 10^{-4}), structure would form very early and densely. Galaxies would be compact enough for stars to collide, and many would collapse to giant black holes. Our value gives galaxies that are big enough to retain heavy elements and sparse enough that planetary systems survive. This post doesn't compute the full structure

chunks.heading: 6. $D = 3$: dimensions of space
chunks.text: Why three? Paul Ehrenfest's 1917 analysis shows that the stability of orbits singles out D=3. In D spatial dimensions Gauss's law makes a central force fall off as r^{-(D-1)} and the potential as r^{-(D-2)}. For a particle with angular momentum L the effective potential is A stable circular orbit needs a minimum of V{{eff}}. - D=3: the attractive -k/r is overtaken by the centrifugal r^{-2} term at small r, producing a stable minimum. Planets can orbit stars. - D=4: both terms go as r^{-2}. There is no minimum at all: for weak angular momentum a particle spirals into the centre, for strong angu

chunks.heading: 6. $D = 3$: dimensions of space
chunks.text: The same argument applies to the Schrödinger equation: in four or more spatial dimensions, hydrogen-like atoms have no stable ground state, so there would be no chemistry. Fewer dimensions have their own problems: in D=2 the gravitational potential is logarithmic, orbits are not closed, and a body can never escape. Max Tegmark's 1997 survey of these arguments is a good modern treatment.

chunks.heading: How seriously should we take all this?
chunks.text: It is worth being clear about what the six-numbers argument does and does not establish. - What it shows is sensitivity: with physics otherwise unchanged, the outcome of these numbers is not robust to large changes. Those scaling arguments, such as M N^{3/2}, the flatness calculation and the orbital stability of D=3, are straightforward calculations. - What it does not show is that the numbers had to be tuned by something. For that you need a probability distribution over possible values of constants, and nobody has a principled one.

chunks.heading: How seriously should we take all this?
chunks.text: Critics, among them Lee Smolin and Sabine Hossenfelder, argue that "fine-tuning" is not well-defined without such a measure, and some of the numbers (like ) may have explanations through dynamics like inflation. - Rees's own response is to take the multiverse seriously: if a very large ensemble of universes exists with different values of N, , Q and so on, then finding ourselves in one that permits observers is no surprise. He is open that this is a hypothesis, not a result, and that it remains controversial. Whichever view you prefer, the numbers provide a clear way to ask what a universe is

chunks.heading: Takeaways
chunks.text: - N 10^{36} sets how big stars are and how long they live: M N^{3/2} and t N. - 0.007 is the fraction of mass released by hydrogen fusion; Rees's examples show it sits in a narrow window. - 0.3 and 0.7 govern the expansion history. The flatness calculation shows the early universe was balanced to about one part in 10^{16}, and is about 10^{-123} of the naive Planck-scale value. - Q10^{-5} sets when and how densely galaxies form. - D=3 is singled out by the stability of orbits and atoms. - The sensitivity arguments are solid. What they mean is still debated.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Almost every atom heavier than helium was made inside a star. The carbon in your cells, the oxygen you breathe and the iron in your blood were assembled by thermonuclear reactions in stellar cores and then scattered by stellar winds and supernovae. This post covers the physics that makes that possible, in three steps: why fusion happens at all at stellar temperatures, how the rates of the main reaction chains depend on temperature, and how Fred Hoyle used the existence of carbon-based life to predict a property of the carbon-12 nucleus before anyone had measured it.

chunks.heading: A short history
chunks.text: Why do stars shine? In 1920 Arthur Eddington argued that stars are powered by turning hydrogen into helium. Four hydrogen nuclei weigh about 0.7% more than one helium nucleus, so the conversion releases energy through E = mc^2. The objection was that stellar cores seemed far too cool: at roughly 10^7 K, protons do not have nearly enough energy to climb the Coulomb barrier. The way out came with quantum mechanics. In 1928 George Gamow showed that nuclei can tunnel through the barrier, and by the late 1930s Hans Bethe (and independently Carl von Weizsäcker) had worked out the reaction chains tha

chunks.heading: A short history
chunks.text: Bethe's 1939 paper laid out the proton–proton chain and the carbon–nitrogen–oxygen cycle. Where do the heavier elements come from? In the 1940s there were two rival ideas. George Gamow and collaborators (Alpher, Bethe, Gamow, 1948) proposed that all the elements were cooked in the first minutes of the Big Bang. That runs into a wall: there are no stable nuclei with mass number 5 or 8, so building up from helium one nucleon at a time stalls, and the Big Bang makes essentially only hydrogen, helium and traces of lithium.

chunks.heading: A short history
chunks.text: Enter Fred Hoyle. Fred Hoyle (1915–2001), a Cambridge astronomer, argued in 1946 that the heavier elements are built inside stars as they evolve. He was, with Hermann Bondi and Thomas Gold, also the author of the steady-state cosmology (1948), a rival to the Big Bang picture. The phrase "Big Bang" itself is usually credited to Hoyle, from a 1949 BBC radio talk. He later said it was meant as a vivid image and not a sneer, though the claim is still debated. Whatever his view of cosmology, his work on nucleosynthesis was right, and it outlived the steady-state theory.

chunks.heading: A short history
chunks.text: The bottleneck was carbon. Stars can make helium, but to get anything heavier they must fuse helium nuclei (alpha particles). Two alphas make beryllium-8, which is unbound and falls apart in about 10^{-16} s. A third alpha has to arrive within that window. Hoyle realised that for this to work at a useful rate in stellar cores, carbon-12 must have an excited state at roughly 7.65 MeV that lines up with the energy of the three-alpha system. In 1953 he pressed this on Willy Fowler's group at Caltech. Fowler's team (Dunbar, Cook, Whaling and colleagues) measured it, and found a 0^+ state at about

chunks.heading: A short history
chunks.text: In 1957 Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, Willy Fowler and Fred Hoyle published "Synthesis of the Elements in Stars", universally known as B2FH. It laid out the processes of nucleosynthesis (hydrogen burning, helium burning, the alpha process, the s- and r-processes of neutron capture, and others) and connected them to observed abundances. Fowler shared the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics for this work (with Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, who was honoured for other research); Hoyle was not included, which many in the field regard as a serious omission. There is also a famous gloss on the Hoyle st

At the nuclear radius (a few femtometres) this barrier is of order an MeV, while the thermal energy at the Sun's core temperature of 1.510^7 K is only kT 1.3 keV. Classical collisions would almost never get through. Quantum tunnelling gives a small but non-zero probability. For relative energy E much below the barrier height, the penetration probability is approximately where mr is the reduced mass, 1/137 is the fine-structure constant and EG is the Gamow energy. chunks.heading: The Gamow peak
chunks.text: Particles in a hot plasma follow a Maxwell–Boltzmann energy distribution, (-E/kT), which favours low energies. Tunnelling probability favours high energies. The reaction rate per particle pair is the integral of their product, where the cross-section is written as (E) = {S(E)}{E}\,e^{-{EG/E}} and the astrophysical S-factor S(E) absorbs the slowly varying nuclear physics. The exponent is minimised at the Gamow peak with the 1/e full width. Reactions with a larger Coulomb barrier have a larger , so they respond far more violently to temperature. The alpha + alpha row is the non-resonant value; the resonant triple-alpha process below is far steeper. For p + p at 1.510^7 K the rate goes roughly as T^4; for proton capture on nitrogen-14 it goes as a much higher power of T. This is why the CNO cy

chunks.text: Both routes convert four protons into one helium-4 nucleus: The energy released is the mass difference. Using atomic masses, m({}^1{H}) = 1.007825 u and m({}^4{He}) = 4.002603 u, That is about MeV per helium nucleus (a bit less reaches the star, since neutrinos carry some away), or % of the rest mass. Assuming the Sun burns about 10% of its hydrogen at its current luminosity, that gives a lifetime of roughly billion years, in line with the Sun's expected main-sequence life. The pp chain begins with the slowest, weak-interaction step: which is the bottleneck, with a characteristic time of billi

chunks.text: This is why the Sun lasts so long. Deuterium then captures another proton, {}^2{H}(p,){}^3{He}, and two {}^3{He} nuclei combine to give {}^4{He} plus two protons (the dominant branch). The CNO cycle uses carbon, nitrogen and oxygen as catalysts, never consumed overall. The slowest step is {}^{14}{N}(p,){}^{15}{O}, which sets the cycle's overall speed and, given the high Coulomb barrier, its steep temperature dependence.

chunks.heading: A reaction network, in general
chunks.text: The abundance of each species i (written as a number fraction Yi = ni/( NA)) obeys a coupled system of ordinary differential equations. For a reaction a + b c + , Real codes solve hundreds of such equations simultaneously. The system is stiff: the fastest and slowest rates can differ by tens of orders of magnitude, so implicit integrators are needed.

chunks.heading: Helium burning and the triple-alpha process
chunks.text: Once the core runs out of hydrogen it contracts and heats up. At around 10^8 K, helium can fuse. The reaction has to proceed through two steps: {}^8{Be} lies only about 92 keV above two free alphas and lives for roughly 10^{-16} s. At stellar temperatures a small equilibrium population of it nonetheless exists, given (up to order-unity factors) by the Saha equation, At 10^8 K (kT 8.6 keV) the Boltzmann factor is only about e^{-10.7}, so beryllium is rare, but not negligibly so. A third alpha capturing on this beryllium would normally be too weak to matter.

chunks.heading: Helium burning and the triple-alpha process
chunks.text: The Hoyle state, however, sits just above the {}^8{Be} + threshold: at 7.654 MeV excitation energy in {}^{12}{C}, it is about 0.287 MeV above the {}^8{Be}+ threshold, or 0.379 MeV above the three-alpha threshold. Capture into it is a resonance, so the cross-section is enormously boosted.

chunks.text: For a narrow resonance, the resulting three-body rate per unit volume is with Q = 379.5 keV the resonance energy above the three-alpha threshold and the effective width. Most Hoyle-state nuclei fall apart again into ^8Be + ; the quantity that matters is the small radiative width 3.7 meV (plus a smaller pair-emission contribution), because only decays by radiation or pair emission produce stable carbon. At T = 10^8 K and = 10^5 g cm^{-3} (the sort of dense, degenerate core in which helium ignites in a low-mass star), this simple estimate gives a helium lifetime of roughly years. At the same tem

chunks.text: The local exponent of this rate is enormous. Since r T^{-3}e^{-Q/kT} (the T^{-3} coming from the thermal factor), At 10^8 K that is , so the rate scales as roughly T^{}. A 10% temperature rise speeds helium burning up by a factor of about . Helium ignition therefore happens abruptly, and in stars with degenerate cores it is explosive (the helium flash).

chunks.heading: What if the resonance were somewhere else?
chunks.text: The factor (-Q/kT) makes the rate exponentially sensitive to the resonance energy. If the Hoyle state were shifted by E relative to its real position, the rate at fixed temperature would change by (- E/kT) (holding all else fixed, which is an idealisation). This sensitivity is what gives the "fine-tuning" discussions their punch. Fairer treatments, though, vary underlying nuclear parameters and track how the resonance energy, the beryllium state and the later burning of carbon into oxygen all respond together. The conclusion that comes out of such studies is more nuanced than "the universe is

chunks.heading: After helium: carbon, oxygen and beyond
chunks.text: Once carbon exists, it can capture another alpha to form oxygen, {}^{12}{C}(,){}^{16}{O}. The competition between this and the triple-alpha process sets the carbon-to-oxygen ratio at the end of helium burning, which controls what a star does afterwards. That rate is known only to limited accuracy, and measuring it more precisely is still an active problem in nuclear astrophysics. In more massive stars the sequence continues in shells and cores: carbon burning ( 610^8 K), neon, oxygen and silicon burning, each stage faster and hotter than the last. The chain stops at iron-group nuclei because t

chunks.heading: Takeaways
chunks.text: - Fusion in stars depends on quantum tunnelling. The reaction rate is the product of two competing exponentials, giving the narrow Gamow peak. - The temperature sensitivity of a reaction, n = (-2)/3, is set by the Coulomb barrier through the Gamow energy. - Hydrogen burning releases about 26.7 MeV per helium nucleus, enough for the Sun to shine for billions of years. - The triple-alpha process needs a resonance, the Hoyle state, to make carbon at a useful rate. Fred Hoyle inferred its existence in 1953, and Fowler's group confirmed it. - B2FH (1957) put stellar nucleosynthesis on a systematic

chunks.text: A thin accretion disk is gas orbiting in the hole's equatorial plane, each ring moving very nearly on a circular geodesic and drifting slowly inwards as friction (in practice magnetic turbulence) carries its angular momentum outwards. For a prograde circular orbit in the Kerr equatorial plane, Bardeen, Press and Teukolsky (1972) give the angular velocity, energy and angular momentum per unit rest mass: and $u^t = dt/d = (r^{3/2} + a)/(r^{3/4}{r^{3/2} - 3r^{1/2} + 2a}). chunks.text: The disk's inner edge sits there. Gas reaching the ISCO has given up 1 - E{ISCO} of its rest-mass energy as heat and light, the radiative efficiency, before it plunges. chunks.text: The light that reaches the camera is not the light the gas emitted. Two effects change its frequency: - gravitational redshift: the photon climbs out of the hole's potential; - Doppler shift: the gas moves at up to half the speed of light, towards the camera on one side and away on the other. General relativity handles both at once. A photon with 4-momentum p has frequency -p u measured by an observer with 4-velocity u. The ray's conserved quantities give p everywhere. chunks.text: All of the physics is in two numbers per ray: the radius where it left the disk, and its b. The factor 1/u^t is the time dilation of the orbiting gas, gravitational and kinematic together, and 1 - b is the Doppler term. Gas moving towards the camera emits photons with b < 0 relative to its motion, so the term is larger than 1 and g grows. The shifts are large. Light from the approaching side arrives up to {python} f"{ghi:.1f}" times its emitted frequency, and from the receding side as little as {python} f"{glo:.2f}" times.

chunks.text: The DNGR paper quotes factors "of order 1.5 and 0.4" for the same disk, combining the Doppler shifts of gas moving at about 0.55c with a gravitational redshift of about 20 per cent. The table of 1/u^t above shows where that 20 per cent comes from: gas at r 10\,M ticks 16 per cent slow.

chunks.text: A frequency shift also changes brightness, through one of the most useful facts in relativistic radiative transfer. Along a ray in vacuum the photon distribution function is conserved (Liouville's theorem), and in terms of the specific intensity I that means So the camera sees I{}^{obs} = g^3\,I^{em}{/g}. For a blackbody that has a remarkably tidy consequence. Planck's law is B(T) = {2h^3/c^2}{e^{h/kT} - 1}, so A shifted blackbody is a blackbody at temperature gT. Integrated over frequency, the brightness scales as g^4, so a factor of 1.5 makes the approaching side five times brighter, and a f

chunks.heading: From spectrum to colour
chunks.text: What colour is a blackbody? The eye's response is summarised by the CIE 1931 colour-matching functions, three weighting curves x, y, z that turn a spectrum into tristimulus values X, Y, Z, with Y the luminance. A fixed matrix takes those to the linear RGB of a standard sRGB display, whose white point is a 6500 K daylight spectrum. The DNGR team made the same choice, setting the virtual camera's white balance so that a 6500 K blackbody comes out neutral, though they used the sensitivity curves of motion-picture film rather than the eye's.

chunks.heading: From spectrum to colour
chunks.text: Visible luminance changes even faster with temperature than bolometric brightness does, because cooling shifts the peak out of the visible band into the infrared. Between the reddest and bluest parts of the disk above, the visible luminance differs by a factor of about {python} f"{round(lumratio, -4):,.0f}". The gas itself, at the ISCO, moves at {python} f"{visco:.2f}"c relative to the local ZAMO.
