chunks.text: This explainer sits behind the Apollo 11 series in the Space section: 1. Launch to translunar injection 2. Translunar coast and lunar orbit 3. Descent and landing Every number in the series lives in one of about a dozen coordinate frames. This post sets out what those frames are, how one becomes another, which mathematics does the work, how a single clock keeps four panels, a 3D scene, a transcript, audio and film in step, and where the data came from and what it forced. The code is in src/apollo11 in the blog's repository.

chunks.heading: The map of frames
chunks.text: There is one working frame, and everything is either computed in it or converted to it at the edges. It is geocentric and inertial, with its axes fixed to the mean equator and equinox of 16 July 1969. The physics is integrated there. Other frames exist for two reasons: to read the 1969 documents, which were written in Earth-fixed, Moon-fixed or spacecraft-local terms, and to draw the views, each of which picks the frame where its story is easiest to see. Arrows show the direction the engine converts in. Every conversion is a rotation, a translation, or both, and each has an exact inverse that

chunks.heading: One clock, three time scales
chunks.text: Every row of every table is keyed by ground elapsed time (GET), seconds from range zero, 13:32:00 UTC on 16 July 1969. GET is the mission's own clock: the transcripts, maneuver PADs and NASA tables all use it, so the reconstruction does too, and nothing in the pages is keyed to anything else. Two physical clocks hang off it. Earth's rotation follows UT1, which in July 1969 ran 0.0115 s ahead of UTC; it sets Greenwich sidereal time, and so where the launch pad and the tracking stations were.

chunks.heading: One clock, three time scales
chunks.text: The planets follow Terrestrial Time (TT), 39.746 s ahead of UTC that day (32.184 s by definition plus 7.5622 s of accumulated leap time); it is the argument of the DE421 ephemeris and of the IAU model of the Moon's rotation. Running Earth's rotation on TT would misplace the launch pad by about 18 km, and running the ephemeris on UT1 would misplace the Moon by about 40 km, so each function asks for the one it needs: with T = ({JD}{UT1} - 2451545)/36525, converted to an angle at 240 s per degree.

chunks.heading: The working frame, and why it is 1969's
chunks.text: Modern ephemerides are referred to the ICRF, which is fixed to distant quasars and is within milliarcseconds of the J2000 equator. NASA's 1969 tables were written in the mean equator and equinox of the launch date: they give right ascension through Greenwich mean sidereal time, against an equator that had precessed by 0.43° between 1969 and 2000. Using the tables' own frame means the anchors go in unaltered, and the only rotation applied is to the modern data, once: where B is the frame bias from the ICRF to the J2000 mean equator (milliarcseconds) and P0 is precession from J2000 to the mean e

chunks.heading: The working frame, and why it is 1969's
chunks.text: P0 is evaluated once, at range zero. Precession over the eight-day mission is about 0.002°, a few hundred metres at the Moon's distance, so treating the frame as inertial costs nothing the tables could show. Nutation, the 18.6-year wobble on top of precession, is left out for the same reason the 1969 tables left it out: "mean" frames exclude it by definition. The Moon and Sun come from JPL's DE421 through the skyfield library, rotated with P0 B and written to ephem1969.csv as hourly positions and velocities. That file is committed, so the engine needs only numpy. Between rows, positions are in

chunks.heading: Reading a 1969 table row
chunks.text: The trajectory tables in Apollo by the Numbers and the Boeing and TRW reports give a state as six numbers: geocentric latitude , longitude , altitude h, space-fixed speed v, flight-path angle (above the local horizontal) and heading (east of north). Turning that into a position and velocity in the working frame is the most frequently used conversion in the project: Two details come straight from the documents. The ellipsoid is the 1960 Fischer ("Mercury") figure, a = 6378.166 km and f = 1/298.3, not WGS-84, because that is what the tables measured altitude from. And the velocity is space-fixed

chunks.heading: The Moon's frames
chunks.text: Moon-centred inertial is the working frame with its origin moved to the Moon, r - r{M}(t), with the Moon's position from the Hermite-interpolated ephemeris. Its axes stay parallel to the working frame's, so no rotation is involved, and velocities subtract the same way. Lunar orbits, perilune and apolune, and the line-of-sight geometry for loss of signal are all computed here. Moon body-fixed turns with the Moon, and gives selenographic latitude and longitude. Its orientation comes from the IAU working group's model (Archinal et al. 2011): the pole's right ascension 0 and declination 0, and the

chunks.heading: The Moon's frames
chunks.text: Heights above the Moon need a reference, and the documents use two. The 1969 lunar tables measure altitude above a 1738.09 km sphere. The landing site lies 8,557 ft below it (TRW), so its radius is 1735.48 km; the descent's altitudes, callouts and computer displays are all relative to that. A PDI altitude of 6.4 n mi in one source and 47,444 ft in another are the same point described from the two references. The same matrix places the Moon's gravity field. The model's two lunar harmonics, J2 (flattening) and C{22} (elongation towards Earth), are defined in body axes, so the acceleration is com

chunks.heading: LVLH: the frame of every burn
chunks.text: Maneuver PADs read up to the crew gave each burn's velocity change as three numbers, "Noun 81", in a local vertical, local horizontal frame built from the spacecraft's own position and velocity relative to whichever body it was orbiting: Impulsive burns add $ vX{ X} + vY{ Y} + vZ{ Z}$. The six-minute lunar orbit insertion is different: the thrust direction is held in LVLH but recomputed at every integration substep as the frame turns with the spacecraft, plus a fitted pitch rate. The fit settled on 0.075°/s, almost the rate at which LVLH itself turns at that height (v/r 0.076°/s), which says t

chunks.heading: Klumpp's guidance frame
chunks.text: For the descent, Eagle's computer worked in a frame centred on its landing site and rebuilt every two-second guidance cycle as the Moon turned: where C has rows { X}G, { Y}G, { Z}G. Velocity here is relative to the turning surface, which is why the Moon's angular velocity {M} appears. The code finds it numerically from two body matrices 60 s apart, W = (M(t+30) - M(t-30))/60 M(t)^{ T}, and reads the vector off that skew-symmetric matrix.

chunks.heading: The site frame $(s, c, h)$
chunks.text: The descent profile, the callouts and the last two minutes use distances along the surface: s downrange and c across, as great-circle arcs times the site radius, and h above the site radius. Flat-plane coordinates would be wrong by the Moon's curvature, which drops 66 km below the tangent plane over the 480 km from PDI. Converting back to a position is a pair of rotations of the site's unit vector by s/R and c/R.

chunks.heading: The views, panel by panel
chunks.text: Each panel picks the frame where its point is easiest to see, then flattens it with a projection. "Basis" means the pair of unit vectors the 3D position is dotted with to get screen coordinates.

chunks.heading: Inside the 3D scenes
chunks.text: Floating origin. A GPU stores positions as 32-bit floats, good to about one part in 16 million. Placed at Earth's centre, the spacecraft would sit 400,000 km out and jitter by tens of metres. So each frame the scene is rebuilt around the spacecraft: the vehicle sits at the origin and Earth, the Moon and the terrain are translated by minus its position. Large objects keep their geometry relative to their own centres, and only the offsets change. Depth. One scene spans 5 cm (the camera's near plane) to 20 million km (the stars).

chunks.heading: Inside the 3D scenes
chunks.text: A logarithmic depth buffer spreads depth precision evenly across that range so the Moon's limb does not flicker through the spacecraft. Earth is a latitude–longitude sphere textured from the same Natural Earth outlines as the 2D globe, flattened by 1/298.3 and turned about z by {GMST}0 + t. The Moon is placed by the body-to-working matrix above. The pages carry that matrix every hour or every 15 minutes, and linear interpolation of a rotation matrix is not quite a rotation, so the code re-orthonormalises it each frame by Gram–Schmidt: normalise the x column, remove its component from z, take y

chunks.heading: Inside the 3D scenes
chunks.text: Attitude. Each spacecraft's orientation is built from two directions and the cross product that completes them. In Part 2 the docked stack points along the burn's LVLH direction during burns and along the ecliptic normal, rolling at 0.3°/s, during passive thermal control; the hand-over into a burn is a quaternion slerp over 15 minutes with a smoothstep weight, so the stack turns instead of snapping. In Part 3 Eagle's thrust axis is the reconstruction's own thrust vector, exported from the simulation, and its windows are found by projecting "up" onto the plane perpendicular to that axis.

chunks.heading: Inside the 3D scenes
chunks.text: The yaw to windows-up at 102:36:57 rotates that window direction 180° about the thrust axis over the documented 62 seconds. Terrain. Part 3's lunar surface is a polar mesh centred on the landing site: 230 rings spaced geometrically from 0.6 m to 950 km, and 360 spokes. Near the LM a cell is decimetres across; at the horizon, kilometres. The mesh is built in the Moon's body frame relative to the site point, so its numbers stay small and precise, and it is placed each frame by the body matrix. Heights are sums of crater profiles; West crater and a handful of large named craters are at their appr

chunks.heading: Inside the 3D scenes
chunks.text: Cameras. "Chase" cameras use local vertical for up and the horizontal part of the velocity for "behind", so the view stays level with the horizon. The "towards the Moon/Earth" views narrow the field of view to keep the body's angular size readable and move the camera back so the spacecraft spans about a third of the frame. "Aldrin's window" sits at the right-hand window in the LM's own axes and looks forward and down about 45°, roughly where the 16 mm camera pointed.

chunks.heading: Keeping it all in step
chunks.text: The pages never integrate physics. All of that happens offline in Python, and the result is one JSON file per part. The browser only interpolates and draws, which is what makes the synchronisation simple: 1. Engine. Python and numpy compute every state in the working frame, keyed by GET and tagged documented, interpolated, propagated or fitted. 2. Data file. One partN.json holds the track table, Moon and Sun tables, events and checks: the same time base and the same frame for every panel. 3. One clock. A single reactive value T (Observable's viewof T) is moved by the slider, the event chips or

chunks.heading: Keeping it all in step
chunks.text: The player. A requestAnimationFrame loop advances T by the elapsed wall-clock time times a rate. The rate is a warp schedule chosen per phase (240× in the coast before DOI, 10× through the braking phase, 2× in the last minutes) times the speed menu, or exactly 1 in Real time. The frame step is capped at 0.1 s so a hidden tab does not leap ahead when it comes back. Reading the state at T. A binary search on the GET column finds the row i with {GET}i T < {GET}{i+1}; every column is then interpolated linearly with f = (T - {GET}i)/({GET}{i+1} - {GET}i), unwrapping longitudes across ±180° first.

chunks.heading: Keeping it all in step
chunks.text: Rows are dense where things change quickly: 1 s in the last minutes of the landing, 2 s in the braking phase, 40 s in lunar orbit, 5 minutes in mid-coast. The few quantities derived in the browser use the same interpolation: Part 2's osculating perilune and apolune (velocity from a centred difference over ±5 s, then the eccentricity vector), the revolution count (from line-of-sight crossings found in the track), and Part 3's landing-point-designator angle.

chunks.heading: Keeping it all in step
chunks.text: Media. Every audio or film clip is mapped to mission time by segments, each a straight line between clip time and GET: The audio reels have rate 1 and re-seek if they drift more than 0.8 s. The 16 mm landing film has rate 5, because it was shot at 6 frames per second and transferred at 30; it plays at a fifth speed and re-seeks beyond 0.4 s. Audio plays only when the player runs at exactly real time; at any other speed the panel says where the next recording starts.

chunks.heading: Keeping it all in step
chunks.text: When paused or scrubbing, the film seeks to the matching frame so it can be stepped with the slider. The transcript highlights the last line at or before T, found by the same binary search, and scrolls itself unless the reader has scrolled it in the last four seconds. Rendering. The 2D panels are rebuilt as SVG in one cell that depends on T. The 3D scene sets its matrices in update(T) and marks itself dirty; its own animation loop renders only when something has changed, so a paused page costs almost nothing.

chunks.heading: Where the data came from, and what it decided
chunks.text: Most sources were used for what they say. Several also forced a design decision, exposed an error in the source, or showed something missing from the model.

chunks.heading: What the data could not settle
chunks.text: The descent engine's efficiency is assumed (specific impulse 303 s), which sets the propellant margin. The braking-phase velocity target, the PDI position along the orbit and its flight-path angle are fitted, not documented. The crater field and maria outlines in the views are illustrative. And the model's lunar gravity has only two terms, so it cannot reproduce the orbit changes the mascons caused; the posts say so wherever it shows.

chunks.text: This report was generated using AI under general human direction. At the time of generation, the contents have not been comprehensively reviewed by a human analyst. Score-based diffusion models generate images (or other data) by starting from pure noise and running a stochastic process that flows toward the learned data distribution. Near the start of that process, a generated sample is maximally ambiguous about which class it will end up as; only later, as the process evolves, does it commit to one class or another. This explainer works through a small, fully analytic toy version of that stor

chunks.heading: The Gaussian mixture model
chunks.text: A Gaussian mixture model describes a density as a weighted sum of Gaussian components: where each component is centered at with shared isotropic variance ^2, and the weights are prior probabilities of each component. Here we use three components ("classes") arranged symmetrically around the origin in 2D, with slightly unequal weights to mimic real-world class imbalance: Why a GMM, specifically? Real generative models learn densities over very high-dimensional data (pixels, tokens, ...), and their exact score function is intractable to write down. A GMM is one of the few densities whose score h

chunks.heading: The Gaussian mixture model
chunks.text: That combination makes it a convenient minimal model for studying the qualitative behaviour of score-based generation — in particular, how a smooth, single density can nonetheless produce sharply distinct, discrete outcomes (the classes) when sampled dynamically. Nothing here is a claim that real data looks like a GMM; it is a controlled setting in which the mechanism of interest (symmetry breaking near an unstable point) can be derived and simulated exactly rather than approximated.

chunks.heading: The score function
chunks.text: The central object in score-based generative modeling is the score, s(x) = p(x) — a vector field pointing in the direction of locally increasing density. Diffusion models are trained to approximate this quantity; here we can differentiate it directly. For a single Gaussian component, $ {N}(x;,^2 I) = -{x-}{^2}\,{N}(x;,^2 I)$, so the gradient of the mixture density is a weighted sum of per-component "restoring forces": a responsibility-weighted average of the pulls toward each mode, where rk(x) is the posterior probability that x "belongs" to component k. Near a single well the responsibility f

chunks.heading: Langevin dynamics
chunks.text: Langevin dynamics is a stochastic differential equation (SDE) that combines deterministic drift up the score field with injected noise: where Wt is a standard Wiener process and g is a (constant, here) diffusion coefficient. This is the overdamped limit of the physical Langevin equation for a particle in a potential U(x) = - p(x) subject to thermal noise, and it is the continuous-time process underlying score-based sampling: under mild conditions, its stationary distribution is exactly p(x). Two competing effects are at work: the drift term s(Xt)\,dt pulls the state toward high-density regions

chunks.heading: Euler-Maruyama discretization
chunks.text: Simulating the SDE above requires discretizing it in time. The Euler-Maruyama method is the direct stochastic analogue of Euler's method for ODEs: replace the continuous drift and diffusion with a single small step t, and replace dWt with a Gaussian increment of the correct variance: The { t} scaling (rather than t) is essential and follows from the Wiener process's defining property {Var}(W{t+ t} - Wt) = t: it is what keeps the discrete-time noise variance consistent with the continuous-time process as t 0. Euler-Maruyama is only first-order accurate (weakly), but it is simple and sufficient

chunks.heading: Simulating the phase portrait
chunks.text: To visualize the potential landscape U(x) = - p(x), evaluate the GMM density on a grid, and overlay a handful of Langevin trajectories started with tiny random offsets from the origin (a stand-in for thermal fluctuations at maximal noise): The contour lines are level sets of U(x): tight closed loops around each mark the three stable wells (learned clean classes), while the region around the origin — equidistant from all three, in a near-symmetric configuration — is comparatively flat and unstable. Each dashed grey path starts with only a tiny random offset from the origin, yet visibly commits

chunks.heading: Bifurcation and the decision boundary
chunks.text: The single-trajectory picture above is suggestive but noisy. To see the bifurcation itself, sweep a deterministic starting position along a fixed cross-section (here, varying x0 at fixed y0=0.2, a line that passes near the origin and separates the Class A and Class B wells), run many independent noisy trajectories per starting point, and record which well each one ends up nearest to. The resulting empirical fraction approximates The transition from "always Class B" to "always Class A" happens over a narrow range of x0 straddling zero — the crossing point of the unstable origin.

chunks.heading: Bifurcation and the decision boundary
chunks.text: This is the discrete analogue of the single-trajectory picture above: whichever side of the (here, effectively one-dimensional) decision boundary a trajectory starts on almost entirely determines its eventual class, and the boundary itself sits exactly at the point where the score field's pulls from competing wells are the most evenly matched.

chunks.heading: Conclusion
chunks.text: Both figures illustrate the same mechanism from different angles: a smooth, unimodal-looking region of the density near the origin is not actually a stable point of the dynamics, but an unstable one. Under Langevin sampling, infinitesimal fluctuations there get amplified rather than damped, and the trajectory is swept into one of several well-separated, stable class basins. This is a simplified but exact picture of the qualitative claim behind score-based generative models: semantic categories emerge dynamically, as the resolution of instability near maximal noise, rather than being explicitly

chunks.heading: Conclusion
chunks.text: This is a toy model, not a reproduction of any specific paper's results: three 2D Gaussian components with hand-chosen weights and variance stand in for a real, high-dimensional, learned data distribution. The value of the exercise is that the score function, Langevin SDE, and Euler-Maruyama discretization are all exact and standard, so the qualitative bifurcation behaviour shown here is a real (if simplified) consequence of the same equations that govern actual diffusion models.

chunks.text: This is the second of four explainers behind Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar's Black Hole: 1. Bending light around a black hole: null geodesics, the photon sphere, and the exact deflection angle. 2. Ray tracing a black hole (this post): from deflection angles to pictures. 3. The Kerr black hole: spin, frame dragging and the D-shaped shadow. 4. Light from the disk: orbits, temperature, redshift and Doppler beaming. Part 1 found how far a non-spinning hole bends a ray from infinity. A picture needs more than that. It needs a camera at a definite place, which in Interstellar is a few dozen M f

chunks.heading: Trace the light backwards
chunks.text: A star sends light in every direction, and almost none of it reaches the camera. Tracing rays forward from the stars would waste nearly all the work. Geodesics are reversible, so instead we start at the camera, send one ray out through each pixel, backwards in time, and ask where it came from. There are three possible answers: - it escapes to large radius, so the pixel shows the point of the celestial sphere (the sky at infinity) in the direction the ray leaves; - it reaches the horizon, so the pixel is black, part of the shadow; - it crosses some light source on the way, such as an accretion

chunks.heading: What a static observer sees
chunks.text: A pixel's direction is measured in the camera's own frame, not in the coordinates (t, r, , ). Start with a static camera, hovering at fixed r by firing rockets. Its local, orthonormal frame has basis vectors along r, and , scaled so that lengths and times are the ones it actually measures: A photon with conserved energy E and angular momentum L (in its orbital plane) has, in this frame, energy and momentum components If the ray makes an angle with the outward radial direction, then = p^{}/E{loc}, so This one line connects a pixel to the theory in part 1. Note the factor 1/{1 - 2/r}: near the h

chunks.text: A ray looking inwards ( > /2) escapes only if b > 33. The edge of the shadow is therefore where b = 3 3, and its angular radius , measured from the direction of the hole, satisfies (Synge 1966). For r 1 this is just 33/r, the angular size of a disk of radius bc. Close in, it grows fast: at the photon sphere, r = 3, the shadow fills exactly half the sky, and inside it the shadow covers more than half.

chunks.text: A real sky is mostly point stars. Each star has a primary image outside the Einstein ring and a secondary image inside it, on the opposite side of the hole, plus fainter higher-order images hugging the shadow. Because is monotonic, all of a star's images can be found directly. If the star lies at angle from the camera's outward direction, its images sit at How bright is each image? Lensing does not create or destroy light, and it conserves surface brightness (specific intensity). This is Liouville's theorem: the phase-space density of photons is constant along a ray. A star passing behind the hole flares enormously as its two images stretch round the ring. The renderer cannot use that formula once the hole spins, because there is no single function (). The general method works for any ray map. Cut the camera's sky into small triangles, two per cell of the ray grid. Each one maps to a spherical triangle on the celestial sphere. chunks.heading: Why not paint the stars on the sky?
chunks.text: The obvious alternative is to paint the stars into the celestial-sphere texture as small dots and let the lookup sample them. The DNGR paper explains why that fails. Near a critical curve such as the Einstein ring, the map magnifies hugely in one direction, so a painted dot becomes a long luminous streak whose length depends on the dot's size, which is an artefact of the texture. A real star, smaller than any pixel, stays a point. It just gets brighter. DNGR solved this by tracing ray bundles (narrow beams whose cross-section is evolved with the equation of geodesic deviation) and feeding each

chunks.heading: Why not paint the stars on the sky?
chunks.text: For extended light, such as the glow of the galaxy or nebulae, painting into a texture is exactly right. Since surface brightness is conserved, a pixel should show the average brightness of the patch of sky it sees. Where the map shrinks the sky (towards the shadow, where one pixel can cover square degrees of sky), the lookup averages over the pixel's footprint using a mip-map pyramid of pre-averaged textures. The renderer here uses both methods: a mip-mapped texture for the diffuse Milky Way, and the triangle method for the stars.

chunks.heading: A moving camera: aberration
chunks.text: A camera hovering near a black hole is a rocket burning hard. The camera in Interstellar is on board a ship in orbit, and an orbiting camera moves through the static frame at high speed. At radius r a circular orbit has speed v = 1/{r - 2} relative to the static observer, which is half the speed of light at r = 6. Motion changes the directions from which light arrives, which is relativistic aberration. A photon arriving along direction n in the static frame arrives, for a camera moving at speed along { x}, from This is the velocity-addition law applied to light.

chunks.heading: A moving camera: aberration
chunks.text: It crowds the sky towards the direction of motion, and in the full renderer it is the first step: map each pixel from the moving camera's frame into the static frame, then trace. For a non-spinning hole that means aberration followed by the same () lookup:

chunks.heading: A moving camera: aberration
chunks.text: Aberration followed by lookup agrees with the full geodesic tracer, which applies the boost to the ray's initial momentum instead, to {python} f"{aberr:.0e}" radians. A moving camera also sees light Doppler shifted, blue ahead and red behind. That matters for the accretion disk and is the subject of part 4.

chunks.heading: The warped star field
chunks.text: Put together, these give the classic image: the night sky seen from a ship orbiting a black hole. Here the camera orbits at 30\,M, as in the film clip by Alain Riazuelo that the DNGR paper uses to introduce lensing. The Milky Way is a texture, and 60,000 stars are lensed as points. Everything here came from the single function (), which is possible only because a non-spinning hole is spherically symmetric. Spin breaks that symmetry: there is no longer one plane per ray or one function for the whole image. Every ray must be integrated through the full equations. Part 3 does that.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Stir a shallow pan of fluid unevenly heated from below, run the Belousov-Zhabotinsky chemical reaction in a dish, or couple an array of lasers together, and — despite having nothing else in common — all three systems can pass through a transition where a uniform, quiescent state gives way to a sea of traveling waves. Remarkably, close to that transition, the envelope of the emerging pattern in all three systems obeys the same one equation: the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation (CGLE). This explainer works through where that equation comes from, what its two free parameters control, and what its

chunks.heading: From Landau's theory of phase transitions to a superconducting order parameter
chunks.text: The story starts with Lev Landau's 1930s mean-field theory of second-order phase transitions: expand the free energy of a system as a power series in a small "order parameter" that vanishes above the critical temperature and grows continuously below it, keep only the lowest-order terms allowed by symmetry, and minimize. In 1950, Vitaly Ginzburg and Landau extended this idea to superconductivity, treating the density of superconducting charge carriers as a complex order parameter ({x}) whose phase encodes the macroscopic quantum coherence of the superconducting state, and whose magnitude vanish

chunks.heading: From Landau's theory of phase transitions to a superconducting order parameter
chunks.text: The Ginzburg-Landau free energy functional, minimized over , gives a static nonlinear equation for ({x}) — a real diffusion-like term coupling neighboring points in space, plus a cubic term that saturates the growth of ||. That static, real-coefficient equation is the ancestor of the one simulated below, but two more ingredients are needed to get there: the equation has to become dynamical (an equation of motion, not just an energy to minimize), and its coefficients have to become complex.

chunks.heading: Amplitude equations and the road to a complex equation
chunks.text: The dynamical step came from a different direction entirely: pattern formation in fluids. Near the onset of Rayleigh-Bénard convection — the striped or hexagonal patterns that appear when a fluid layer is heated from below past a critical temperature gradient — Newell and Whitehead showed that the envelope of the convection rolls (not the fast-oscillating roll pattern itself, but the slowly-varying amplitude modulating it) obeys a real Ginzburg-Landau equation, derived by a weakly nonlinear multiple-scales expansion around the instability threshold [@newellwhitehead1969]. This is the general m

chunks.heading: Amplitude equations and the road to a complex equation
chunks.text: This is the same universality argument used throughout bifurcation theory (see the companion explainer on Langevin dynamics and bifurcation for a related but distinct flavor of symmetry-breaking): the amplitude equation doesn't care about the chemistry of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction or the viscosity of the convecting fluid, only about the type of instability and a couple of real numbers describing it.

chunks.heading: Amplitude equations and the road to a complex equation
chunks.text: The complex Ginzburg-Landau equation is what falls out of this same argument for an oscillatory (Hopf) instability in an extended medium: a spatially distributed field of identical, weakly coupled oscillators, each individually just past the threshold of sustained self-oscillation. Yoshiki Kuramoto derived exactly this reduction for reaction-diffusion systems modeling chemical oscillators — the mathematical root of both the CGLE and the more famous Kuramoto model of coupled-oscillator synchronization — and used it to explain the onset of "chemical turbulence" in the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reacti

chunks.heading: Amplitude equations and the road to a complex equation
chunks.text: Cross and Hohenberg's canonical review of pattern formation situates the CGLE as one member of a small family of universal amplitude equations that recur across fluid dynamics, nonlinear optics, and chemical physics [@crosshohenberg1993pattern], and Aranson and Kramer's dedicated review catalogs just how rich its behavior is — plane waves, spiral defects, and full spatiotemporal chaos, all from the same three-term equation [@aransonkramer2002world].

chunks.heading: The equation
chunks.text: The version simulated here, in one spatial dimension with periodic boundary conditions, is where A(x,t) {C} is the complex envelope, and c1, c3 {R} are the two free parameters of the model (their coefficients on the linear growth and cubic terms have been rescaled to 1 by an appropriate choice of time, space, and amplitude units — the genuinely universal content of the equation is just c1 and c3). Reading it term by term: - A: linear growth. Every point is individually just past a Hopf bifurcation, so left alone (no coupling), |A| would grow exponentially from any small perturbation.

chunks.heading: The equation
chunks.text: This is what makes the flat A=0 state in the simulation below unstable to the tiny initial noise. - (1+ic1)\,^2x A: spatial coupling between neighbors. The real part (coefficient 1) is ordinary diffusion, which smooths out spatial differences in amplitude. The imaginary part, ic1\,^2x A, has no analogue in the static Ginzburg-Landau theory: it couples spatial curvature into the local phase, which is what lets a spatially extended field of oscillators lock into traveling waves rather than just synchronizing to a spatially uniform, purely time-oscillating state. c1 is often called the linear dis

chunks.heading: The equation
chunks.text: - -(1-ic3)\,|A|^2 A: cubic self-saturation. The real part is the same amplitude-limiting nonlinearity as in the static theory — it's what stops the linear growth term from blowing up, pinning |A| near 1 once the system saturates. The imaginary part, ic3|A|^2 A, is a nonlinear frequency shift: the local oscillation frequency depends on the local amplitude, the way a Kerr-nonlinear optical medium's refractive index depends on light intensity. c3 is the nonlinear frequency-renormalization coefficient.

chunks.heading: Plane waves and the Benjamin-Feir-Newell criterion
chunks.text: Before running the simulation, it's worth asking what the CGLE predicts analytically, because the prediction is exact and gives a sanity check for the numerics. The simplest nontrivial solutions are traveling plane waves, A(x,t) = R\,e^{i(kx - t)} with constant real amplitude R and wavenumber k. Substituting into the equation and separating real and imaginary parts gives so a family of plane-wave solutions exists for every $|k| 0, $$ and unstable otherwise. When it's unstable, small perturbations to a plane wave grow rather than decay, and the system is driven toward "defect turbulence" or "ph

chunks.heading: Plane waves and the Benjamin-Feir-Newell criterion
chunks.text: For the parameters used here, 1 - c1 c3 = 1 - ()() = , which is positive — so the plane-wave regime should be linearly stable, and the simulation should settle into a single coherent traveling wave rather than turbulence. That's the prediction to check against the numerics below.

chunks.heading: Where the criterion comes from
chunks.text: The criterion is short enough to derive in full. Take the uniform (k=0) plane wave, which from the formulas above has R=1 and =-c3, so A0 = e^{ic3t}. Perturb it, A = (1 + u + iv)\,e^{ic3 t}, with u (amplitude) and v (phase) small and real. Substituting and keeping terms linear in u, v gives (u+iv) = (1+ic1)\,^2(u+iv) - 2(1-ic3)\,u. Try a single Fourier mode, (u, v) e^{iqx + t}: One eigenvalue is always close to -2. That is the amplitude mode: disturb |A| and it relaxes back to 1 quickly.

chunks.heading: Where the criterion comes from
chunks.text: The other is the phase mode, which for long waves (q 0) is To leading order, a slow modulation of the phase therefore obeys a diffusion equation, = (1-c1c3)\,^2, with an effective diffusion coefficient D = 1 - c1c3. When D > 0, phase ripples smooth out. When D < 0 the diffusion runs backwards: every long-wavelength ripple grows, which is the Benjamin-Feir-Newell instability. Its growth is cut off at shorter wavelengths by the O(q^4) terms. Near the threshold, those terms turn the phase equation into the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, the classic model of phase turbulence [@kuramoto1984chemical

chunks.heading: Where the criterion comes from
chunks.text: This is checkable. The chunk below starts the 1-D equation from the uniform plane wave with a tiny phase ripple of wavenumber q, measures how fast the ripple grows or decays, and compares that rate with the exact eigenvalue of the 22 matrix above. It does this for the stable parameters used in the 1-D run and for the two unstable sets used later in 2-D. The simulation reproduces the linear theory: for the longest waves the measured and predicted rates agree to within %. The residual comes from the forward-Euler time step and the finite-difference Laplacian.

chunks.heading: Where the criterion comes from
chunks.text: For the stable parameters every ripple decays. For both unstable sets a band of long waves grows, much faster for c1 = 2 than for c1 = 1, and the curves explain the choices made in 2-D below. The weakly unstable set (c1 = 1, c3 = 1.3) has a peak growth rate of only , at a wavelength of about . That is why its run below uses a 20×20 domain and a long simulated time.

chunks.heading: Simulating the equation
chunks.text: The equation is solved by explicit finite differences on a periodic ring: the spatial Laplacian at each grid point is approximated by the standard second-order central difference, with the two boundary neighbors wrapped around the ring, and the whole field is advanced in time by a single forward-Euler step. The time step has to respect the explicit scheme's stability limit, and the complex diffusion coefficient makes that limit tighter than for ordinary diffusion. The shortest grid mode has ^2 -4/dx^2. Forward Euler multiplies it by 1 - 4\,dt\,(1+ic1)/dx^2 each step, and that factor has modulu

chunks.text: That is here, half the real-diffusion limit dx^2/2, and dt = 0.04 is inside it. (In 2-D the limit halves again, to dx^2/(4(1+c1^2)). Both 2-D runs below respect it, the first with little room to spare.) The field starts from the unstable state A 0, seeded with tiny uniform random noise — a stand-in for the fact that any real physical realization of this instability starts from some unavoidable microscopic fluctuation, not from an exact, infinitely fine-tuned zero.

chunks.heading: Checking the plane-wave prediction against the final state
chunks.text: Before plotting the full space-time history, it's worth directly comparing the simulation's final state to the plane-wave formula derived above. The periodic domain only permits wavenumbers k = 2 n/L for integer winding number n, so unwrapping the final phase profile across the ring reads off exactly which k the system selected. The field settles into (almost exactly) a single winding of phase around the periodic domain — the lowest nonzero wavenumber the ring permits, k = 2/L — and the observed amplitude is uniform to a part in a thousand.

chunks.heading: Checking the plane-wave prediction against the final state
chunks.text: It sits % above the plane-wave prediction R={1-k^2} . That gap is not noise. It is a systematic error of the forward-Euler time step: each Euler step slightly over-rotates and over-stretches a uniform oscillation, and the amplitude at which the discrete map stops growing is , which matches the observed . As dt 0 it converges on the exact R. Apart from that numerical offset, this is the exact analytic solution derived above, reappearing as the attractor of the full nonlinear simulation.

chunks.heading: Reading the space-time picture
chunks.text: The two top panels are plotting the same complex field, split into its polar coordinates, and they show almost entirely different things. Panel A (amplitude) grows out of the noisy initial condition and then goes essentially flat — the plane-wave analysis above is exact evidence that this should happen, not a numerical artifact, since |A| genuinely is spatially uniform for an ideal plane wave. Panel C makes the transient legible. The spatial spread of |A| peaks while patches of different phase are still competing. It falls below 0.01 by t , and after that it decays slowly and exponentially, at

chunks.heading: Reading the space-time picture
chunks.text: That slow tail is the phase mode of the previous section at work. The last long-wavelength phase irregularities relax diffusively, and the amplitude, slaved to the phase gradients, follows them down. The predicted rate for the slowest phase mode on this ring, (1-c1c3)q^2 with q = 2/L from the exact eigenvalue, is . The tail rate is of the same order. The two need not match exactly, since the linear analysis was about the k=0 wave and the ring has selected k = 2/L.

chunks.heading: Reading the space-time picture
chunks.text: Panel B (phase) is where the structure lives, because for a plane wave {Arg}(A) = kx - t is linear in both space and time. With k as small as the ring allows, the field oscillates almost in unison at -c3, which gives the horizontal stripes. The single winding of phase round the ring tilts each stripe by exactly one period across the domain: the travelling wave. It is a phase phenomenon, encoded in the winding of the argument of A around the periodic domain, not in any spatial modulation of its magnitude.

chunks.heading: Extending to two dimensions: spiral defects and phase turbulence
chunks.text: Everything above stayed in one spatial dimension, where the Benjamin-Feir-Newell criterion has a clean binary reading: 1-c1c3>0 gives a stable traveling plane wave, and 1-c1c3<0 gives some form of spatiotemporal chaos. In two dimensions, the same instability opens onto a richer phase diagram, because the phase field {Arg}(A) can now wind around a point rather than only accumulating along a line. Where the phase winds by a full 2 around some point (x,y), continuity forces the amplitude to vanish exactly at that point — these are the topological defects of the CGLE, and away from the defect core

chunks.heading: Extending to two dimensions: spiral defects and phase turbulence
chunks.text: Aranson and Kramer's review catalogs how, once 1-c1c3<0, the system can settle into two qualitatively distinct chaotic regimes depending on how far into the unstable region the parameters sit: a defect-free phase turbulence, where the phase field is chaotic but the amplitude stays bounded away from zero everywhere, and a defect (or amplitude) turbulence, where point defects continually nucleate, wander, and annihilate in pairs, each one the core of a rotating spiral [@aransonkramer2002world]. The equation itself only needs the Laplacian promoted to two dimensions:

chunks.heading: Detecting a topological defect numerically
chunks.text: A defect is a point around which the phase winds by a full turn. On the grid, that's checked by walking around each elementary 2x2 plaquette of grid points, summing the (wrapped, so always in (-,]) phase differences between adjacent corners, and dividing by 2: a plaquette encloses a defect of charge +1 or -1 exactly when that sum is 2, and encloses no defect when it's zero. This is the same discrete circulation-counting argument used to find vortices in superfluids or dislocations in a crystal lattice — a defect is, by construction, a place where a per-point quantity (the phase) is discontinuo

chunks.text: 1-c1c3<0 is necessary for either chaotic regime, but it's a statement purely about the linear growth rate of long-wavelength perturbations to the k=0 plane wave, and that growth rate vanishes continuously as the parameters approach the line from the unstable side. That has a concrete numerical consequence: sitting just barely past the line, the instability takes a very long time (and a large domain, to admit small enough wavenumbers) to grow out of infinitesimal noise, and — checked directly, by starting a run near the line and simply watching for a long time — it does not automatically produc

chunks.heading: Choosing two parameter sets on the unstable side of the line
chunks.text: Nucleating an actual point defect is a separate, finite-amplitude event: it requires some region of the field to be driven all the way to A=0, which is a much larger fluctuation than "phase is a bit ragged." So two runs are used here, both satisfying 1-c1c3<0, chosen to sit on either side of that further, empirical threshold:

chunks.heading: The two regimes, side by side
chunks.text: Fully developed phase turbulence, a chaotic but defect-free phase field, needs a domain many unstable wavelengths across, and a correspondingly long and expensive simulation. "Phase turbulence" names the regime, chaotic in the dynamical-systems sense; it is not a promise of visual complexity at this size.

chunks.heading: The two regimes, side by side
chunks.text: Both runs sit on the unstable side of the same Benjamin-Feir-Newell line derived in one dimension above — the criterion doesn't care about dimensionality, since it comes from linearizing around the same uniform plane wave — but only one of them turns that linear instability into topological defects. This is the sense in which the two-dimensional CGLE is a genuinely richer object than its 1D restriction: a 1D "defect" would require the amplitude to hit zero at an isolated point in spacetime, an event fine-tuned enough to be essentially unobservable from generic initial conditions, whereas in 2D

chunks.heading: How literal is the biological framing?
chunks.text: It is tempting to describe A(x,t) as a "morphogen field" and to draw an analogy with the segmentation clocks that lay down somites in vertebrate embryos. That framing should be treated as a narrative device, not a claim that this equation is a validated model of any particular developmental system. Real segmentation clocks (the traveling wavefront of Hes/Her gene expression oscillations in the vertebrate presomitic mesoderm) are usually modeled with delay-coupled genetic oscillator networks tied to a receding determination front, not a CGLE-type amplitude equation, and the classic Turing-type

chunks.heading: How literal is the biological framing?
chunks.text: Where the CGLE genuinely does apply as a first-principles model — not just an analogy — is anywhere a spatially extended medium of near-identical oscillators is weakly coupled to its neighbors just past a Hopf bifurcation: coupled chemical oscillators in the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction, traveling and spiral waves in some models of cardiac tissue, arrays of coupled lasers, and convecting fluids with an oscillatory (rather than stationary) primary instability. The reason the same three-term equation keeps reappearing across such physically unrelated systems is precisely the universality argume

chunks.heading: Conclusion
chunks.text: Four things are worth taking away. First, the historical arc: a static, real mean-field theory for superconductivity became a dynamical, complex amplitude equation once the same symmetry-and-scaling argument was applied to oscillatory rather than stationary instabilities — and that equation turned out to be universal across a wide range of unrelated physical systems. Second, the concrete numerical lesson from the 1D simulation: splitting a complex field into |A| and {Arg}(A) is not a neutral choice of coordinates. There, essentially all of the interesting spatiotemporal structure was carried b

chunks.heading: Conclusion
chunks.text: Third, the stability of those plane waves comes down to one number. A slow phase modulation diffuses with coefficient 1-c1c3, and when that coefficient turns negative, long phase ripples grow instead of smoothing out: the Benjamin-Feir-Newell instability, confirmed above by direct measurement of growth rates. Fourth, moving to two dimensions changes the picture: past the same line, the amplitude stops being a passive, uniform background and can itself develop structure. chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Last of four explainers behind The Martian Tripod. Parts 1 and 2 covered geometry: where the feet are and how to put them there. Part 3 covered force, and ended on an awkward discovery. With a foot in the air, the tripod's grasp matrix loses a rank: nothing the legs do can resist a tip about the line through the two planted feet. A walking tripod is never in static equilibrium. It is always falling, and each footfall catches it. There are two ways to walk like that.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: The static way, the project's first gait, carries the centre of mass to the edge of the next two-foot support, stops, lifts the foot, lets the body topple onto the new foot, and settles. It works at about 1.1 mph. The dynamic way, which reaches 5.6 mph, plans the fall in advance and keeps the body moving throughout. This post builds that planner from the ground up.

chunks.heading: From a falling pole to a linear model
chunks.text: Picture the machine's whole mass m at its centre of mass c, held at height h above the ground by massless legs. The ground pushes on the feet, and the net ground force F acts through some point z on the ground. Two conditions fix everything. - Vertical: if the height is held constant, the vertical force just carries the weight: Fz = mg. - Rotational: a point mass has no angular momentum about itself, so the net force on it must point through it. The force's line of action runs from z on the ground to c in the air, so its horizontal and vertical components are in the ratio of the horizontal and

chunks.heading: From a falling pole to a linear model
chunks.text: with the same equation in x and y, independently. It is linear, which is the whole point: an inverted pendulum with a fixed-length leg is nonlinear, but holding the height constant makes the dynamics exactly linear. The point z is the zero-moment point (ZMP, Vukobratović, 1972). It is the point on the ground about which the ground forces have no horizontal moment. When every foot is on flat ground, it is simply the centre of pressure, the load-weighted average of the foot positions: Since every f{i,z} 0 (the ground can only push), z is a convex combination of the feet.

chunks.heading: From a falling pole to a linear model
chunks.text: It must lie inside the support polygon, their convex hull. This is the barycentric-coordinate result from part 3 read backwards. There, the centre of mass's position fixed the foot loads. Here, choosing the foot loads places the ZMP anywhere in the polygon, and the ZMP steers the centre of mass. That is the planner's whole control authority. The legs choose where the ZMP is, within the support polygon, and the centre of mass falls away from it.

chunks.heading: What the pendulum does
chunks.text: With z held still, write x = c - z for one axis. The solution of x = ^2 x is is conserved, so trajectories in the (x, x) plane are hyperbolas. This is the LIPM's orbital energy (Kajita & Tani, 1991). If E > 0, the centre of mass has enough speed to pass over the ZMP and carry on. If E < 0, it falls back the way it came. The boundary lines x = x are the eigenvectors of the dynamics. Along x = - x the body glides in and stops exactly above the ZMP. Along x = + x it falls away exponentially.

chunks.heading: The divergent component and the capture point
chunks.text: Change variables to split the stable and unstable parts. Define the divergent component of motion (DCM) Differentiating and substituting the LIPM gives two first-order equations: The second equation is stable: the centre of mass simply chases with time constant 1/. All the instability is in the first. runs away from the ZMP exponentially. The control problem has halved in size: keep under control, and the centre of mass looks after itself. There is a striking special case. Put the ZMP exactly at and hold it there. Then {} = 0, and the centre of mass coasts to a halt directly above the ZMP.

chunks.heading: The divergent component and the capture point
chunks.text: So is the point on the ground where you must step, or put the centre of pressure, to stop. That is why it is also called the capture point (Pratt and colleagues, 2006). If the capture point leaves the region where any future support polygon could reach it, the fall can no longer be stopped.

chunks.heading: The divergent component and the capture point
chunks.text: There is another way to read the equation for . Solving it forward from time t and asking that stays bounded (the robot does not fall over) forces The DCM now is a discounted average of all future ZMPs, with a discount time of 1/ = 1.67 s. A walk that doesn't fall must therefore be planned with the future in view: where the ZMP will be over the next few seconds determines what the body must do now. That one equation is why the tripod needs a predictive planner, and how far ahead it must look.

chunks.heading: The hinge, in pendulum terms
chunks.text: On three feet the ZMP can go anywhere in the triangle. On two feet the support polygon collapses to the line segment between them. Resolve the motion along and across that line. Along it, the ZMP can still slide, so that component is controlled. Across it, the ZMP is pinned at zero offset, and the equation becomes a pure, uncontrolled fall: part 3's hinge again. The tripod spends 60% of its walking time on two feet, so 60% of the time it is free-falling sideways. The fall is slow, because 1/ = 1.67 s for a 27 m pendulum, but it cannot be stopped from two feet. The planner's job on three feet i

chunks.heading: The hinge, in pendulum terms
chunks.text: The last line shows the DCM's predictive power. The body starts 1 m on one side of the hinge but moving towards it fast enough that its DCM is on the other side, so it crosses over. Where it ends up is decided by the side of the line the DCM is on, not the side the body is on.

chunks.heading: Discretising exactly
chunks.text: The planner works on a time grid of t = 0.1 s, with the ZMP held constant during each interval. Because the LIPM is linear with constant coefficients, the state after one interval is exact, not an approximation like Euler's method: The eigenvalues e^{ t} are the discrete version of the stable/unstable split. One mode shrinks by 6% per step, the other grows by 6%.

chunks.heading: The ZMP planner as a quadratic programme
chunks.text: Now set up the planning problem. Stack everything over a horizon of N steps into one vector of decision variables: the states x0, , xN (position and velocity, in x and y) and the ZMPs z0, , z{N-1}. Then - keep the walking speed; - keep up with the footstep timeline; - move the ZMP smoothly; - keep the ZMP near the middle of the support (around the centroid { p}k of the planted feet). The constraints are all linear. A triangle is three half-planes, ne^ z ne^ ae - {margin} for each edge e with outward normal ne.

chunks.heading: The ZMP planner as a quadratic programme
chunks.text: A two-foot line is an equality across it plus two bounds along it. A quadratic cost with linear constraints is a quadratic programme (QP). It is convex, so there is one global optimum and fast, reliable solvers find it. The tripod uses OSQP, an operator-splitting solver designed for exactly this kind of sparse, repeated problem.

chunks.heading: A one-dimensional warm-up
chunks.text: Before the full planar version, here is the same QP stripped to one dimension, written out from scratch: a walker on a line. The footsteps advance 7.33 m every 2 s. For 0.8 s of each step the ZMP may be anywhere between the rear and front feet; for the next 1.2 s it is confined to a 1 m patch around the front foot, the 1-D stand-in for the hinge. Read the picture from left to right. To get going from rest, the planner first puts the ZMP well behind the body: the only way to accelerate forward is to fall forward.

chunks.heading: A one-dimensional warm-up
chunks.text: Once walking, each three-foot phase sweeps the ZMP forward from the rear foot to the front one. In the narrow phase the ZMP is pinned at the front foot while the body vaults over it, slowing as it climbs towards the foot and speeding up as it falls past. That is the steady ripple in the speed. The capture point always leads the body by c/, about 6 m at this speed, and keeps ahead of the footsteps. The body has always just enough momentum to reach the next support. The last line confirms the integral formula: the DCM computed from the state equals the discounted sum of the planned future ZMPs.

chunks.heading: The real thing: the tripod in the plane
chunks.text: The tripod's planner (tripod/planner.py) is the same QP in two dimensions with the real support polygons. A footstep schedule says which leg swings when and where it lands. Steps take 2.0 s: 0.8 s on three feet, then 1.2 s with one leg in the air. Each step moves one foot by a 22 m stride, in the order 1, 2, 0. Over a 14 s horizon at 0.1 s resolution there are 140 ZMP knots and 141 states, about 850 variables, solved in roughly 10 ms.

chunks.heading: How far ahead must it look?
chunks.text: The DCM integral says the present depends on the future ZMP, discounted with a 1.67 s time constant. A planner that looks only a second or two ahead cannot see the supports it will need, so it plans motions that look fine within its horizon and are doomed just beyond it. It has no notion that the body must still be catchable when the horizon ends. This is easy to test: run the receding-horizon loop on the pendulum with different horizons. Horizons of four seconds or less fail.

chunks.heading: How far ahead must it look?
chunks.text: Every individual QP is feasible, and the planner never reports a problem, yet the walk diverges: within a few steps for horizons of 1–3 s, after about ten steps at 4 s. From six seconds on, one full gait cycle (three steps of 2 s), the walk is stable and longer horizons change little. The rule of thumb in humanoid robotics is a preview of one to two steps; for this slow, tall pendulum on a three-step cycle, that means a whole cycle. The project uses 14 s for margin.

chunks.heading: Model-predictive control: replanning from what actually happened
chunks.text: A plan computed once and followed blindly is open-loop. The pendulum is unstable, so any error — a gust, a misplaced foot, a modelling error — grows like e^{ t}, doubling every 1.15 s. The cure is to re-solve the QP frequently from the measured state. Execute only the first part of each plan, then plan again. This is receding-horizon or model-predictive control (MPC). The tripod re-plans at every change of support and every 0.4 s in between. To see the difference, push the walking pendulum sideways at t = 10 s, and compare the MPC loop with one that stops re-planning at the moment of the push.

chunks.heading: Model-predictive control: replanning from what actually happened
chunks.text: The frozen plan does not merely drift. Its error grows exponentially, the straight line on the log scale, because the push has moved the DCM and the old plan's ZMP no longer contains it. MPC sees the new state at the next re-plan and moves the ZMP to absorb the push over the following steps. The deviation decays steadily, and the robot rejoins its path.

chunks.heading: In the full MuJoCo simulation
chunks.text: The tripod model has extra machinery on top of this. Its whole-body controller adds a spring-damper pulling the centre of mass towards the plan. While three feet are down, friction at the feet can resist sideways forces directly. In the full simulation, a 2 m/s lateral push of 0.5 s duration during the walk hardly disturbs it. The pure pendulum above, with nothing but the ZMP to steer with, shows the planner's contribution on its own.

chunks.heading: From plan to torques
chunks.text: The planner outputs a centre-of-mass trajectory and a ZMP. Turning those into motor commands uses everything from the earlier parts, about 500 times a second. 1. Desired force. Compute the force that keeps the centre of mass on the plan: the planned acceleration m{ c}{plan} as feedforward, plus a spring-damper on the tracking error, plus the weight. Compute a moment that keeps the hood level. 2. Share it among the planted feet. Solve the grasp-matrix least-squares problem from part 3, with every foot pushing and inside its friction cone.

chunks.heading: From plan to torques
chunks.text: On two feet, drop the moment component about the hinge, which can't be produced. 3. Torques. Map each foot force through = g( q) - J^ f, the virtual-work law of part 3. 4. Swing leg. Move the lifted foot along its task-space arc using closed-form IK (part 2) and a joint servo, landing on the next scheduled foothold. - 15 steps in 30.6 s, covering 77 m at 5.6 mph; - 59% of the time on two feet; - the hood never tilting more than 2.7°. That is five times the speed of the wait-and-topple gait, with a sixth of its tilt.

chunks.heading: What this planner leaves out
chunks.text: The LIPM and a fixed footstep schedule are the classic starting point, not the state of the art. Some refinements, roughly in order of how much they would help the tripod: - Footstep optimisation. Here the footholds are fixed in advance and only the ZMP moves. Letting the QP also choose where the feet land, as a capture-point stepping strategy does, gives far more authority against pushes. That matters on two feet, where the ZMP has no sideways authority at all. - Height and angular momentum. Holding the height constant is what made the model linear.

chunks.heading: What this planner leaves out
chunks.text: Allowing the body to bob, or the hood to pitch, adds more ways to control the body. The usual tool is the centroidal dynamics model, solved by nonlinear MPC. - Leg dynamics. Each 28 t leg weighs a ninth of the machine, and swinging it shoves the body. The LIPM ignores this; whole-body MPC includes it. - Learning. Much of modern legged locomotion is trained by reinforcement learning in simulators like MuJoCo, often with a model-based planner like this one providing structure or reference motions. The main post discusses why MuJoCo became the standard simulator for that work.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: - Holding the centre of mass at constant height gives the linear inverted pendulum { c} = ^2( c - z). The ZMP z is the centre of pressure and must stay in the support polygon. - The divergent component = c + { c}/ carries all the instability. It equals the discounted future ZMP, so walking must be planned ahead. It is also the capture point: put the ZMP there to stop. - On two feet the support polygon is a line, and the motion across it is a pure fall.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A walking tripod is falling sideways 60% of the time. - Exact discretisation plus linear support constraints make ZMP planning a convex QP, solved by OSQP in about 10 ms. - The horizon must cover about one gait cycle; shorter horizons produce feasible plans that still fall. - Re-planning from the measured state (MPC) turns an exponentially unstable open-loop plan into a robust walk.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: This is the first of four explainers behind The Martian Tripod: Walking a Fighting-Machine in MuJoCo. That post moved quickly through the mathematics of making a three-legged machine walk. These explainers slow down and work through it properly: 1. Forward kinematics (this post): given the joint angles, where is the foot? 2. Inverse kinematics: given where the foot should be, what are the joint angles? 3. Statics and the Jacobian: what torques must the motors supply to hold the machine up? 4. Planning the falling walk: how do you plan a gait in which the machine is always falling? Every formul

chunks.heading: Joint space and task space
chunks.text: A robot is described in two ways. Its configuration is the list of joint angles, q = (q1, , qn); that is what the motors and encoders know. Its task is described in space: where the foot is, which way the hood points. Kinematics is the map between them, ignoring forces and masses entirely. Forward kinematics (FK) goes from joints to space, p = f( q). It is always easy: there is exactly one answer, found by composing one rigid motion per link. Inverse kinematics goes the other way and is harder: there may be no answer, one, several or infinitely many. That is the subject of part 2. This post bu

chunks.heading: Rotations
chunks.text: A rotation is a 3 3 matrix R whose columns are the rotated frame's axes, written in the original frame. Those axes stay unit length and mutually perpendicular, so Matrices with these two properties form the special orthogonal group SO(3). The inverse of a rotation is just its transpose, which is why R^ appears so often below. The three basic rotations about the coordinate axes are - Rotations do not commute. Ry(a)Rz(b) Rz(b)Ry(a) in general, so the order of joints along the chain matters. - A positive rotation about +y tips the x-axis down. Ry() sends (1,0,0) to (, 0, -). The tripod's hip and

chunks.heading: Homogeneous transforms
chunks.text: A rigid motion is a rotation followed by a translation, x R x + t. Writing points as ( x, 1) turns this into a single matrix product: These 4 4 matrices form the special Euclidean group SE(3). Read {}^{A}T{B} as "the pose of frame B in frame A". Poses then chain like fractions cancelling, and the inverse is cheap: ${}^{B}T{A} = {pmatrix}R^ & -R^ t\\ 0^ & 1{pmatrix}$. That chain rule is all of forward kinematics. Give every link a frame and write each frame's pose relative to its parent. That pose is a fixed offset (the link's geometry) times a rotation by the joint angle. Then multiply down th

chunks.heading: One leg, link by link
chunks.text: Each leg hangs from the underside of the hood. Its chain, from the hood's centre to the foot, is: Because the hip and knee both turn about the same y axis, their angles add. The thigh's direction is set by qh and the shin's by qh + qk. In terms of elevation angles above the horizontal, 1 = -qh for the thigh and 2 = -(qh + qk) for the shin. The foot, in the leg's own vertical plane, is then and the yaw turns that plane round the vertical: This closed form is what the project's kinematics.footfk computes.

chunks.heading: One leg, link by link
chunks.text: Below, the same thing is built by brute-force matrix multiplication, so the two can be checked against each other. With the hood at the origin, the standing foot sits 22 m out and 28.9 m down, in the foot sphere's centre. The hip angle is slightly negative: the thigh points 3° above horizontal, and the knee folds the shin down through 86° to stand almost vertical.

chunks.heading: The workspace
chunks.text: The workspace is the set of all points the foot can reach. In the leg plane, with no joint limits, the two-link arm reaches exactly the annulus which for the tripod is between 12 m and 44 m from the hip. The outer rim is the leg fully straight, and the inner rim fully folded. Real joints have limits, though: in the MuJoCo model the hip pitch is limited to [-1.2, 1.4] rad and the knee to [-0.3, 2.6] rad, and the limits carve pieces out of the annulus.

chunks.heading: The workspace
chunks.text: The quickest way to see the workspace is to sample joint space and push every sample through FK. - The workspace is a crescent, not the annulus. The knee limit of 2.6 rad (149°) stops the leg folding completely, so the inner rim is never reached. The hip limits stop the leg swinging right round, so the crescent runs from the leg pointing nearly straight up to the foot curled in under the body. - The knee almost never bends backwards. Its range is [-0.3, 2.6], so it can only overextend by 17°.

chunks.heading: The workspace
chunks.text: Positive knee angles are the knee-up shape. A point in the workspace can usually be reached by a knee-up and a knee-down configuration, but here the knee-down one only exists in a thin sliver along the outer rim. The joint limits have nearly removed the ambiguity that part 2 has to resolve. - The stance sits well inside the workspace, with margin in every direction. That margin is what lets the hood rise, sway and tilt while the feet stay planted.

chunks.heading: The workspace
chunks.text: Adding the yaw sweeps this plane through 0.8 rad ( 46^) about the vertical through the hip. The 3-D workspace is a thick wedge of a spherical shell. Three such wedges, one per leg at 120° apart, overlap only a little. Each foot has its own patch of ground, and a gait has to keep every foot inside its own patch.

chunks.heading: Checking against MuJoCo
chunks.text: MuJoCo builds the same chain from the model file. Each has a position and orientation relative to its parent, and each adds a rotation about its axis. mjkinematics multiplies everything down the tree and stores every body's world pose in data.xpos and data.xmat. There is one subtlety in the configuration vector. The hood is attached to the world by a free joint: three translations and an orientation stored as a unit quaternion (w, x, y, z). A quaternion has four numbers but only three degrees of freedom, so qpos (the positions) has one more entry than qvel (the velocities).

chunks.heading: Checking against MuJoCo
chunks.text: The transform chain agrees with MuJoCo to within a fraction of a millimetre across 300 random poses, with the hood flung about at random orientations. Leg 0 agrees to machine precision. The tiny residual on legs 1 and 2 is not a kinematics error: the model file writes each mount's azimuth with six significant figures (2.0944 rad for 120°). A rounding error of a few millionths of a radian, swung through a 44 m leg, moves the foot a tenth of a millimetre.

chunks.heading: Another way to write it: the product of exponentials
chunks.text: The link-by-link chain needs a frame on every link. A more modern formulation, the product of exponentials (Brockett, 1984; the standard form in Lynch & Park's Modern Robotics), needs only two things: - the home pose M of the foot when every joint is at zero; - for each joint, its screw axis Sj = (, vj) in the home configuration. For a hinge, is the unit axis direction and vj = - rj, where rj is any point on the axis. where [] is the skew-symmetric matrix with [] x = x, and the exponential is the matrix exponential.

chunks.heading: Another way to write it: the product of exponentials
chunks.text: Each factor is "rotate everything beyond joint j about joint j's axis by qj", applied from the tip backwards. No intermediate frames are needed. The screw axes are also exactly the columns of the Jacobian at the home pose, which part 3 builds on.

chunks.heading: Another way to write it: the product of exponentials
chunks.text: For leg 0 the axes are simple. The yaw is a vertical axis through the hip at r = (2.6, 0, -2). At home, the hip and knee are horizontal y-axes through the hip and through the point 16 m further out. The two formulations agree to rounding error. The PoE form is popular for exactly this reason: it is defined by physical axes you can point at on the machine, it has no special-case conventions, and its Jacobian falls straight out of it.

chunks.heading: What about Denavit–Hartenberg parameters?
chunks.text: Older textbooks and many industrial controllers describe chains with Denavit–Hartenberg (DH) parameters. That is four numbers per joint (a, , d, ), which fix each link's frame by a strict convention: z along the joint axis, x along the common normal to the next axis. DH is compact, but the conventions (there are two incompatible ones, "standard" and "modified") are a famous source of errors. MuJoCo, URDF and most modern software instead give each link an arbitrary pose relative to its parent, as in the table above. The PoE form avoids link frames altogether.

chunks.heading: Velocities: a look ahead
chunks.text: Differentiate the foot position with respect to time and every term picks up a joint velocity: The matrix J of partial derivatives is the Jacobian. It turns joint speeds into foot speed and, by a duality explained in part 3, foot forces into joint torques. It is also the engine of numerical inverse kinematics in part 2. Each column is "the foot's velocity if only this joint moves". For a hinge, that is ( p - rj): the foot circles the joint's axis. A finite-difference check on the standing pose shows the idea: Read the columns of J one at a time.

chunks.heading: Velocities: a look ahead
chunks.text: - Yaw moves the foot purely sideways (y), at 19.4 m/rad. That is its horizontal distance from the yaw axis. - Hip moves the foot inward (26.9 m/rad) and down (19.4 m/rad). Positive qh swings the whole leg downward round the hip. The foot is far below the hip, so it swings back towards the body as well as dropping. The downward part equals the foot's horizontal reach from the hip, the lever arm. - Knee moves the foot almost purely horizontally. The shin hangs nearly vertically below the knee, so turning the knee swings the foot sideways along a near-horizontal arc. That last point has consequen

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: - A configuration is a vector of joint angles; forward kinematics maps it to the pose of a point of interest by composing one rigid transform per link. - Rotations live in SO(3) (R^ R = I, R = 1); poses live in SE(3) and chain by matrix multiplication. - The tripod's leg is yaw–pitch–pitch: a yaw that turns a vertical plane, inside which a two-link arm reaches an annulus between 12 m and 44 m, trimmed by joint limits. - The hand-built chain, the closed form and the product of exponentials all agree with MuJoCo to within the precision of the model file. - Differentiating FK gives the Jacobian,
