chunks.text: - K. M. Lynch and F. C. Park, Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control (Cambridge, 2017), chapters 3–4. Free online, and the clearest treatment of the product of exponentials. - B. Siciliano, L. Sciavicco, L. Villani and G. Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control (Springer, 2009), chapter 2, for the DH convention. - The MuJoCo documentation, "Computation" and "XML reference" chapters, for how bodies, joints and the free-joint quaternion are laid out.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Second of four explainers behind The Martian Tripod. Part 1 built the forward map from joint angles to foot position, p = f( q). Every gait needs the reverse: the planner decides where the feet and the hood should be, and something has to turn that into joint angles. That is inverse kinematics (IK): solve f( q) = p^ for q. FK always has exactly one answer. IK can have none (the target is out of reach), several (the leg can bend either way), or infinitely many (the robot has more joints than the task needs). This post works through each case on the tripod.

chunks.heading: Divide and conquer: the yaw first
chunks.text: The tripod's leg is yaw, then pitch, then pitch. The yaw turns a vertical plane; the hip and knee then work entirely inside that plane. So the 3-D problem splits in two. 1. Express the target in the hip's own frame (undo the hood's pose, the mount offset and the mount's azimuth), giving (x, y, z). 2. The leg's plane must contain the target, so the yaw is [equation] and within that plane the foot must reach horizontal distance = {x^2 + y^2} and height z. 3. Solve the planar two-link problem for (qh, qk).

chunks.heading: Divide and conquer: the yaw first
chunks.text: Step 2 already hides a choice. + with reach - points the plane the other way and reaches back through the body. It is a valid solution of the equations, but it is far outside the yaw limit of ±0.8 rad, so it is discarded. Step 2 also has a singularity: when the target is directly below the hip ( = 0), every yaw works. A tripod never puts its foot there, but a humanoid's hip faces exactly this problem when the foot passes under it.

chunks.heading: The planar two-link problem
chunks.text: Put the hip at the origin and the foot target at (, z), a distance d = {^2 + z^2} away. The thigh, the shin and the line from hip to foot make a triangle with sides L1, L2 and d. The law of cosines gives the angle at the knee, and so the knee bend (the shin's direction relative to the thigh's): A solution exists only if -1 1, that is |L1 - L2| d L1 + L2: the reachable annulus from part 1. When it exists there are two solutions, , mirror images across the hip–foot line. The thigh's elevation 1 is then the direction to the foot, corrected by the angle between the thigh and that line:

chunks.heading: The planar two-link problem
chunks.text: The second term is the angle at the hip in the hip–knee–foot triangle. Writing it with {atan2} rather than an keeps the right sign for both branches and stays accurate near the edge of reach. Finally the joint angles are qh = -1 and qk = -(2 - 1), using part 1's convention that a positive rotation about +y swings a link downward. Geometrically the knee must lie on a circle of radius L1 round the hip and on a circle of radius L2 round the foot. Two circles cross in zero, one or two points, which is the whole existence-and-uniqueness story in one picture. The joint limits then choose between the

chunks.heading: Checking it everywhere
chunks.text: A closed-form IK should invert FK exactly wherever a solution exists. Throwing 50,000 random targets at it, in and out of the annulus, tests every branch of the code. Every reachable target round-trips to rounding error, and every unreachable one is reported as such. Most of the geometrically reachable points in this square, about three in five, need a joint beyond its limit. They are behind the hip, above it, or curled under it. So a real IK solver must check limits as well as reach.

chunks.heading: Singularities: where IK becomes ill-conditioned
chunks.text: At the edge of reach, d L1 + L2, the leg is straight and the two branches merge. The knee angle depends on d through an arccos, whose derivative is infinite at 1: Near a straight leg, moving the foot a centimetre outward demands a large knee rotation. Past the rim it demands an impossible one. That is a kinematic singularity, and it is the same thing as the Jacobian losing rank (part 3 computes J = \,L1L2 qk). It matters in practice: a controller that tracks a foot target near full reach will command huge joint velocities.

chunks.heading: Singularities: where IK becomes ill-conditioned
chunks.text: Standing, the leg is at 75% of full reach and well conditioned: about 4° of knee per metre of foot travel. Reared up to look round, it is at 89% of reach and the sensitivity is up by a third. The steep part of the curve is not far beyond. That is one reason the machine in the main post's video stops to rear up rather than walking tall.

chunks.heading: Whole-body IK: posing the hood
chunks.text: A walking machine rarely thinks about one foot at a time. With all three feet planted, the question is: where can the hood go? Give the hood a pose (position p{hood} and orientation R{hood}), keep the feet fixed, and solve IK for each leg separately. Each leg sees its foot target transformed into its own hip frame, which is the project's footik. The hood's pose has six degrees of freedom and the three legs have nine joints between them, but with the three feet pinned (nine constraints) the nine joints are fully determined by the six numbers of the hood pose.

chunks.heading: Whole-body IK: posing the hood
chunks.text: The legs form a parallel mechanism, like a flight simulator's Stewart platform. In a serial arm, FK is easy and IK is hard; in a parallel mechanism it is the other way round. Here, IK of the hood is just three independent leg IKs.

chunks.heading: Whole-body IK: posing the hood
chunks.text: The useful question is which hood poses are feasible: every foot within reach and every joint within its limits. Three different limits shape the region. At the standing height it is a rounded triangle set by the yaw limits: move the hood too far sideways and some leg has to swing more than 46° from its radial direction. The region is the same from about 20 m to 30 m. Above that, reach takes over and the region shrinks fast, from about 720 m² at 30 m to 230 m² at 38 m: a tall machine can lean less far before a leg runs out of length.

chunks.heading: Whole-body IK: posing the hood
chunks.text: Below about 20 m, the knee and hip limits start to cut pieces out of it as the legs fold up (the green outline at 16 m). Notice too that the region pokes outside the support triangle. Kinematically the hood can lean beyond its feet; whether it stays up is a question of statics and dynamics, taken up in parts 3 and 4. The planning explainer moves the centre of mass several metres from side to side every step, and this map shows how much room it has to do so.

chunks.heading: Numerical IK: Newton's method on the Jacobian
chunks.text: The closed form works because this leg is simple. A general chain, such as a seven-joint arm or a humanoid with a flexible spine, usually has no closed form, and IK is solved numerically. The workhorse is Newton's method. Linearise FK about the current guess using the Jacobian J = f/ q: and choose the step that zeroes the error e = p^ - f( q): Near a singularity J^{-1} explodes. When the target is unreachable it doesn't exist at all. The standard fix is damped least squares, also called Levenberg–Marquardt.

chunks.heading: Numerical IK: Newton's method on the Jacobian
chunks.text: It minimises \|J q - e\|^2 + ^2\| q\|^2, which gives The damping trades accuracy for step size. Far from singularities it behaves like Newton. Near one, it refuses to take huge steps and settles for the closest point it can reach. A third, cruder option is the Jacobian transpose step, q = J^ e. It never inverts anything and always moves downhill on \| e\|^2, but it converges slowly.

chunks.heading: Numerical IK: Newton's method on the Jacobian
chunks.text: Newton converges quadratically: once it is close, the number of correct digits roughly doubles each iteration, which is the plunge in the left panel. From this guess it recovers the closed-form joint angles exactly. From a different guess, with the hip raised and the knee nearly straight, it converges just as fast to the knee-down branch, which breaks the joint limits. Numerical IK finds a solution, usually the one nearest the starting guess, and knows nothing about branches or limits unless they are added. That is why walking controllers warm-start it from the previous timestep's answer.

chunks.heading: Numerical IK: Newton's method on the Jacobian
chunks.text: With the target out of reach, Newton has nothing to converge to, and its steps blow up near the straight-leg singularity. Damped least squares with enough damping does what you would want: it straightens the leg towards the target and stops exactly 5 m short. With too little damping it can stall at a bent-knee configuration, where the error is perpendicular to every direction the foot can move: a local minimum of \| e\|^2. Choosing is a real engineering decision, and practical solvers adapt it as they go. Every serious IK library uses some form of damping for this reason.

chunks.heading: Moving the foot: task space vs joint space
chunks.text: IK is rarely solved for one point; a swing leg needs a whole path. There are two ways to get from the lift-off configuration to the touch-down one. - Interpolate the joints: blend the joint angles from start to finish. This is cheap and smooth for the motors, but the foot traces whatever curve FK makes of it. - Interpolate the foot: design the foot's path in space (the gait uses a smooth forward motion plus a -shaped lift), and solve IK at every instant. For a walking machine the foot's path is what matters: it must clear obstacles and must not scuff the ground.

chunks.heading: Moving the foot: task space vs joint space
chunks.text: So the gaits in the main post plan in task space and call IK at every control step, a few hundred times a second. Closed-form IK is cheap enough for that. A numerical solver warm-started from the last step converges in one or two Newton iterations.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: - IK solves f( q) = p^. It may have no solution, a finite number, or a continuum. - The tripod's leg decouples: yaw by {atan2}, then a planar two-link problem solved by the law of cosines, with two mirror-image branches; the joint limits pick the knee-up one. - Near full reach the solution becomes ill-conditioned: a kinematic singularity, where the Jacobian loses rank. - Hood poses are found by three independent leg IKs, because the planted legs form a parallel mechanism. The feasible region shrinks as the hood rises. - Numerical IK uses Newton's method on the Jacobian; damped least squares ke

chunks.heading: Further reading
chunks.text: - K. M. Lynch and F. C. Park, Modern Robotics (2017), chapter 6 (inverse kinematics). - S. R. Buss, "Introduction to inverse kinematics with Jacobian transpose, pseudoinverse and damped least squares methods" (2004). A short, clear survey of the numerical methods. - C. W. Wampler, "Manipulator inverse kinematic solutions based on vector formulations and damped least-squares methods", IEEE Trans. SMC (1986). The origin of damped least squares in robotics.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: This is the third of four explainers behind Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar's Black Hole: 1. Bending light around a black hole: null geodesics, the photon sphere, and the exact deflection angle. 2. Ray tracing a black hole: cameras, celestial spheres, Einstein rings and multiple images. 3. The Kerr black hole (this post): spin, frame dragging and the D-shaped shadow. 4. Light from the disk: orbits, temperature, redshift and Doppler beaming. Gargantua spins. In the story it spins within a whisker of the maximum, which is what makes an hour on Miller's planet cost seven years on Earth.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Spin breaks the spherical symmetry that made part 2 so economical: a ray no longer stays in one plane, and no single function of one angle describes the image. This post sets up the equations that DNGR, the code behind Interstellar, actually integrated, builds a ray tracer from them, and checks it against the few results for a spinning hole that are known exactly.

chunks.heading: The Kerr metric
chunks.text: Roy Kerr found the spacetime of a spinning black hole in 1963. In Boyer–Lindquist coordinates (t, r, , ), with G = c = M = 1 and spin parameter a = J/M (the angular momentum per unit mass, 0 a 0, out to r = 1 + {1 - a^2^2}. Inside the ergosphere frame dragging is so strong that nothing can stay still relative to the distant stars. Everything there is swept round with the hole.

chunks.heading: Observers who do not rotate
chunks.text: Which observer should hold the camera? Near a spinning hole there are no static observers inside the ergosphere, and outside it they are not the natural choice either. The natural one is the zero-angular-momentum observer (ZAMO), the "fiducial observer" or FIDO of the DNGR paper. It moves on the line = t + {const}, carried round by frame dragging but with no angular momentum of its own. Its orthonormal basis vectors point along the coordinate lines: Any real camera moves relative to the local ZAMO with some velocity , and its view is the ZAMO's view, aberrated as in part 2.

chunks.heading: Three constants for a light ray
chunks.text: In Schwarzschild spacetime a ray has energy E and angular momentum L, and spherical symmetry supplies the rest. The Kerr metric is independent of t and , which again gives E = -pt and Lz = p. But it is only axially symmetric, so total angular momentum is no longer conserved, and two constants are not enough to determine a path in three dimensions. In 1968 Brandon Carter found a third. Write the Hamilton–Jacobi equation for null geodesics, and try S = -Et + Lz + Sr(r) + S().

chunks.heading: Three constants for a light ray
chunks.text: With E = 1 (so that b = Lz/E is the axial impact parameter), the inverse Kerr metric turns the equation into The left side depends only on r and the right side only on , so both equal a constant, -q. That separability is the hidden symmetry of the Kerr metric, and q is the Carter constant (divided by E^2). The radial and polar motions then decouple: A ray can only be where R 0 and 0. A ray that crosses the equator has q 0, and q = 0 means a ray confined to the equatorial plane.

chunks.heading: The ray equations
chunks.text: Integrating pr = R/ directly runs into trouble at every turning point, where the square root changes sign. DNGR instead integrated Hamilton's equations for the super-Hamiltonian H = 12 g^{}p p, which handle turning points smoothly. With pt = -1 and p = b fixed, and Hamilton's equations, x = H/ p and p = - H/ x, give the five equations that are the heart of the renderer: These are equations (A.15) of the DNGR paper. The combination $(R + )/ = P^2/ - (b-a)^2 - ^2\,(b^2/^2 - a^2) does not involve q at all, so q$ is never used during integration. Its conservation is therefore a genuine test of the

chunks.heading: Initial conditions from a pixel
chunks.text: The camera supplies a direction. A pixel's unit vector N (from camera to sky) in the camera frame becomes, for the arriving photon, a propagation direction n = - N. Aberration converts it to the ZAMO frame, giving nF. The photon's energy measured by the ZAMO is then These satisfy H = 0 automatically. The ray is then integrated backwards, -, until it escapes, reaches the horizon, or hits the disk.

chunks.heading: The integrator
chunks.text: The tracer (kerr.trace) is a Dormand–Prince 5(4) Runge–Kutta integrator with adaptive steps. It is compiled with numba and runs one ray per thread. Steps are small where the ray bends sharply near the hole and long far away. A ray that crosses the equator inside the disk's radius is stopped there, the crossing located to 10^{-10} in by secant iteration (part 4). Here it traces the rays of one image of a fast-spinning hole and checks the constants it is not told about: The Carter constant, which the equations never use, is conserved to {python} f"{dqmax:.0e}" or better along every ray, through

chunks.heading: Photon orbits
chunks.text: A Schwarzschild hole has one photon sphere. A Kerr hole has a whole shell of spherical photon orbits: rays that stay at constant r while oscillating in and winding round the axis. They exist where R(r) = 0 and R'(r) = 0 at once, which fixes the two constants as functions of the radius (Bardeen 1973; equations (A.5) of DNGR): for r between the prograde and retrograde equatorial photon orbits, These orbits are all unstable. A ray launched exactly onto one stays there only as long as rounding error allows, and then peels off exponentially.

chunks.heading: Photon orbits
chunks.text: The tracer shows both behaviours: The deviation from the orbit grows by a factor of about {python} f"{growth:.0f}" with every turn round the axis. This is the Kerr version of the winding rays of part 1, and the DNGR paper pictures one such orbit (their Figure 11). Rays that pass close to this shell are what pile up the multiple images near the shadow's edge.

chunks.heading: The shadow
chunks.text: The edge of the shadow is made of rays that, followed backwards, approach a spherical photon orbit asymptotically. For a distant observer at inclination from the spin axis, each orbit radius r gives two points on the observer's sky (Bardeen 1973): in units of M. Here x runs in the direction of the hole's rotation and y along the projected spin axis. This curve is an exact, independent result, so it is the natural test of the ray tracer. The test is to place a camera very far away (r = 10^5 M) and bisect, along rays out from the shadow's centre, for the boundary between captured and escaping ra

chunks.heading: The shadow
chunks.text: This flattened edge is why Interstellar did not show Gargantua at its story spin. Christopher Nolan and Paul Franklin judged that the flattened shadow, with the multiple disk images along it and an off-centre disk, would confuse a mass audience. For the pictures they turned the spin down to a = 0.6, where the shadow is still almost round (part 4 and the main post).

chunks.heading: The camera's motion matters as much as the spin
chunks.text: Close to a fast-spinning hole, the choice of camera changes the picture more than anything else. The DNGR paper makes this point with a checkerboard sky seen from r = 2.6\,M around a hole with a = 0.999, inside the photon region and just outside the ergosphere, by three cameras at the same point: - one on a prograde circular orbit; - one at rest relative to the local ZAMO; - one static relative to the distant stars, which takes a rocket working very hard against frame dragging.

chunks.heading: The camera's motion matters as much as the spin
chunks.text: The speeds match the DNGR paper's figures exactly: relative to the orbiting camera, the ZAMO moves at {python} f"{borb:.3f}"c and the static camera at {python} f"{relstatic:.3f}"c (the paper gives 0.546c and 0.813c). The static camera, racing backwards against the hole's rotation, sees the shadow swell to cover more than half its sky. The orbiting camera sees it shrink. Yet the pattern of images, how many copies of each piece of sky appear and where the critical curves fall, is the same for all three. The caustics belong to the light cone at that point, not to whoever is looking.

chunks.heading: Stars round a spinning hole
chunks.text: The DNGR paper's first image of a spinning hole (their Figure 4) is a star field seen from a camera in a circular equatorial orbit at rc = 6.03\,M around a hole with a = 0.999. Here is the same configuration, with this renderer's synthetic sky: a mip-mapped Milky Way and 30,000 point stars lensed by the triangle method of part 2. With a spinning hole there is nothing left to tabulate, so every pixel is a full geodesic integration. On a laptop with numba that takes seconds for an image of a few million rays. DNGR rendered 23-million-pixel IMAX frames with ray bundles, at 30 minutes to several h

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: This is the first of four explainers behind Gargantua: Rebuilding Interstellar's Black Hole. That post renders the black hole from Interstellar, with and without the Doppler shifts the film left out. These explainers work through the mathematics it rests on: 1. Bending light around a black hole (this post): how a non-spinning black hole deflects a light ray, and why it casts a shadow. 2. Ray tracing a black hole: how to turn that deflection into a picture: cameras, celestial spheres, Einstein rings and multiple images. 3. The Kerr black hole: what spin adds: frame dragging, the Carter constant

chunks.heading: The Schwarzschild metric
chunks.text: In 1916, a few weeks after Einstein published his field equations, Karl Schwarzschild found their solution outside a spherical, non-rotating mass M. In coordinates (t, r, , ) the spacetime interval is The radius r is defined so that a sphere at r has area 4 r^2, and t is the time kept by a clock at rest far away. The metric becomes singular at the Schwarzschild radius rs = 2GM/c^2. That singularity is a feature of the coordinates, not of spacetime, but the sphere at rs is real: it is the event horizon, from inside which nothing escapes.

chunks.heading: The Schwarzschild metric
chunks.text: From here on we use geometrised units, G = c = 1, and measure lengths in units of M (strictly GM/c^2). The metric is then and the horizon is at r = 2. To convert back, multiply lengths by GM/c^2: In the film, Gargantua has a mass of 100 million Suns, so one unit of length is about 1.5 × 10⁸ km, which is roughly the distance from the Earth to the Sun.

chunks.heading: Light rays are null geodesics
chunks.text: A free particle follows a geodesic, a path of extremal proper time. A geodesic x^() extremises the action of the Lagrangian where is an affine parameter along the path. For light the interval vanishes, g{} x^ x^ = 0, so a light ray is a null geodesic. The Schwarzschild metric depends on neither t nor , so the Euler–Lagrange equations for those coordinates give two conserved quantities: E is the photon's energy as measured at infinity, and L is its angular momentum about the axis. Spherical symmetry lets us choose the orbital plane to be the equator, = /2.

chunks.heading: Light rays are null geodesics
chunks.text: The null condition is then Rescaling the affine parameter rescales E and L together, so only their ratio matters for the shape of a ray. That ratio is the impact parameter which, far from the hole, is the perpendicular distance between the incoming ray and a parallel line through the centre. Dividing by L^2, This is a one-dimensional problem. A ray coming in from infinity moves inwards while 1/b^2 > V(r) and turns round where 1/b^2 = V(r).

chunks.heading: The photon sphere and the critical impact parameter
chunks.text: V(r) has a single maximum. Setting V'(r) = -2/r^3 + 6/r^4 = 0 gives At r = 3M, the photon sphere, light can travel on a circular orbit, an unstable one, balanced on top of the potential. A ray with spirals in towards that orbit forever. This splits all incoming rays into two families: - b > 3 3: the ray meets the potential barrier, turns round at a radius r0 > 3, and escapes back to infinity. - b < 3 3: the ray passes over the barrier and falls through the horizon. The turning point r0 and the impact parameter are related by 1/b^2 = V(r0), that is and inverting this means solving the cubic r0^

chunks.heading: The photon sphere and the critical impact parameter
chunks.text: The consequence for a picture is immediate. Look towards the hole from far away: every line of sight with impact parameter less than 33\,M ends on the horizon, so the hole appears as a black disk of radius which is more than two and a half times the size of the horizon itself. This dark disk is the black hole's shadow. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope imaged the ring of light around the shadow of M87. For its mass and distance the formula predicts an angular diameter of which is close to the 42 ± 3 µas ring the collaboration reported. (The ring of emission sits slightly outside the shadow's

chunks.heading: The orbit equation
chunks.text: To get the shape of a ray, trade the affine parameter for the angle . Using = L/r^2 and u = 1/r, Without the right-hand side this is the equation of a straight line, u = / b. The term 3u^2 (in ordinary units 3GMu^2/c^2) is all of the bending. It is the same correction that makes Mercury's orbit precess, here acting on a particle with no rest mass. Integrating it for a fan of parallel incoming rays shows the whole story at once:

chunks.heading: The exact deflection angle
chunks.text: A ray from infinity that turns round at u0 = 1/r0 sweeps out an angle 0^{u0} du/{P(u)} on the way in and the same on the way out. A straight line would sweep exactly , so the deflection is Two ways to evaluate this are worth having, because each checks the other. Quadrature. The integrand blows up like (u0 - u)^{-1/2} at the turning point. The substitution u = u0 - s^2 removes this, since du = -2s\,ds and {P} s{-P'(u0)}, which leaves a smooth integrand for adaptive quadrature.

chunks.heading: The exact deflection angle
chunks.text: Elliptic integrals. P(u) is a cubic, 2(u - u1)(u - u2)(u - u3), with roots u1 33. A standard reduction (Byrd and Friedman, formula 233.00) gives, for any starting point y, where F is the incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind. With y = 0 this is half the swept angle, in closed form. The two agree to {python} f"{maxdiff:.0e}" radians over the whole range, from rays that graze the photon sphere to rays that pass 10^4\,M away.

chunks.heading: Far from the hole: Einstein's 1.75 arcseconds
chunks.text: For b 1, expanding the integral in powers of 1/b gives Restoring units, the leading term is = 4GM/(c^2 b), twice what you get by treating light as a Newtonian particle, because space is curved as well as time. For a ray grazing the Sun this is which is the deflection the 1919 eclipse expeditions led by Eddington and Dyson set out to measure.

chunks.heading: Close to the photon sphere: winding without limit
chunks.text: As b bc from above, the turning point approaches the photon sphere and the ray winds round it more and more times. Near the critical value the deflection diverges logarithmically. Bozza (2002) derived the strong-field limit The coefficient of the logarithm, exactly 1 for Schwarzschild, carries a physical meaning. Each extra half-turn round the hole adds to . To add , the distance from the critical value, b - bc, must shrink by a factor of e^{-} 0.0432. Solving (b) = n exactly confirms it: The ratio settles to {python} f"{ratiolast:.4f}", against e^{-} = 0.0432.

chunks.heading: Close to the photon sphere: winding without limit
chunks.text: The rate = at which neighbouring rays peel away from the photon sphere is its Lyapunov exponent per half-orbit. The same number reappears in a picture: next to the shadow's edge sits a stack of ever-thinner rings, the second, third and later images of the whole sky, each about 23 times thinner than the last. Only the first one or two are ever visible, but they are there.

chunks.heading: Where this leaves us
chunks.text: For a non-spinning hole, everything a renderer needs is now in hand: - rays with b 33\,M escape, deflected by the exact (b) above; - near the critical value, rays wind round the photon sphere, which gives infinite sequences of images packed against the shadow's edge. What is missing is the camera. These formulas describe rays from infinity seen from infinity, while Interstellar's camera sits a few dozen M from the hole, and possibly moves. The next explainer puts the camera in place and turns (b) into images.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: This is the first of three short refreshers behind two earlier posts — Reproducing a Phase Transition in Diffusion Models and Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models — both of which lean on ideas from Sclocchi, Favero & Wyart (2024) [@sclocchi2024phase] that are easy to gloss over if you haven't seen them recently. This one covers Markov chains; the next two cover mean-field analysis and the generative diffusion process itself.

chunks.heading: What makes a process "Markov"
chunks.text: A process is Markov if its next state depends only on its current state — not on the path that got it there. Formally, P(x{t+1} xt, x{t-1}, , x0) = P(x{t+1} xt). That's it; the entire history collapses into whatever's true right now. A simple weather model makes this concrete: three states, and a transition matrix giving the probability of tomorrow's weather given today's. The same transition matrix, drawn as a state diagram, makes the "only today matters" structure visually explicit — every arrow starts from a single current state, with no memory of how the chain got there: Knowing today is S

chunks.heading: Where does it settle? Two ways to find out
chunks.text: Run the chain long enough and the fraction of time spent in each state converges to a fixed stationary distribution , satisfying P = — a left eigenvector of P with eigenvalue 1. Two independent ways to find it should agree: Eigenvector: Sunny , Cloudy , Rainy . A long simulated path lands close to the same numbers — the chain has "forgotten" where it started and settled into its long-run behaviour. This idea — a distribution that's a fixed point of an update rule — will come back in the next post, where a self-consistency equation plays exactly the same role.

chunks.heading: Why an eigenvector, and how `eigen()` actually gets it
chunks.text: The stationary condition P = treats as a row vector multiplying P from the left — a left eigenvector of P with eigenvalue 1. Transposing both sides turns it into an ordinary right-eigenvector problem: P^ ^ = ^. That's why the code above calls eigen(t(P)) rather than eigen(P) — R's eigen() only ever returns right eigenvectors, so finding a left eigenvector of P means first transposing. An eigenvalue-1 solution is guaranteed to exist. Every row of P sums to 1, so P{1} = {1}: the all-ones vector is a right eigenvector of P with eigenvalue 1.

chunks.heading: Why an eigenvector, and how `eigen()` actually gets it
chunks.text: P and P^ share the same eigenvalues (they have the same characteristic polynomial, since (P^ - I) = ((P - I)^) = (P - I)), so 1 is also an eigenvalue of P^ — guaranteeing a satisfying P = exists, though not automatically that it's unique or non-negative (that extra guarantee comes from Perron–Frobenius, since every entry of P here is strictly positive).

chunks.heading: Why an eigenvector, and how `eigen()` actually gets it
chunks.text: Under the hood, eigen() finds all three eigenvalues of P^ as the roots of (P^ - I) = 0, then for each eigenvalue finds a vector spanning the null space of (P^ - I) — solved numerically via matrix decomposition rather than by hand, but conceptually just "solve (P^ - I)v = 0." Doing that null-space step explicitly for = 1, independently of eigen()'s eigenvector output, should recover the same up to scale: eig$values shows one eigenvalue at 1 and two others strictly smaller in modulus — consistent with the all-ones-vector argument above and with a unique stationary distribution.

chunks.heading: Why an eigenvector, and how `eigen()` actually gets it
chunks.text: A has rank out of 3, meaning (P^ - I)$ has a 1-dimensional null space — exactly one free direction, which svd() extracts as the singular vector paired with a (numerically) zero singular value. pimanual matches pistat from eigen() up to floating-point noise, since both are just different numerical routes to the same null space.

chunks.heading: Why an eigenvector, and how `eigen()` actually gets it
chunks.text: Those two smaller eigenvalues aren't wasted information either: the second-largest one in modulus governs how fast the chain forgets its starting state and converges to — larger gap to 1, faster mixing. That's a thread this post won't pull further, but it's the same kind of "look at the eigenvalues away from the fixed point" reasoning that shows up when analyzing stability in the mean-field post next.

chunks.heading: DDPM's actual Markov chain
chunks.text: Diffusion models run a Markov chain too, just with a continuous state and Gaussian transition kernels rather than a lookup table. Forward and reverse processes run along the same chain of latents x0, x1, , xT, in opposite directions: Each xt is a latent variable — same shape as the data (an image's pixel array, say), but not itself an observed data point except at the two ends of the chain. x0 is a real, clean data sample; xT is (by construction, after enough steps) indistinguishable from pure Gaussian noise; everything in between, x1, , x{T-1}, is a progressively noisier, unobserved intermedi

chunks.heading: DDPM's actual Markov chain
chunks.text: "Latent" here just means: a random variable in the model that generative code manipulates and a network learns to reverse, but that's never seen directly in the training data. The subscript t indexes position along the chain (equivalently, how much noise has accumulated), not real time.

chunks.heading: DDPM's actual Markov chain
chunks.text: The forward (noising) process is fixed by construction, defined, exactly as in Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) [@ho2020denoising], by: Each step nudges x{t-1} slightly toward the origin and adds a little Gaussian noise, with controlling how much. This is precisely the recurrence used in guideddiffusion/gaussiandiffusion.py, the codebase reproduced in the diffusion-phase-transition post. (0, 1) is the noise schedule — a small, hand-chosen number per step (Ho et al.'s schedule ramps it linearly from 10^{-4} at t=1 to 0.02 at t=T) fixing how much variance gets injected at step t.

chunks.heading: DDPM's actual Markov chain
chunks.text: It's not learned; it's a fixed hyperparameter sequence chosen before training even starts. := 1 - is just a convenient rename — close to 1 when is small — so that the update reads xt = {}\, x{t-1} + {1-}\,: shrink the previous state slightly, add noise to make up the variance budget. Their product across steps, := {s t} , is what actually appears in the closed-form jump below — it tracks how much of the original signal x0 survives after t compounded steps, and it's what decays toward 0 as t T in @fig-gaussian-chain, driving xt toward pure {N}(0, I) noise.

chunks.heading: The closed-form jump
chunks.text: Simulating 1000 sequential steps every time you need a noisy sample would be wasteful, and because each step's kernel is Gaussian, it's also unnecessary: the composition of t Gaussian steps is itself Gaussian, in closed form: You can jump straight from x0 to any xt in one draw. This is exactly qsample in the reproduced code, and it's what makes the "forward-diffuse-partway-then-reverse" experiment in the diffusion-phase-transition post practical on real images. Worth actually checking it's true rather than taking it on faith: At t=, 200,000 step-by-step Monte Carlo draws give mean and variance

chunks.heading: The reverse chain
chunks.text: The reverse process p(x{t-1} xt) is modelled the same way — Markov, approximately Gaussian for small — but its mean isn't known in closed form for real data; that's what a neural network is trained to approximate. The next explainer is a detour into a different piece of machinery this paper needs (mean-field analysis); the third comes back to build a toy reverse chain where, unusually, the right answer is known exactly.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Second of three short refreshers behind Reproducing a Phase Transition in Diffusion Models and Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models. The first covered Markov chains; read it first only if that material feels unfamiliar — this one stands alone.

chunks.heading: The problem mean-field theory solves
chunks.text: A ferromagnet is a lattice of interacting spins: each one wants to align with its neighbours, but the neighbours are themselves fluctuating, coupled to their neighbours, and so on. Tracking the full joint distribution over every spin is intractable for anything but tiny systems. The mean-field trick: replace each spin's actual, fluctuating neighbours with their average value. A many-body problem becomes a single spin sitting in an effective field set by everybody else's average behaviour — and that's tractable, at the cost of ignoring fluctuation correlations between neighbours. Sclocchi et al

chunks.heading: Curie-Weiss, derived
chunks.text: Give each spin z neighbours, coupling strength J, at inverse temperature . Averaging over its neighbours' fluctuations, a spin's effective field is proportional to the mean magnetization m, and self-consistency (the average spin must reproduce the magnetization that produced its own field) gives: Folding , J, z into the single parameter K is the standard textbook reduction — the actual critical temperature is = 1/(Jz), i.e. K=1 exactly. Below K=1 the only solution is m=0 (paramagnetic: no net alignment); above it, two new nonzero solutions appear (ferromagnetic: spontaneous alignment, sign cho

chunks.heading: Solving it
chunks.text: m=0 satisfies (K 0) = 0 for every K — it's always a trivial root, present whether or not the interesting nonzero one exists. Searching for the nonzero branch means excluding it explicitly: bracket uniroot away from zero. Below K=1, only m=0; above it, a genuine phase transition. Three independent checks on the nonzero branch agree: at K=2, uniroot gives m=, and simply iterating m (2m) a thousand times from m=0.5 converges to — the same fixed point found two different ways. Near the critical point, mean-field theory predicts m {3(K-1)}; at K=1.01 that asymptotic gives against uniroot's — agreem

chunks.heading: The same move, in belief propagation
chunks.text: The Random Hierarchy Model's disordered production rules play the role of the Ising model's disordered neighbour spins. Tracking every possible realization of the hierarchy's rules exactly is just as intractable as tracking every spin's actual neighbours. Sclocchi et al. take the identical shortcut: average over the ensemble of rule realizations (the "annealed" approximation) rather than conditioning on one specific (quenched) realization, and a complicated random recursion collapses into the single deterministic belief-propagation map already implemented and solved in Fixed Points, Phase Tran

chunks.heading: The same move, in belief propagation
chunks.text: That post doesn't re-derive the annealed approximation; this is the missing piece that justifies why F(p) is allowed to be written down as a plain deterministic function at all. The same self-consistency structure — and the same {K-1}-type critical scaling — also shows up throughout my own dissertation on renormalization-group critical phenomena, where the RG fixed point plays the role K=1 plays here.

chunks.heading: What's next
chunks.text: The final post in this series builds a complete toy diffusion model from scratch — forward noising, the score function, and exact reverse sampling — using the closed-form Markov chain from the first post.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Third of four explainers behind The Martian Tripod. Part 1 found where the foot is; part 2 found the joint angles that put it there. Both were pure geometry. This part brings in force. The machine weighs 257 tonnes and stands on three point feet, so how hard must each motor push? One matrix answers that: the Jacobian, the derivative of forward kinematics. It maps joint velocities to foot velocity, and its transpose maps foot forces back to joint torques. This post derives it for the tripod's leg, checks it against MuJoCo, and then uses it to explain the spider-like stance. It ends by sharing t

chunks.heading: Velocity kinematics
chunks.text: Forward kinematics gives the foot position as a function of the joints, p = f( q). Differentiate with respect to time: J is the Jacobian. For the tripod's leg it is 33: three joints in, three components of foot velocity out. Column j is the foot's velocity when joint j alone turns at 1 rad/s. Part 1 gave the foot in the leg's own plane, horizontal reach and height z relative to the hip, in terms of the elevation angles 1 = -qh and 2 = -(qh + qk): The yaw turns that plane about the vertical, so with = ai + (mount azimuth plus yaw) the foot is at (,\ ,\ z) relative to the hip. Differentiating te

chunks.heading: Velocity kinematics
chunks.text: The first column is the yaw: it moves the foot round a horizontal circle of radius . The other two act within the leg's plane. MuJoCo computes Jacobians for any point on any body (mjjac, mjjacSite). Here they are side by side for all three legs in the standing pose. The analytic Jacobian matches MuJoCo's. Leg 0 agrees to machine precision; the others differ only by the six-figure rounding of their mount angles noted in part 1. For legs 1 and 2 the same numbers appear, rotated by 120° and 240°.

chunks.heading: Singularities
chunks.text: The Jacobian is invertible except where its determinant vanishes. Expanding along the bottom row and simplifying gives a compact result: There are three ways to lose a degree of freedom. - = 0: the foot is directly below the yaw axis, and turning the yaw does nothing. This is the yaw singularity from part 2. - qk = 0: the leg is straight. Hip and knee then both move the foot perpendicular to the leg, and nothing can move it along the leg. This is the edge of reach. - qk = : the leg is folded back on itself. The joint limits rule this out.

chunks.heading: Velocity and force ellipsoids
chunks.text: Push unit-speed joint motions, \|{ q}\| = 1, through J and the foot velocities fill an ellipsoid. Its axes are the singular vectors of J, and its semi-axis lengths are the singular values. This is the manipulability ellipsoid. Where it is long the foot moves fast; where it is thin the leg is close to a singularity in that direction. Forces behave in the opposite way. As derived below, a foot force f needs joint torques = J^ f. The foot forces that unit joint torques can produce, \|\| = 1, form the force ellipsoid f^(JJ^) f = 1. It has the same axes, with reciprocal lengths. A direction in whic

chunks.heading: Virtual work: τ = Jᵀf
chunks.text: Now the key result. Suppose the ground pushes on the foot with force f, and the leg is in equilibrium, held there by joint torques . Imagine a tiny joint displacement q. The foot moves p = J\, q. In equilibrium the total work done in any such virtual displacement is zero. The work the motors do equals the work done against the ground: This is the principle of virtual work. It needs no free-body diagrams, no reaction forces at the joints and no geometry beyond the Jacobian already computed.

chunks.heading: Virtual work: τ = Jᵀf
chunks.text: Each row of J^ f is a dot product: joint j's torque is the foot force projected onto the direction joint j moves the foot. For a hinge, Jj = ( p - rj), so which is just the moment of the foot force about joint j's axis. That is the familiar lever law, recovered from the Jacobian.

chunks.heading: Adding the legs' own weight
chunks.text: The legs themselves are heavy: each weighs 28 t. Gravity on each part does work too, so each part contributes its own J^ term, using the Jacobian of its centre of mass: The sign follows the equations of motion, $M{ q} + c( q, { q}) = + J^ f. With everything at rest, the motor torque must cancel the gravity term g( q) and the ground force. MuJoCo calls the term c$ (gravity plus Coriolis and centrifugal terms, which vanish at rest) qfrcbias. The tripod's balance controller computes exactly this: bias - J.T @ force for every planted leg.

chunks.heading: The check: torques from measured contact forces
chunks.text: The strongest test is to let MuJoCo settle the standing machine and then measure the contact forces from its contact solver. Those are numbers the controller never sees directly. Then predict the joint torques from them with = g( q) - J^ f, and compare with what the motors are actually commanding. Prediction and simulation agree to every printed digit. The feet carry nearly pure vertical loads that add up to the machine's weight. Foot 0 carries a little less than the others because the centre of mass sits about 0.24 m behind the hood's centre, pulled back by the carrier basket.

chunks.heading: Why the spider stance
chunks.text: For a vertical foot load Fz the virtual-work formula gives a striking result. The yaw column has no vertical component, so the yaw torque is zero. The hip and knee torques come from the bottom row of J: Here is the foot's horizontal distance from the hip, and L22 is its horizontal distance from the knee. A joint's torque from a vertical load depends only on how far the foot is from it horizontally. The leg's shape doesn't matter, nor does its height or the angle of the thigh. The legs' own weight modifies this. It hangs on the inboard side of the foot and partly offsets the load, which is why

chunks.heading: Why the spider stance
chunks.text: This is why a heavy walker stands like a daddy long-legs (harvestman). The hip must sit 19.4 m inboard of the foot, because the feet must be spread wide for stability, so the hip carries a large torque whatever happens. But the knee can be put almost directly above the foot. Then the knee torque is nearly zero, and the shin becomes a column in compression. The hip torque map is a set of vertical bands: it depends only on . The knee map has a cool valley along the line where the knee sits above the foot.

chunks.heading: Why the spider stance
chunks.text: The standing pose sits near that valley, with the foot only 3.4 m horizontally from the knee. Statically the 40 MN·m motors could hold a third of the machine's weight with the foot anywhere out to 40/0.84 47 m from the hip, which is beyond reach. So standing is never torque-limited. The limit comes when walking. The motors have only about three times the standing hip torque in hand, and the main post found that the swing legs saturate once the gait is pushed much past 5–6 mph.

chunks.heading: Sharing the weight between three feet
chunks.text: So far each leg had its own foot force. Where do those come from? The machine as a whole must be in equilibrium. The ground forces f1, f2, f3 acting at the feet pi must balance the weight acting at the centre of mass c: where g = (0, 0, g). Stack the nine force components into one vector and these six equations become linear: G is the grasp matrix, a name borrowed from robot hands, where fingers share the job of holding an object. Here the "object" is the machine itself and the "fingers" are the ground contacts.

chunks.heading: Sharing the weight between three feet
chunks.text: Nine unknowns and six equations leave a three-dimensional null space. Those are the internal forces: combinations of foot forces that cancel exactly, adding no net force or moment. For three point feet they are pairs of feet pushing against each other, squeezing or stretching along each edge of the triangle.

chunks.heading: Sharing the weight between three feet
chunks.text: - The minimum-norm solution is the one MuJoCo found. It is purely vertical, with no internal squeeze. The project's controller solves the same least-squares problem (BodyController.distribute), with two extra conditions explained below. - The edge squeezes span the null space. Any amount of push-apart or pull-together along the three edges can be added without disturbing equilibrium. A real controller uses this freedom to keep the feet away from slipping, by pushing them inward so friction is not needed, or to reduce the hip torques. - Vertical loads are barycentric coordinates.

chunks.heading: Sharing the weight between three feet
chunks.text: For vertical forces, moment balance says the weighted average of the foot positions, weighted by each foot's share of the load, must equal the centre of mass's position over the ground. Those weights are exactly the barycentric coordinates of the centre of mass in the foot triangle. MuJoCo's measured shares match them to four figures. - The ground can push but not pull. A foot's vertical force must be positive, f{i,z} 0. Its sideways force must stay inside the friction cone, {f{i,x}^2 + f{i,y}^2} f{i,z}. These inequalities turn the least-squares problem into a constrained one. The controller h

chunks.heading: Unloading a foot
chunks.text: The barycentric picture explains how to take a step. Move the centre of mass towards the edge between two feet, and the third foot's barycentric coordinate, and so its load, falls linearly to zero. Once it is unloaded it can be lifted without the machine noticing. Go any further and it would have to pull: the machine tips.

chunks.heading: On two feet, the machine is a hinge
chunks.text: Lift a foot and G shrinks to 66, with just two feet. You might expect six equations and six unknowns to have a unique solution. But one combination is impossible: no pair of forces applied at two points can make a moment about the line through those points, since every such force either passes through the line or crosses it. G loses rank. The missing direction has no force part and a moment part along the line through the two feet: a pure moment about that line (the sign of a singular vector is arbitrary).

chunks.heading: On two feet, the machine is a hinge
chunks.text: Nothing the legs do can resist a tip about that line. Wherever the centre of mass is relative to it, the machine rotates about it freely, like a door on its hinges. The controller acknowledges this explicitly: on two feet it projects the hinge component out of the moment it asks for (the hinge argument of distribute) instead of fighting it. So a walking tripod is never in static equilibrium while a foot is in the air. It is always falling sideways about the hinge, and the next footfall has to catch it. Planning that fall is the subject of the final part.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: - The Jacobian J = f/ q maps joint velocities to foot velocity. For the tripod's leg, J = \,L1L2 qk. It is singular with the foot under the hip, with the leg straight, or with the leg folded. - Virtual work gives = J^ f. Velocity and force are dual: the leg moves fast in the directions where it pushes weakly. - With gravity, = g( q) - J^ f. This predicts MuJoCo's standing torques exactly, from contact forces measured in the simulation. - A vertical load costs torque in proportion to horizontal distance.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: So the knee sits above the foot, and the hip does the work. - Balance is a 69 linear system with a 3-D null space of internal forces. Vertical loads are the barycentric coordinates of the centre of mass. On two feet the system loses a rank: the hinge.

chunks.heading: Further reading
chunks.text: - K. M. Lynch and F. C. Park, Modern Robotics (2017), chapter 5 (velocity kinematics and statics) and chapter 12 (grasping and the grasp matrix). - R. M. Murray, Z. Li and S. S. Sastry, A Mathematical Introduction to Robotic Manipulation (CRC, 1994), chapter 5, for internal forces and friction cones. - T. Yoshikawa, "Manipulability of robotic mechanisms", International Journal of Robotics Research 4(2), 1985. The origin of the manipulability ellipsoid.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Third and final part of a series behind Reproducing a Phase Transition in Diffusion Models and Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models. This one assumes the first post's closed-form jump q(xt x0); the second is a self-contained detour and isn't needed here.

chunks.heading: Noising a whole distribution
chunks.text: The first post applied the forward chain to a single starting point, x0=2. Real data isn't a point, it's a distribution — so apply the same closed-form jump to a batch of samples instead. Take something with actual structure to destroy: a two-component mixture, two bumps at -2 and +2. By t=, mean and sd — the two bumps have merged into plain {N}(0,1), no trace of where they started.

chunks.heading: What a denoiser actually needs: the score
chunks.text: Reversing this requires knowing which direction "more like the data" is, at every noise level. That direction is the score, pt(x) — the gradient of the log-density of the noisy marginal at time t. Tweedie's formula relates it directly to the optimal denoiser: the best single-step estimate of the clean signal given a noisy xt is a simple function of the score. This is the modern way to think about what a diffusion model's network is trained to produce — not "the clean image" directly, but a time-indexed family of score estimates, one per noise level.

chunks.heading: The one case you don't need a network for
chunks.text: For almost any real data distribution, the score has no closed form and has to be learned. But a Gaussian mixture is a rare exception: convolving a Gaussian mixture with Gaussian noise gives another Gaussian mixture, so the noised marginal at every t — and hence its score — stays exactly computable: Checked against a numerical derivative of pt(x) at t=100, four test points: numeric gives , the closed form gives — matching to the precision shown.

chunks.heading: Reversing it, exactly
chunks.text: The ancestral-sampling reverse update, written in terms of the score: Ordinarily pt is what a trained network approximates. Here it's the closed form from the previous section — nothing learned, nothing approximate. Generation recovers both modes: mean/sd of the lower cluster / against a true -2/0.4, and the upper cluster / against a true 2/0.4. A two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test against the original data gives D=, p= — nowhere near rejecting "same distribution."

chunks.heading: What this stands in for
chunks.text: The diffusion-phase-transition post does exactly this same procedure — forward-diffuse partway, then reverse — but on real ImageNet images, with a trained U-Net standing in for the score computed here in closed form [@ho2020denoising]. The abrupt class-flip reported there is a direct consequence of how that (learned, not closed-form) score behaves across noise levels for hierarchically-structured data — the same mechanics as this toy, just with a far richer p0 than two Gaussian bumps [@sclocchi2024phase].

chunks.heading: Series wrap-up
chunks.text: Three explainers, one underlying machine: a Markov chain moves data toward noise and, run in reverse with the right score function, moves noise back toward data; mean-field/annealed averaging is how you get a tractable equation for when that reversal preserves the "shape" of the data versus loses it; and the toy model here makes both pieces concrete enough to check by hand. With all three in place, Reproducing a Phase Transition in Diffusion Models and Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models should read as engineering and analysis built on genuinely solid ground, rather than mach

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: The Meccano steam shovel turned out to be a lesson in number theory: a construction set built on a ½-inch grid is full of Pythagorean triples, and its gears were sized so that every pair lands on the grid. LEGO is a lattice too, but a stranger one. Its studs are 8 mm apart, while its plates are 3.2 mm tall, so the vertical and horizontal grids do not match, and that one ratio shapes how everything in the system fits together. The second half of the post is a famous counting problem.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: For decades LEGO said that six 2×4 bricks could be combined in 102,981,500 ways. The true figure, found by the mathematician Søren Eilers, is 915,103,765. The post works out where the old number came from, reproduces the published counts with a short program, and looks at how fast the count grows.

chunks.heading: About the sources
chunks.text: The counts of LEGO buildings are from Søren Eilers and his collaborators, as published on his page and in the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (links at the end); the program below reproduces the ones a laptop can reach. LEGO's dimensions are the widely published nominal ones. The list of Technic gears is from memory of the system, so check it against a parts reference before quoting it.

chunks.heading: Two grids that do not match
chunks.text: The ratio that matters is {plate} : {pitch} = 3.2 : 8 = 2 : 5. A brick, three plates, is 6/5 of a pitch. So a stack of b bricks and p plates is which is a whole number of studs only when 3b + p is a multiple of 5. The smallest stack that lands back on the horizontal grid is five plates: one brick and two plates make exactly two studs. Every serious builder knows that rule. It is why Technic bricks, whose holes run sideways through them on the stud pitch, are stacked with two plates between each pair. The holes then fall on a square grid, two studs apart in both directions.

chunks.heading: Building sideways
chunks.text: Modern models often turn parts on their sides, the technique builders call SNOT (studs not on top). A sideways part brings its own lattice, rotated a quarter turn: one stud along what was the height, 0.4 of a stud along what was the width. The two lattices coincide only at points that are on both: because {2}{5}k is an integer only when 5 divides k, and then it is even. So upright and sideways building can only meet every two studs in each direction. That is why sideways work is full of special parts (brackets, jumper plates with a single central stud, headlight bricks) whose job is to make up

chunks.heading: Pythagoras in Technic
chunks.text: Technic beams have holes on the stud pitch, so a diagonal beam, like a Meccano strip, fits exactly only when its length is a whole number of holes. On the flat, that again means Pythagorean triples: the (3, 4, 5) triangle and its multiples are the only exact diagonals inside ten studs. What happens when the diagonal climbs through a stack of Technic bricks and plates? Then one side is x studs across and the other is p plates up, 0.4p studs, and The right-hand side is a multiple of 25, so 5 2p, so 5 p: an exact diagonal can only rise by whole studs, in steps of one brick and two plates. Plates

chunks.heading: Which gears mesh
chunks.text: Technic gears are cut to a module of 1 mm, so a gear with N teeth has a pitch diameter of N mm. Two meshing gears sit (N1 + N2)/2 mm apart, which is The gears come in two families. The spur gears have 8, 16, 24 and 40 teeth: multiples of 8. The double-bevel gears have 12, 20, 28 and 36: each 4 more than a multiple of 8. Within a family N1 + N2 is a multiple of 8, so d is a whole or half number of studs and the pair can be mounted on the grid (on half studs with the right beams).

chunks.heading: Which gears mesh
chunks.text: Across the families N1 + N2 4 8, so d ends in a quarter stud, and a spur gear and a double-bevel gear never mesh in line on the grid. Meccano's gears, by contrast, were all odd multiples of 19 teeth, which made every pair fit.

chunks.heading: Which gears mesh
chunks.text: The one whole-stud diagonal among Technic gears is the pair of 40-tooth gears, 5 studs apart, which can sit at the (3, 4) offset of the Pythagorean triangle. Three pairs that are 2.5 studs apart fit at a half-stud offset across and one brick and two plates up, which is the (3, 4, 5) triangle again, at half scale.

chunks.heading: Two bricks: 24
chunks.text: Put one 2×4 brick down and press a second one onto it. If the second brick is parallel to the first, its four-by-two footprint can be shifted 7 ways along and 3 ways across and still overlap by at least one stud: 21 placements. If it is turned crosswise, it can be shifted 5 ways each way: 25 placements. That makes 46. But a building does not know which brick was put down first or which way round it stands. Turning the whole thing half a turn about the vertical gives the same building, and maps most placements to a different one of the 46.

chunks.heading: Two bricks: 24
chunks.text: Burnside's lemma counts the buildings that remain: the number of distinct buildings is the average number of placements left unchanged by each symmetry. The identity leaves all 46; the half turn leaves only the 2 that are centred, one parallel and one crossed. So

chunks.heading: Towers, and LEGO's famous number
chunks.text: The figure LEGO quoted for many years, 102,981,500 ways to combine six bricks, goes back to a 1974 company newsletter. It counted only towers: buildings six bricks high, each brick on the one below. Each brick can sit on the one beneath it in 46 ways, so there are 46^5 towers before symmetry. The half turn pairs them up, except for the towers it leaves unchanged, those with every brick centred on the one below, either parallel or crossed: 2^5 of them. Burnside again: That is LEGO's number, four short; Eilers suggests the original sum was done on a calculator that could not hold nine digits. Bu

chunks.heading: Counting every building
chunks.text: A building here is any set of n bricks joined into one piece by their studs, counted once however it is turned about the vertical. Counting them by hand is hopeless after two or three bricks, but they can be generated: 1. Every connected building of n bricks has at least one brick whose removal leaves it connected (a leaf of a spanning tree of its connections). So every building of n bricks can be made by adding one brick to some building of n-1. 2. Starting from one brick, add a brick in every possible place: above or below any existing brick, in either orientation, at every offset that overl

chunks.heading: Counting every building
chunks.text: 3. Reduce each result to a canonical form: rotate it through four quarter turns, move each rotation to the origin, sort its bricks, and keep the smallest. Two buildings are the same exactly when their canonical forms are equal, so a Python set removes the duplicates.

chunks.heading: Counting every building
chunks.text: The program reproduces every published count it reaches, split by height, and the formula gives the tallest column of each row, ending in LEGO's 102,981,504. Beyond four bricks the numbers outgrow a simple Python set: there are about ten million buildings of five bricks. Eilers and Mikkel Abrahamsen counted six bricks with a careful program that never stores the buildings, only counts them, which is how the 915,103,765 was found.

chunks.heading: How fast it grows
chunks.text: The published counts now run to eleven bricks; the eleventh term was added to the integer-sequence encyclopedia only this month. The ratio of each count to the one before tells how many new buildings each extra brick multiplies the total by. Towers grow by a factor of 46 per brick, but buildings grow faster and faster: each new brick can go on any of the others, and side by side as well as on top. The factor passes 100 at ten bricks and is still rising. The towers' share falls from all of the two-brick buildings to about a ninth of the six-brick ones, which is why LEGO's figure was out by a fa

chunks.heading: How fast it grows
chunks.text: Durhuus and Eilers proved that the number of buildings grows exponentially, T(n) ^n in the long run, and pinned the base between roughly 78 and 191. The ratios above suggest it lies somewhat above 100, but the exact value is still unknown: a simple question about a children's toy that remains open.

chunks.heading: Next
chunks.text: The lattice and the count are the static half of LEGO. Two follow-ups would put the bricks into motion in MuJoCo: a Technic walking linkage whose link lengths must be whole numbers of holes, and the structural question of how far a brick cantilever can reach when its studs can pull apart.

chunks.heading: Sources
chunks.text: - Søren Eilers, A LEGO counting problem, including the history of the 102,981,500 figure. - OEIS A112389 (buildings of n 2×4 bricks) and A112390 (by height). - Bergfinnur Durhuus and Søren Eilers, On the entropy of LEGO (2005).

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: An orrery is a clockwork model of the solar system. They take their name from Charles Boyle, Earl of Orrery, for whom one was made in the early 1700s, but the idea is far older: the Antikythera mechanism, built in Greece some two thousand years ago, already modelled the Moon's cycles with bronze gears. The hard part has never been the mechanism. It is the arithmetic. A pair of gears turns at a ratio of whole numbers of teeth, and the sky does not run on whole numbers: there are 365.2564 days in the year and 29.5306 days from one new Moon to the next.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: The previous post found that LEGO Technic gears come in only eight sizes, with 8 to 40 teeth. This post asks how well an orrery built from those eight sizes can keep time, finds the best gear trains by search, builds the machine in MuJoCo with every gear a real moving part, and runs it for a simulated year.

chunks.heading: About the model and the sources
chunks.text: The astronomical periods are the standard modern values. The orrery is a design, simulated rather than built: every gear and every mesh is in the model, at real Technic sizes, but the layout has not been tested with physical parts. The history in the introduction is general knowledge; check details before quoting them.

chunks.heading: Two kinds of day, two kinds of month
chunks.text: The Earth turns once on its axis relative to the stars in a sidereal day, about 23 hours 56 minutes. But while it turns, it also moves a little way round its orbit, so it has to turn slightly further before the Sun is overhead again. That longer turn is the solar day, the 24 hours of the clock. Over a year the difference adds up to exactly one turn: the Earth turns 366.2564 times relative to the stars in a year, but only 365.2564 times relative to the Sun.

chunks.heading: Two kinds of day, two kinds of month
chunks.text: The Moon has the same pair of periods. It goes round the Earth relative to the stars in a sidereal month of 27.32 days, but because the Earth has moved on round the Sun meanwhile, it takes 29.53 days to return to the same phase, the synodic month. The rates add like the days:

chunks.heading: The epicyclic trick
chunks.text: The orrery's year arm carries the Earth round the Sun. Gears mounted on a moving arm form an epicyclic (planetary) train, and they obey Willis's rule: what a gear train on an arm transmits is not the rotation of the input shaft but its rotation relative to the arm. If the central shaft turns at and the arm at , a train on the arm with ratio g turns its output at - The Earth's spin. Let the crank turn the central shaft once per sidereal day, and carry its turning out along the arm to the Earth through a chain of gears with g = 1.

chunks.heading: The epicyclic trick
chunks.text: Then {Earth} = : the Earth turns once per sidereal day relative to the stars. Relative to the arm, which always points at the Sun, it turns at - , which is once per solar day. The solar day costs no gears at all; it falls out of the geometry, exactly as it does in the sky. - The Moon. A second train on the arm reduces ( - ), the solar day, by a ratio Rm to drive the Moon's carrier relative to the arm. The Moon then goes round once per Rm solar days relative to the Sun direction.

chunks.heading: The epicyclic trick
chunks.text: So Rm must be the synodic month, 29.5306, and the sidereal month comes out automatically. The third train is fixed to the table: it reduces the central shaft to the arm's hub by Ry, the number of sidereal days in a year, 366.2564. So everything rests on two numbers that gears have to approximate: 366.2564 and 29.5306.

chunks.heading: Fractions that cannot be built
chunks.text: The classic way to approximate a number by a fraction is its continued fraction. Its truncations, the convergents, are the best rational approximations for their size: no fraction with a smaller denominator comes closer. They give the famous calendar fractions: 36514 for the Julian year, and 235/19 for the Moon, the Metonic cycle of 235 lunations in 19 years, which the Antikythera mechanism used. A gear train can make a fraction only if it can be factored into gear ratios. Its numerator must be the product of the driven gears' tooth counts and its denominator the product of the drivers'.

chunks.heading: Fractions that cannot be built
chunks.text: The Metonic 235/19 needs a 47 and a 19; the year's 1465/4 needs a 293. The Antikythera mechanism's makers cut whatever tooth counts they needed, including a gear of 223 teeth, a prime. LEGO's tooth counts are 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 36 and 40, and every one of them is built from the primes 2, 3, 5 and 7. So every ratio a Technic gear train can make is a 7-smooth rational number, of the form and not one of the convergents above is of that form. The best fractions mathematics has to offer are unbuildable.

chunks.heading: Searching every train
chunks.text: The alternative is brute force: try every train that can be built. A reducing stage is a pair of gears from the same family (spur with spur, or double-bevel with double-bevel, which the previous post showed are the pairs that mesh on the grid), or a worm driving a spur gear. Building the trains up a stage at a time, every ratio reachable with k stages comes from one reachable with k-1. Because all the ratios are 7-smooth with small exponents, the sets stay remarkably small. The best trains are long.

chunks.heading: Searching every train
chunks.text: The Moon needs six stages to come within 210^{-5}, using a fraction no textbook would suggest: against the true 29.530589. Its numerator is 945 = 3^3 5 7 and its denominator 2^5, both as smooth as the parts require. The year needs seven stages to reach 46875/128 = 366.2109 (that is, 3 5^6 / 2^7), about a part in eight thousand. Worms do not help either target: their single tooth makes big, coarse steps, and the best trains are built from the gentle ratios 3:2, 5:2 and 7:3 instead.

chunks.heading: The machine
chunks.text: The orrery uses the two winning trains and a 1:1 chain for the Earth's spin: - The year train, seven stages, is coiled round the central shaft on the base: the axles stand on a circle that starts and ends at the centre, so the last gear meshes with the year arm's hub, coaxial with the shaft. A plain idler gear in the loop makes the arm turn the same way as the crank. - The spin chain runs out along the arm: 24, 40, 24, 40, 24 teeth. The first and last gears are equal, so the ratio is 1, and an even number of meshes keeps the direction. - The Moon train, six stages, runs along the arm above it,

chunks.heading: The machine
chunks.text: Both trains on the arm are exactly 128 mm long, 16 studs, which is why the Earth sits there. In MuJoCo, every gear is a body on a hinge joint, carried either by the base or by the arm. Each mesh is a constraint on the joints' angles. For two gears with N1 and N2 teeth, turning by 1 and 2 relative to whatever carries them, rolling without slipping means That is a linear combination of joint angles. MuJoCo calls such a combination a fixed tendon, and an equality constraint holds it at zero. The epicyclic meshes, between the central shaft and gears riding on the arm, are expressed exactly the sam

chunks.heading: Running it for a year
chunks.text: Turning the crank until the arm has gone once round the Sun, and reading every angle from the simulation: The machine does exactly what its gears say: 366.2109 sidereal days to the year, within a few millionths, and the constraints hold the meshes to within a fraction of a milliradian. Two numbers in the table were never put into the design. The solar days in the year come from the epicyclic arm, and so does the sidereal month, which comes out within a thousandth of a day of the real one.

chunks.heading: Running it for a year
chunks.text: The errors are what the arithmetic allowed. The year is short by about 0.045 days, so the orrery's Earth gains a day on the real one every 22 years or so. The Moon's month is long by 0.0007 days, which takes over a century to add up to a day.

chunks.heading: The Moon's phases, and eclipses
chunks.text: The Sun in the model is a light. MuJoCo's lights are spotlights, so the sunlight that falls on the Earth and Moon comes from a lamp riding on the year arm at the Sun's surface, aimed along the arm. It always faces the Earth, as the real Sun does. The video below rides on the arm beside the Earth for two months, lit by the Sun alone. The Earth turns its day side to the Sun once per solar day, and the Moon goes through its phases. Because this Moon orbits in the same plane as the Earth, it also passes through the Earth's shadow at every full Moon: a lunar eclipse every month. The real Moon's orb

chunks.heading: What would make it better
chunks.text: - A tilted Earth. A real orrery keeps the Earth's axis pointing the same way all year, to show the seasons. That takes one more train: a fixed gear on the central shaft driving an equal gear on the Earth's mount through idlers, so the mount turns backwards exactly as fast as the arm turns forwards. - Better arithmetic with a differential. A Technic differential averages two rotations, so trains can be combined into sums and differences as well as products. A sum of smooth numbers need not be smooth: 1465/4 = 360 + 25/4, for instance, is out of reach of any product of LEGO ratios but within rea

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: The Earth–Moon orrery showed that LEGO Technic gears can only make ratios built from the primes 2, 3, 5 and 7, and that a search over every train the parts allow finds surprisingly good approximations to the year and the month. This post takes the same idea to its limit: a grand orrery with all eight planets, from Mercury, which goes round the Sun in under three months, to Neptune, which takes 165 years.

chunks.heading: About the model and the sources
chunks.text: The planets' mean longitudes and their rates are from JPL's Approximate Positions of the Planets (link at the end). The orrery is a design, simulated in MuJoCo with every gear a moving part; it has not been built. Its sizes and distances are not to scale, as in every real orrery.

chunks.heading: One crank, eight ratios
chunks.text: Let one turn of the crank be one year, and fix the Earth's arm straight to the crank shaft. Every other planet then needs a gear train whose ratio is its orbital period in Earth years. JPL tabulates each planet's mean longitude, the angle it would have reached if it moved round the Sun at a steady rate, and how fast that angle grows. The ratio of each planet's rate to the Earth's is the gear ratio the orrery needs. Mercury and Venus are faster than the Earth, so their trains must speed up rather than slow down. In the Earth–Moon orrery every stage was a reduction; here a stage may go either wa

chunks.heading: Fast planets are hard
chunks.text: How good does a ratio have to be? An orrery is judged by where its planets point, so the natural measure is the angle a planet drifts from the sky over a century. If a train's ratio is off by a fraction , a planet making n orbits per century drifts by about The same fractional error costs Mercury, with 415 orbits a century, nearly 700 times as much as it costs Neptune, with 0.6. A slow planet can be geared roughly; a fast one needs a fine ratio.

chunks.heading: Fast planets are hard
chunks.text: The search below builds every train of up to eight stages, now with stages in both directions, and reports the best drift each planet can reach. The orrery takes, for each planet, the shortest train that drifts less than 2° a century, or, where none does, the shortest train that reaches the best accuracy eight stages allow:

chunks.heading: Fast planets are hard
chunks.text: Some of the winners are pleasingly simple. Uranus is 84 to one, made as 2233{7}{3}, and drifts less than a tenth of a degree a century. Others are the opposite: Mercury's best eight-stage ratio is a fraction no one would write down by hand, and it still drifts by tens of degrees a century. Mercury is the planet a LEGO orrery cannot keep up with.

chunks.heading: The machine
chunks.text: The trains are stacked into a tiered tower round the crank shaft, the classic layout of a grand orrery: - Order of the tiers. The outer planets are at the bottom with the longest arms and the inner planets at the top with the shortest, so the post carrying each planet up to the common height never meets an arm above it. - Each tier is one planet's train. It starts with a gear on the shaft at the bottom of the tier and coils round the shaft on a circle of axles, ending on the planet's hub at the top.

chunks.heading: The machine
chunks.text: The hub is a tube on the shaft, carrying the planet's arm. A train with an odd number of meshes gets an idler, so that every planet goes round the same way. - The Earth has no tier of its own: its arm is fixed to the crank shaft.

chunks.heading: The machine
chunks.text: As in the Earth–Moon orrery, every mesh in MuJoCo is a fixed tendon, a linear combination of joint angles held at zero, so the crank is the only thing driven and everything else follows through the gears. One liberty: the hubs are concentric tubes on a single shaft, eight deep. Real LEGO has no nested tubes, so a physical build would carry the arms on stacked turntables or bring the drives in from outside. The arithmetic does not change.

chunks.heading: Running it
chunks.text: The arms are set at each planet's mean longitude for 27 October 2026. Turning the crank for a century of simulated years, and reading each planet's angle from the simulation: The simulation reproduces every train's ratio to five or six figures, and after a century the planets have drifted from the sky by just what the arithmetic predicted: a degree or two for the outer planets, 8° for Mars, 20° for Venus and 46° for Mercury. The second video looks straight down on the orrery for one whole orbit of Neptune, 165 years. Mercury goes round nearly seven hundred times, far too fast for the camera to

chunks.heading: What the gears cannot do
chunks.text: Two things separate this machine from the sky, and only one is the arithmetic. - Rational ratios. Every LEGO train is a ratio of 7-smooth numbers, and the search shows how far that limits each planet. The cure is the one from the Earth–Moon orrery: differentials, which add rotations together, reach ratios no product of LEGO gears can. A watchmaker's alternative is simply to cut the tooth counts the sky asks for. - Steady motion. Gears turn at constant rates, so the orrery shows each planet's mean longitude.

chunks.heading: What the gears cannot do
chunks.text: Real planets move on ellipses, faster near the Sun and slower far from it, by Kepler's second law. The true position swings either side of the mean by up to about twice the orbit's eccentricity, in radians: roughly 24° for Mercury, 11° for Mars and 2° for the Earth. Mechanical orreries have answered this since antiquity with eccentric gearing; the Antikythera mechanism used a pin-and-slot pair of gears to make its Moon speed up and slow down. A LEGO version, with a pin on one gear driving a slotted liftarm on the next, would be a good next build.

chunks.heading: Sources
chunks.text: - JPL Solar System Dynamics, Approximate Positions of the Planets, Table 1 (mean longitudes and rates, valid 1800–2050).
