chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: The two photographs below show a Meccano steam shovel: a face shovel of the kind that dug railway cuttings and canals. It is built in green girders and red plates, with a brass engine, a perforated boiler and a bucket on a long dipper stick. This post rebuilds it in MuJoCo, one strip, girder and nut at a time, and then asks how it works: - why a construction set built on a ½-inch grid is full of Pythagorean triples, and why its gears always fit; - how one rope, led over a pulley at the boom head and through a pulley block, both lifts the bucket and swings the stick; - why the stick is really a

chunks.heading: About the model and the sources
chunks.text: The code lives in the meccano-shovel project alongside this blog, and every number printed below comes from running it. The model's dimensions were measured from the two photographs, using the hole spacing as a ruler, so they are a reconstruction rather than a published plan. The notes on Meccano's parts (tooth counts, slotted holes) are from memory of the system; check them against a Meccano parts list before quoting them.

chunks.heading: From two photographs to a model
chunks.text: Meccano gives the modeller a gift: a ruler built into every part. The holes are on ½-inch centres, so counting holes along a girder in a photograph gives its length, and the scale of the whole picture follows. The model was measured that way, then every length was rounded to a whole number of holes, as the original builder had to. The cameras in the simulation were placed to match the photographs, and the renders are set beside them below. Each part is generated as a mesh from a 2-D outline with real holes, then extruded: strips with rounded ends, angle girders with round holes in one flange a

chunks.heading: The lattice: Pythagoras on a half-inch grid
chunks.text: Every Meccano part is pierced on the same ½-inch grid. Write positions in holes, so that a point on a flat assembly is a pair of integers (a, b). A strip with n holes spans n-1 pitches between its end holes. To brace two points (0,0) and (a,b) with a straight strip, the distance between them must be a whole number of pitches: So every exact diagonal in a Meccano model is a Pythagorean triple. Horizontal and vertical members are trivial; the first true diagonal is the (3, 4, 5) brace, a 6-hole strip across a 3-by-4 rectangle of holes, and the next primitive ones are (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17) and

chunks.heading: The lattice: Pythagoras on a half-inch grid
chunks.text: Meccano's answer is the slotted hole. Angle girders carry slots in one flange, which give a millimetre or two of play. That turns the exact condition into an approximate one: and a near miss becomes buildable. The figure counts how many brace angles each rule allows. The shovel itself uses the lattice in a less obvious way. The A-frame, the back-stays and the boom all run at angles that are not lattice angles, because each is a long girder pinned only at its ends, where a single bolt lets it take any angle. Only the short ties between them have to land on holes, and on the model those ties spa

chunks.heading: Why Meccano gears always fit
chunks.text: Gears have their own version of the problem. Two meshing gears must sit with their centres one pitch radius plus the other apart, and those centres are holes on the grid. Meccano gears are cut to a diametral pitch of 38 teeth per inch of diameter, and the classic sizes are multiples of 19 teeth: a ½-inch pinion with 19 teeth, a 1½-inch gear with 57, then 95 and 133. Writing a gear's tooth count as N = 19k, its pitch diameter is k half-inches, and the centre distance of a pair is All the classic k are odd (1, 3, 5, 7), so k1 + k2 is always even and every pair lands exactly on the grid.

chunks.heading: Why Meccano gears always fit
chunks.text: The 19 and 57 meshing in the shovel's hoist drive sit (1+3)/2 = 2 holes apart. A 57 and a 133 sit 5 holes apart, so they can even be mounted on a diagonal, at the (3, 4) offset of the Pythagorean triple above.

chunks.heading: How the rope lifts the stick and the bucket
chunks.text: The shovel has one hoist rope, and it does most of the work. Follow it from the engine: 1. It is wound on the hoist drum in the machinery house, which the engine turns through two pairs of gears. 2. It runs up beside the boom to the head sheave, the cream pulley at the top of the boom, and over it. 3. It drops to the pulley block, the red pulley hanging on the bucket's bail, passes round it, 4. and rises again to be tied off at the boom head. So the block hangs in two parts of rope, the two falls. In the model the rope is a MuJoCo spatial tendon through four points, drum, sheave, block and boo

chunks.heading: The pulley block: two falls, twice the force, half the speed
chunks.text: Treat the sheaves as frictionless, so the tension T is the same all along the rope. The block hangs in two falls, each pulling up on it with T, so when the falls are vertical the block is lifted by The same factor appears in the motion. If the block rises by h, both falls shorten by h, so the drum must wind in 2h of rope. The rope's length L and the block's height are tied by {d}L = -2\,{d}h. Force goes up by two and speed goes down by two, and the work done is unchanged, as it must be: T 2h = 2T h. This is the mechanical advantage of the block: 2, for two falls.

chunks.heading: The bucket is lifted by a moment, not a force
chunks.text: The block does not simply lift the bucket straight up. The stick, bucket and block hang together from the shipper shaft S halfway up the boom, and they can only turn about it. What the rope supplies is a moment about S, and the hanging weight Mg, acting at the centre of mass G, supplies the opposing moment. In equilibrium where rB is the block and { u}{1,2} point up the two falls. Solving for T gives the rope tension from the geometry alone. There is a neater way to the same answer: virtual work. Let the stick turn by a tiny angle with the crowd held still. The rope shortens by {d}L and the ce

chunks.heading: The bucket is lifted by a moment, not a force
chunks.text: The tension is the hanging weight times a pure ratio of speeds: how fast the centre of mass rises for each unit of rope wound in. The block, the falls and the moment arms are all hidden inside that one derivative, which MuJoCo can compute directly by moving the joint and measuring the tendon length. The three answers can be set side by side: All three agree to a fraction of a percent; the small difference is the hoist servo still settling. The printout also shows how the load is shared.

chunks.heading: The bucket is lifted by a moment, not a force
chunks.text: Each part of the rope pulls with only about a third of the hanging weight. The block, with its two falls, lifts about two thirds of it, and the shipper shaft carries the rest, because G lies closer to S than the falls do. The block has the longer lever, so the rope needs only a small pull.

chunks.heading: How hard the rope must pull, all the way up
chunks.text: As the rope is wound in, the stick swings up about S and the geometry changes. The falls lean, the lever arm of the block about S shortens, and the centre of mass moves out. The virtual-work formula gives the tension at every point of the swing without simulating anything: sweep the shipper angle, and differentiate zG with respect to L. The crowd setting slides the stick in or out through the shipper, which changes both arms. The crowd setting matters more than the height. Running the stick out (red) carries G further from the shipper shaft, so the rope must pull harder, but the pull hardly ch

chunks.heading: How hard the rope must pull, all the way up
chunks.text: With the stick drawn in (blue), the pull starts small, because G hangs almost under the shaft and the shaft takes nearly all the weight, and then climbs steeply as the bucket swings out and up. The dots are full dynamic simulations at three rope settings, and they sit on the lines.

chunks.heading: The drum and the gearing
chunks.text: At the house end, the rope is wound on a drum of radius rd, so holding a tension T takes a torque T rd on the drum shaft. The drum is driven from the engine's crankshaft through two identical stages, each a 19-tooth pinion driving a 57-tooth gear: Both stages sit on 2-hole centres, as the lattice rule above promised. Putting numbers on the hoist stroke of the dig below: These are small numbers, and a toy electric motor delivers them easily, which is why the real model could work under its own power. On a full-size shovel the same equations hold with the forces scaled up by the cube of the size

chunks.heading: What the boom and its rods carry
chunks.text: The boom is a strut, pinned at its foot and held up at its head by the suspension rods running back to the top of the A-frame. Three loads arrive on it: - at the head, the rope: one part leading back down to the drum and two falls pulling down toward the block, T({ e}{drum} - { u}1 - { u}2); - at the shipper shaft, everything the rope does not carry: the weight of the stick and bucket less the lift of the block, T({ u}1 + { u}2) - Mg\,{ z}; - its own weight, at its middle. Taking moments about the boom foot gives the tension in the rods; the force balance then gives the thrust into the foot pi

chunks.heading: What the boom and its rods carry
chunks.text: The rope loads the boom head from both sides of the sheave, the lead down to the drum and the falls down to the block, so it pulls on the boom harder than the shipper shaft does. The rods hold the head back, and what is left is a thrust straight down the boom into its foot pin, more than twice the weight of everything hanging below. The boom is a strut in almost pure compression. A long, slender strut in compression fails by buckling sideways rather than by crushing, and the cure is bracing, which is why the photographs show the boom as a lattice of paired girders braced across, not a single s

chunks.heading: The stick is a pendulum
chunks.text: Nothing in the machine drives the angle of the dipper stick. The crowd motion slides the stick in and out through its saddle on the shipper shaft; on the model a chain from a sprocket in the house drives the black wheel on the shipper shaft. The hoist shortens the rope. The stick's angle is whatever balances the rope against gravity: the stick is a pendulum, and the rope is its string. A rope can pull but not push. In MuJoCo this is a servo on the tendon whose force is allowed to be negative (pulling) but not positive.

chunks.heading: The stick is a pendulum
chunks.text: Physically it is a complementarity condition between the tension T and the slack s, the difference between the rope paid out and the distance it has to span: Either the rope is taut and carries load, or it is slack and carries none. When the rope is paid out far enough, the bucket comes to rest on the ground and the stick's angle is set by the ground instead.

chunks.heading: Where the bucket can reach
chunks.text: With the rope taut, each pair of lever settings, crowd c and rope length L, puts the teeth at one point: the stick hangs at the angle where the rope's length matches L. The map below draws that grid in the side view, together with the floor. Beyond the floor line the rope goes slack and the bucket sits on the ground; along the floor, only the crowd moves the teeth. The map explains the shape of the dig, which was found by trial before it was understood.

chunks.heading: Where the bucket can reach
chunks.text: On the floor, the teeth can only be moved by the crowd. Lifting them off the floor is only possible along the lines of constant crowd, which curve up and out, because the stick is swinging about the shipper. So a cut into a bank has two strokes: crowd out along the floor into the foot of the bank with the rope slack, then hoist, so the teeth sweep up the face on an arc and the bucket fills. That is how a full-size face shovel digs too.

chunks.heading: The dig
chunks.text: The dig was run with 260 stones in a three-sided bin of Meccano plates. The figure follows the two levers' forces and the number of stones in the bucket through the cut and the lift. Two things stand out. Cutting into the bank is the hard part: the crowd pushes at its 80 N limit for about two seconds as the teeth go in, more than twenty times what the hoist rope pulls. And the bucket fills across the change of stroke. Stones start to come in as the crowd drives the mouth into the foot of the bank, and they come fastest as the hoist starts and the teeth turn up the face on their arc, as the rea

chunks.heading: The dig
chunks.text: A few fall back out over the lip as the bucket tips up clear of the bank. The close-up below shows both strokes. After the lift, the superstructure slews a quarter turn and the trip cord pulls the catch on the bucket's door. The door is hinged along its top edge, so the load swings it open and falls out, as in the video at the top of the post.

chunks.heading: Coda: why gravel is hard
chunks.text: Granular material is a notoriously difficult thing to simulate, and the shovel's gravel took more iterations than the shovel. - Spheres roll. The first heaps of spheres collapsed into a single layer and rolled away across the floor. Real gravel stands at an angle of repose because its stones interlock; spheres cannot. Giving each contact rolling resistance (MuJoCo's six-dimensional contacts, with torsional and rolling friction) made the spheres behave like gravel and stand in a bank. - Angular stones are expensive. Small boxes stood well, but box-to-box contacts are much costlier than sphere c

chunks.heading: Coda: why gravel is hard
chunks.text: - Every contact is several constraints. A six-dimensional contact in MuJoCo's pyramidal friction model is ten constraint rows, so a few hundred touching stones make thousands of rows. Switching the solver from Newton's method to conjugate gradient, which suits this many loosely coupled contacts, cut the cost of a step by about three quarters. - A bank needs walls. Even rough spheres slump without a wall to lean on, so the gravel sits in a three-sided bin open toward the shovel, which is also a fair picture of the working face of a quarry.

chunks.heading: Next steps
chunks.text: - Model the crowd drive properly, with the chain turning a pinion on the shipper shaft against a rack on the stick, so the crowd force comes from the engine as the hoist does. - Let the boom be raised and lowered on its suspension, which turns the boom into a third control. - A Meccano lorry to dump into, and a full dig-swing-dump-return loop. - Export the model to a path tracer for photographic lighting to match the original prints.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: A sailing yacht is two wings. One, the sails, works in air. The other, the keel, works in water. The wind pushes on the sails with a force that points mostly sideways, and the keel pushes back with a force that also points mostly sideways, and what is left over, a small forward component, drives the boat. Everything else about sailing (why you cannot sail straight into the wind, why the boat leans over, why it goes fastest with the wind on the beam and slows down when the wind is directly behind) comes from how those two forces, and the twisting moment between them, balance.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: This post works that balance out for a real boat, the J/109, a 35-foot racing and cruising yacht designed by Rod Johnstone and built by J/Boats since the early 2000s. It is a common boat in handicap racing, which matters here: every boat racing under the Offshore Racing Congress (ORC) rule carries a certificate listing its predicted speed at each wind speed and angle, and 43 J/109 certificates from nine countries for 2024 are public. They are the check.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: A second post takes the same model through the sailing modes: the best angles upwind and downwind and why the fastest route downwind is not straight downwind, what a tack or a gybe costs, simulated second by second, and what a tidal current does to the wind a boat sails in.

chunks.heading: How this post is built
chunks.text: The approach is the one used in the Apollo 11 series: documented numbers as anchors, physics between them, and a small number of quantities fitted so that the physics passes through the anchors. - The boat's dimensions come from its ORC certificates (displacement, crew weight, wetted surface, draft, sail areas: the median of the 43) and from the J/109 class association (waterline length, ballast, rig dimensions). - The sails are described by the ORC's published lift and drag coefficients for a mainsail, a jib and an asymmetric spinnaker, measured in wind tunnels and refined against real boats.

chunks.heading: How this post is built
chunks.text: - The hull's wave-making resistance comes from the ORC's resistance surfaces, derived from towing-tank tests of systematic series of yacht hulls; friction from the standard turbulent flat-plate line. - The keel and rudder are treated as wings, with lifting-line theory for their lift and induced drag. - Two numbers nobody publishes are fitted to the certificates: the hull's stability (its metacentric height, GM) and its effective sailing length. At every true wind speed and angle the program then finds the boat speed, heel and leeway at which the forces balance, and picks the sail trim that giv

chunks.heading: Sail the J/109
chunks.text: Set the wind speed and the boat's angle to the true wind, or press Sweep to swing the boat from close-hauled to dead downwind. The boat is on starboard tack: the wind comes over its right-hand side and the sails are out to the left. The 3D view shows the sail force (red), split into the drive along the course (green) and the side force across it (orange), and the water's force on the keel and hull (blue). Switch on Lift and drag to see the sail force split the other way, relative to the wind the sail feels, and Righting to see the weight and buoyancy that hold the boat up.

chunks.heading: Sail the J/109
chunks.text: The arrows are to scale with each other; the wind arrows above the mast are the true wind (dark blue) and the apparent wind (light blue). The compass rose on the water gives bearings in degrees true: set the direction the wind comes from, and the boat's heading (where its bow points) and its course through the water (the heading plus the leeway) follow. Try Underwater to see the keel and the rudder that the water pushes on. Drag to look around and scroll to zoom.

chunks.heading: The wind the sails feel
chunks.text: A moving boat makes its own wind. If you motor at 7 knots on a calm day, you feel a 7-knot headwind. Under sail the same thing happens, and the wind the sails actually feel, the apparent wind, is the vector sum of the true wind and that headwind. With the true wind speed w at angle to the course and the boat moving at v, where is the apparent wind angle. Two refinements matter. The wind is slower near the water than at the masthead, so the model scales the true wind with height using a logarithmic profile, w(z) (z/z0) with roughness length z0 = 5 mm, as the ORC does. And when the boat heels, t

chunks.heading: The wind the sails feel
chunks.text: Close-hauled in 12 knots of true wind at 38°, the J/109 sails at 6.4 knots, and its sails feel 16.7 knots at 22°: more wind than there is, from further ahead. On a run the boat's speed is subtracted from the wind instead, which is why running in a breeze feels calm and warm, and beating into the same breeze feels cold and wet.

chunks.heading: Wind, sea and the Beaufort scale
chunks.text: Sailors describe the wind by its Beaufort force, a scale drawn up by Francis Beaufort, a Royal Navy officer, in 1805 for describing the effect of the wind on a warship's sails, and later tied to measured wind speeds and to the state of the sea. The J/109's certificates cover forces 2 to 6: The Met Office's wave heights are for a sea that has had the wind blowing over it long enough, and over enough open water, to be fully developed. Most racing happens in coastal waters where the fetch, the distance of open water upwind, is much shorter, and the waves stay smaller and shorter. The standard rel

chunks.heading: Wind, sea and the Beaufort scale
chunks.text: and the wavelength of deep-water waves of period T is gT^2/2. The 3D view uses these for 20 km of fetch, with a few wave trains travelling downwind at their own speeds and white crests from force 4, and the boat pitching, rolling and heaving on them. The waves are for show: the speed model assumes flat water. Waves slow a real boat, most of all upwind, where it climbs every one of them; that is one reason the ORC's own program is more detailed than this one.

chunks.heading: The sail is a wing
chunks.text: A sail set at a small angle to the apparent wind turns the airflow, and the turning produces a lift force at right angles to the apparent wind and a smaller drag force along it. Both scale with the dynamic pressure of the apparent wind and the sail area A: The coefficients CL and CD depend on the apparent wind angle and the type of sail. The ORC publishes them for a mainsail, a jib and several kinds of spinnaker; they are the backbone of every modern handicap rating: Solid lines are lift, dashed drag; dots are the ORC's published points and the lines the smooth curves through them used in the

chunks.heading: The sail is a wing
chunks.text: Lift and drag are defined relative to the apparent wind, but the boat needs them relative to its course. Resolving them gives the drive along the course and the side force across it: Close to the wind is small, so most of the lift becomes side force and the drag subtracts directly from the drive. In the example above the sails produce 4,190 N of lift and 725 N of drag, which turn into 926 N of drive and 4,150 N of side force: the sails push the boat sideways 4.5 times as hard as they push it forward.

chunks.heading: The sail is a wing
chunks.text: Turn on Lift and drag in the 3D view to see the two decompositions of the same force. The drag here includes more than the sails' profile drag. A finite wing sheds tip vortices, and the energy in them shows up as induced drag, C{Di} = CL^2/(\,h{eff}^2/A), which depends on the rig's effective height h{eff}, set by the ORC's formulas from the mast height and the apparent wind angle. The mast, rigging and topsides add their own windage.

chunks.heading: The keel is a wing too
chunks.text: The side force has to be resisted, or the boat would just blow sideways. It is resisted by the keel, and the keel can only do that by meeting the water at an angle, which means the boat moves slightly sideways as well as forward. That angle is the leeway, . Like the sail, the keel produces lift in proportion to its angle of attack: where S is the keel's area and {A}e its effective aspect ratio. The hull acts as a mirror at the keel's root, so {A}e is twice the geometric value.

chunks.heading: The keel is a wing too
chunks.text: The rudder and the canoe body carry part of the side force too, the rudder more as the boat heels. Water is about 840 times denser than air, so the keel, at a few square metres, can balance sails of 70 m² at a leeway of only 2.7° in the example. The cost is the keel's own induced drag, F^2/(12 v^2\,\, b{eff}^2) for an effective span b{eff}, which grows as the square of the side force and falls as the square of the speed. That is why a boat sailing slowly close to the wind is so inefficient, and why a deep keel points higher than a shallow one.

chunks.heading: Resistance: friction and waves
chunks.text: The drive has to equal the water's resistance to the hull moving forward. There are three main parts: - Friction, from the water dragged along the hull's wetted surface, RF = 12 v^2 Sw CF({Re}), with the friction coefficient from the turbulent flat-plate line CF = 0.066/({10}{Re} - 2.03)^2, and the same for the keel and rudder. - Wave-making resistance, the energy that goes into the bow and stern waves. It depends on the Froude number {Fn} = v/{gL}, and on the hull's slenderness: its length against the cube root of its displaced volume.

chunks.heading: Resistance: friction and waves
chunks.text: The model takes it from the ORC's resistance surfaces. - Induced drag of the keel, rudder and hull, from the side force (above). Friction dominates in light air; above about 7 knots the waves take over, and they grow so fast that the boat runs into what sailors call hull speed. At {Fn} 0.4 the wave the boat makes is as long as the boat itself, and the boat sits in the trough of its own wave with its bow climbing the face. The old rule of thumb puts this at 1.34{L} knots for a waterline L in feet: 7.7 knots for the J/109's sailing length. It is not a hard limit, as the polar shows: in strong wi

chunks.heading: Resistance: friction and waves
chunks.text: The fit put the J/109's effective sailing length at 10.09 m against a static waterline of 9.30 m. The boat has overhangs, particularly at the stern, which immerse as it heels and as its own wave lifts the stern, so it sails longer than it floats. The ORC rule measures the same effect.

chunks.heading: Heel and the righting moment
chunks.text: The sail's side force acts high up, at the centre of effort 7.1 m above the water in the example, and the keel's side force acts below the water. They form a couple that tries to roll the boat over. The boat resists with a righting moment: when it heels, the centre of buoyancy moves to the low side while the centre of gravity (with 1.77 tonnes of ballast in the keel, low down) stays put, and weight and buoyancy form a couple of their own. For small angles the lever arm between them is GZ = GM, where GM is the metacentric height.

chunks.heading: Heel and the righting moment
chunks.text: The crew, sitting on the windward rail, add their own lever: The boat heels until the two moments are equal. The fit put the J/109's GM at 1.05 m, which with 5.7 tonnes sailing displacement and 620 kg of crew on the rail gives a righting moment of 33 kN·m at 25° of heel; about 24% of that comes from the crew. Heel is costly: it tilts the sails away from the wind, reduces the keel's effective span and increases its induced drag, and makes the hull asymmetric in the water. Racing crews keep a boat like this at or below about 25 to 30°, and the model allows at most 30°.

chunks.heading: Heel and the righting moment
chunks.text: When the wind gets up, the boat cannot use all the force its sails could make. The model then depowers: it flattens the sails and twists their upper parts off to leeward, which reduces lift (and heeling moment) more than it reduces drive, and when that is not enough it reefs. Both are what a crew does: flattening by tensioning the backstay, outhaul and cunningham and easing the traveller, reefing by tying down the bottom of the mainsail. In the panel above, power is the fraction of the sails' full lift being used. Up to about 10 knots of true wind the J/109 sails close-hauled at full power; be

chunks.heading: Why you cannot sail into the wind
chunks.text: Put the three balances together and a simple relation appears, usually credited to the aeronautical pioneer Frederick Lanchester and known in yacht design as the course theorem. The sail's total force leans back from the perpendicular to the apparent wind by the sail's drag angle = (D/L). The water's total force leans back from the perpendicular to the course by the hull's drag angle = (R/F{keel}). In steady sailing the two forces are equal and opposite, and the geometry forces The apparent wind angle a boat can sail at is the sum of the inefficiencies of its two wings.

chunks.heading: Why you cannot sail into the wind
chunks.text: No sail is drag-free and no hull is resistance-free, so can never be zero. A J/109 needs an apparent wind angle of at least about 22°, which with its speed comes to a true wind angle in the high thirties; anything closer and the sails luff and the boat stops. That wedge either side of the wind is the no-go zone, shaded on the polar. To go upwind a boat zigzags, beating on alternate tacks. Every improvement in sailing efficiency, from better sail cloth to deeper keels, is an attack on or .

chunks.heading: The polar, checked
chunks.text: Solving the balance at every angle and wind speed gives the polar diagram, the boat's speed in every direction. The ORC certificates contain the same thing, predicted by the ORC's own, far more detailed, velocity prediction program from each boat's measured hull, rig and sails. Comparing the two at the certificates' 64 points: The root-mean-square difference is 0.15 knots. The spread among the 43 real boats, the gap between the 10th and 90th percentiles, is typically 0.16 knots, from differences in sails, keel, weight and measured stability. The largest differences are where a simple model wou

chunks.heading: The polar, checked
chunks.text: The certificates also give the best upwind and downwind angles and the velocity made good (VMG) at each wind speed: the speed directly towards or away from the wind, v. These were part of the fit upwind: Upwind, the model's best angles are within 2° of the certificates' (on the model's 2° grid). Its VMG is within 0.08 knots from 12 knots of wind upwards, but up to 0.19 knots low in lighter air, where the real boat's sails, trimmed fuller and with less twist than the model's two-parameter trim allows, make more of a little wind.

chunks.heading: The polar, checked
chunks.text: Downwind, without being fitted, the VMG is within 0.18 knots at every wind speed. The best downwind angles differ more, because near the optimum VMG hardly changes with angle, so small details decide where the optimum sits. In 16 and 20 knots the certificates' optimum is almost dead downwind (174° and 176°), while the model's is 166° and 156°. Why the best way downwind is usually not straight downwind is the subject of the next post.

chunks.heading: Points of sail
chunks.text: Sailors name the angle to the wind by the way the boat is sailed. The boundaries are loose, but the physics behind them is in the sections above: The red dot follows the true wind angle set above. With the wind on the starboard side the boat is on starboard tack; on the other side, port tack. The next post looks at each of these in turn and at moving between them.

chunks.heading: The words, and where they come from
chunks.text: Sailing has its own vocabulary, much of it centuries old and most of it borrowed from the languages of the North Sea, where the European sailing ship developed. Dutch, the Scandinavian languages and Old English supply most of it, and because sailors' stories travel better than their documents, it also carries more than its share of folk etymology. The origins below are from the Online Etymology Dictionary and Merriam-Webster, with naval history from the sources linked on each entry. Each is marked established where the dictionaries agree, probable where they hedge, and disputed where there are

chunks.heading: The words, and where they come from
chunks.text: Dates are first recorded uses in English. A few things stand out. Starboard is the steering side: Old English steorbord, the side the steering oar hung from. Early Germanic boats were steered from the right; that this was because most people are right-handed is a plausible explanation rather than a documented one. The left side was larboard until an Admiralty order of 1844 replaced it with port in the Royal Navy (the US Navy followed in 1846). The usual explanation is that larboard and starboard were too easily confused when shouted into a gale, though at least one historian of the words argue

chunks.heading: The words, and where they come from
chunks.text: Heel in the sense of leaning over has nothing to do with feet; it is Old English hieldan, "to lean", which lost its final d in the 16th century. Tiller comes from weaving, through the stock of a crossbow. Yacht is Dutch jacht, short for jachtschip, a fast ship for chasing. And leeward, the side away from the wind, is still pronounced "loo-ard" by sailors.

chunks.heading: The words, and where they come from
chunks.text: The best stories are usually the least certain. The spinnaker is first recorded in 1866; the popular account that it is a corruption of Sphinx, a yacht that carried an early one, is not supported by the publications of the time, and the word's origin is unknown. The genoa is named after the Italian city, but whether the sail was first shown there by the Swedish yachtsman Sven Salén, or by an Italian sailmaker a year earlier, depends on which account you read. And "port out, starboard home" as the origin of posh is a story without evidence: the acronym is only recorded decades after the word.

chunks.heading: Method and sources
chunks.text: The model is a three-degree-of-freedom velocity prediction program: at each true wind speed and angle it solves for boat speed, heel and leeway so that drive equals resistance, the sails' side force equals the side force from keel, rudder and hull, and the heeling moment equals the righting moment. The sail trim (a flattening factor scaling the lift and, through the ORC's drag multiplier, the drag, and a reefing factor scaling the area and the height of the centre of effort) is chosen for the highest speed with at most 30° of heel. Upwind the boat carries its mainsail and jib; from 70° it may

chunks.text: Two quantities are fitted by least squares to the median of the 43 certificates' 64 polar speeds and their 8 best upwind VMGs: the metacentric height GM = 1.05 m and the sailing length 10.09 m. Several dimensions are assumed, because no source gives them: the waterline beam (3.00 m), the canoe-body draft (0.50 m), the keel's and rudder's planforms, the heights of the deck and boom above the water at the mast, and the crew's average distance from the centreline (1.45 m). The sail shapes and sheeting in the 3D view are drawn for illustration. What the model leaves out: waves and the motion they

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Part 1 built a model of the J/109, a 35-foot racing yacht, that balances the forces on its sails, keel and hull at every wind speed and angle, and checked it against 43 of the boat's rating certificates. It answers the question "how fast does the boat go on this heading?". Sailing is about more than that. A boat that has to go upwind cannot point at its destination; one that has to go downwind usually should not; and at the corners of every zigzag it has to turn through the wind, losing speed in the process.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: All of this happens on water that is itself moving. This post takes the Part 1 model through three questions: 1. Which way to point. The best angles to the wind upwind and downwind, and why they are what they are. 2. What a tack or a gybe costs. The model extended in time, so that the boat can turn through the wind and slow down and speed up again, second by second. 3. What a current does. The same boat on moving water, and the real reason behind the sailor's lore about "lee-bowing" the tide.

chunks.heading: Which way to point
chunks.text: What matters on a race course is rarely the speed through the water. It is how fast the boat gets towards (or away from) the wind, its velocity made good, {VMG} = v, where is the true wind angle. The polar from Part 1 gives v at every angle, so finding the best angle is a one-dimensional optimisation, and it has a neat geometric form: on the polar diagram, the best upwind angle is where a line square to the wind just touches the curve. Upwind the optimum is a compromise between speed and direction.

chunks.heading: Which way to point
chunks.text: Pointing higher than the best angle shortens the distance sailed but the boat slows faster than the angle improves; pointing lower gives more speed but sends it too far sideways. For the J/109 the best angle narrows from about 46° to the true wind in a light breeze to about 36° in a strong one, because in more wind the boat reaches its maximum speed at higher angles too, and pointing higher costs less. Upwind, the angle between the two tacks, the tacking angle, is twice that: from about 70° to 90°.

chunks.heading: Which way to point
chunks.text: Downwind the same logic gives a less obvious answer. Running straight downwind, the boat's own speed is subtracted from the wind: at 5.6 knots of boat speed in 12 knots of true wind, the sails feel only about 6.2 knots, from dead astern, where the spinnaker works by drag alone. Heading up 20 or 30° brings the apparent wind forward, onto the side of the sails, where they produce lift, and the speed rises more than the cosine falls. So boats downwind zigzag too, gybing between broad reaches. The best angle is 156° in 12 knots, a gybing angle of 48°. In very light wind the effect is strongest: th

chunks.heading: The tack
chunks.text: In a tack the boat turns its bow through the wind, from close-hauled on one side to close-hauled on the other. For a few seconds the boat points almost straight into the wind, its sails flap and produce no drive, and it coasts on its momentum. Then the sails fill on the new side, the boat is going slowly, and it has to accelerate back to its target speed. Part 1's model is a steady state: it finds the speed at which the forces balance. A tack is not steady, so the model has to be extended in time. The helmsman's turn is prescribed (the heading follows a smooth curve over a given time), and the

chunks.heading: The tack
chunks.text: The first is Newton's second law along the track: the boat's mass m, plus the water it carries with it (added mass ma), accelerates under the difference between the sail drive and the resistance, both from Part 1's model. The second is the same for roll: the heel swings across as the sails' heeling moment reverses, with the boat's roll inertia I and some damping. Three more pieces make it a tack rather than just a slowdown: - The sails luff. Inside about 20° of apparent wind angle the sails stop producing lift and flog, adding drag.

chunks.heading: The tack
chunks.text: Once the bow is through the wind, the jib is briefly backed on the old side, then released and sheeted in on the new side over a few seconds. - The keel turns the boat. To make the boat follow a curved path, something must push it towards the centre of the turn: a centripetal force m u r, where r is the rate of turn. That force comes from the keel and rudder, which need extra leeway and produce extra induced drag to supply it. A fast turn costs drag; a slow one leaves the sails luffing for longer. - The crew move across to the new windward side.

chunks.heading: The tack
chunks.text: Choose the manoeuvre, the wind speed and how long the helmsman takes over the turn, and press play. The yellow line across the water is where a boat sailing at its steady VMG would be: the gap between it and the boat is the distance lost. Bearings are in degrees true: set where the wind comes from, and the compass rose on the water and the readouts give the boat's heading and course as it turns. Watch the speed trace. It falls by between a fifth and almost a half during the turn, depending on the wind and the turn, bottoms out near the end of the turn, then climbs back slowly.

chunks.heading: The tack
chunks.text: And watch the distance lost: in a quick turn it hardly grows at all while the boat is turning. With its sails flapping the boat still has momentum, and while its bow points into the wind that momentum carries it straight to windward, which is exactly where it is trying to go. The loss comes afterwards, in the seconds spent accelerating at well below target speed. In 12 knots of wind with an 8-second turn the J/109 takes 22 seconds to get back to 95% of its speed; in 6 knots, 39.

chunks.heading: The tack
chunks.text: A tack costs the J/109 between 0.5 and 1.3 boat lengths in the model. Sailing coaches' rules of thumb are about one boat length for a keelboat tacking in flat water (Sailing World) and one to two lengths typically (US Sailing), with more in waves. The model sits at the low end of that range, as it should: it sails on flat water, its crew never fumble a sheet, and the boat comes out of the tack exactly on its best upwind angle rather than a little low to build speed, as real crews do.

chunks.heading: The tack
chunks.text: Two things in the plot are worth noticing. In light air the turn time matters little and the cost is dominated by the long, slow acceleration: there is little wind to accelerate the boat. In a breeze a quick turn is clearly better, because the slower the turn, the longer the sails spend luffing and the further the speed falls. And above about 16 knots every tack costs a little more again, because the boat comes out of the tack overpowered at low speed, with its keel at high leeway.

chunks.heading: The gybe
chunks.text: In a gybe the boat turns its stern through the wind, from a broad reach on one side to a broad reach on the other. Choose Gybe above to see it. The physics is the same, but the outcome is very different, as the right-hand panel of the plot shows: a gybe costs the J/109 between a few hundredths and four tenths of a boat length, the most in light air, where the boat has least wind to accelerate it again. The reason is that the sails never stop working.

chunks.heading: The gybe
chunks.text: Turning through dead downwind, the apparent wind stays behind the boat, and the sails keep producing drag-driven force throughout; the mainsail's boom swings across, and the spinnaker is gybed (its sheet released on one side and trimmed on the other) while it partly collapses for a few seconds. Nothing equivalent to the flapping sails of a tack happens, and the boat never slows much.

chunks.heading: The gybe
chunks.text: What a gybe costs instead is risk. The boom crosses the boat in a second or so, carrying the force of the whole mainsail, and in strong wind an uncontrolled gybe can break gear or injure anyone in its path. That is why a crew gybing in a breeze pulls the boom to the centreline first, and why sailing by the lee, with the wind on the same side as the boom, is uncomfortable: the boom can come across without warning. The model's crew always gybe cleanly.

chunks.heading: On moving water: current
chunks.text: Everything so far has assumed the water is still. In tidal waters it rarely is. A current carries the boat with it, and the physics of that is simple: the boat sails through the water exactly as it would on still water, and the water moves over the ground. Velocities just add: where {c} is the current. The surprise is what the current does to the wind. The wind a boat sails in is the air's motion relative to the water it floats in, not to the ground. If the current carries the boat along at 2 knots, the boat feels a 2-knot breeze from the direction the current is going towards, added to the re

chunks.heading: On moving water: current
chunks.text: a different speed and, unless the current runs exactly with or against the wind, a different direction. Sailors call the difference the tidal wind. Set the current below: the calculator finds, for each tack, the heading relative to the wind over the water that makes the most progress towards the true (ground) wind, using the Part 1 polar. - Current with the wind or against it. A current running straight downwind carries both tacks the same amount the wrong way, and also takes away from the wind over the water (2 knots of current in 12 knots of wind leaves 10).

chunks.heading: On moving water: current
chunks.text: Running against the wind it does the opposite: the boat is carried upwind and also gets more wind to sail in. Both tacks are affected equally. - Current across the wind. Now the current carries both tacks sideways by the same amount: on its own it favours neither. But the wind over the water has swung, towards the side the current comes from. With 2 knots of current across 12 knots of wind it swings by about 9°. For the tack heading into the current that is a lift, a wind shift that lets it point closer to the true upwind direction; for the other tack it is a header.

chunks.heading: On moving water: current
chunks.text: In that case the favoured tack makes 5.7 knots towards the wind over the ground and the other 4.4. - Lee-bowing. The favoured tack is the one with the current coming against its lee bow, the bow on the side away from the wind. Sailors have long known that "lee-bowing the tide" pays, and the usual explanation is that the current pushes the boat to windward. The calculation says otherwise: the current's push is the same on either tack. What differs is the wind the boat sails in, and the lee-bowed tack gets the lift. (A current that varies across the course, stronger in one place than another, ad

chunks.heading: On moving water: current
chunks.text: Current also changes the waves. Where the current runs against the wind, the waves it raises meet a current that slows them and squeezes them shorter, and they grow steeper: the short, breaking sea of wind against tide that every coastal sailor knows. Where wind and current run together the sea flattens out. The 3D views in these posts use waves for still water.

chunks.heading: What the model leaves out
chunks.text: The manoeuvre model is a first step from a steady state towards a full simulation, and several of its numbers are assumed rather than measured: - The turn is prescribed: a smooth change of heading over 5, 8 or 12 seconds, coming out exactly on the best angle. A real helmsman steers by feel, often turning faster at the start, and comes out a little low to build speed. - The boat's dynamic properties: added mass (5% of displacement in surge), roll radius of gyration (1.45 m), added roll inertia (30%) and roll damping (15% of critical), all typical values for a boat of this kind, not J/109 measur

chunks.heading: What the model leaves out
chunks.text: - The crew's timing: sheets released and trimmed, and crew moving across, over 3 to 4 seconds; the spinnaker partly collapsing for 3 seconds in a gybe. - Flapping sails add drag with a coefficient of 0.15 on the full sail area. - Sideways motion is quasi-steady: the keel takes whatever leeway it needs, up to a stall at 12°. - Yaw is not modelled: the rudder and the sails' turning moments, which set how fast a real boat can turn and how hard the helmsman has to work, would need yaw coefficients nobody publishes for this boat.

chunks.heading: What the model leaves out
chunks.text: - Waves are not in the physics, and they are the largest omission: in a seaway each tack costs much more, because the boat stops in the waves and has to climb them again while accelerating. The steady-state parts (sails, hull, keel, stability) are exactly Part 1's, so a boat sailing straight on holds its speed to within a thousandth of a knot.

chunks.heading: Method and sources
chunks.text: The manoeuvre simulation integrates surge and roll with a second-order (Heun) method at 0.02-second steps, using Part 1's sail, hull and keel forces at each step; leeway is solved quasi-statically from the side force the keel and rudder must carry, including the centripetal force of the turn. The current calculator uses Part 1's polar, interpolated in wind speed and angle, and optimises each tack's heading for progress over the ground. Code: src/sailing/manoeuvre.py in the blog's repository; Part 1's model is src/sailing/vpp.py. - The J/109 model, its data and sources: Sailing, Part 1.

chunks.heading: Method and sources
chunks.text: - US Sailing, Tacking Tips Part II: The Acceleration: keelboat tack losses "between one and two boat lengths", more if the boat comes out straight onto a close-hauled course. - M. Ingham, A Guide to Tactical Risk Management, Sailing World (2024): about one boat length per tack for a larger keelboat in flat water, three in waves; gybes cost little.

chunks.text: Sclocchi, Favero and Wyart's A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models Reveals the Hierarchical Nature of Data [@sclocchi2024phase] makes a simple, sharp claim about how diffusion models generate images. Take a real image, run the forward noising process partway to some timestep t, then run the backward (denoising) process the rest of the way back to t=0. If t is small, you get back almost exactly the image you started with. If t is large, you get a plausible image of the same rough kind but with different fine details. The paper's finding is that the switch between these two regimes isn't gradua

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: This post reproduces that experiment end to end: real pretrained weights, real ImageNet-derived images, run locally on a Mac (Apple Silicon, no CUDA) rather than the multi-GPU cluster the paper used. The code lives in forward-backward-diffusion, the paper's own release — I had to fix a couple of bugs in it and add Apple GPU (MPS) support to get it running here; the how and why of that is at the bottom of the post.

chunks.heading: Scaling it down to run on a laptop
chunks.text: The paper's own experiment uses OpenAI's 256×256 unconditional ADM diffusion model over the full ImageNet-1k validation set (1000 classes, 10 images each), resampled to 250 diffusion steps, swept across the full 0–250 range of reversal points. Doing that on a single Mac would take a very long time, so this reproduction keeps every piece of the pipeline real but turns the dials down: So: same model, same classifier, same underlying mechanism, real (if smaller) ImageNet-derived data — just a coarser grid and a tenth-scale image set, sized to finish in about 20 minutes on a laptop instead of hour

chunks.heading: Where does the class identity break?
chunks.text: For each reversal point t, we forward-diffuse every starting image to t, denoise it back to a clean image, and ask ConvNeXt-Base what class it thinks the result is — then compare that to what it originally said about the untouched image. samplecorrect and startcorrect track agreement with the true (Imagenette) label; predunchanged tracks whether reconstruction preserved the classifier's own original prediction, which is the more direct read on "did the reverse process preserve identity" independent of whether the classifier was right to begin with.

chunks.heading: A hierarchy of breakdown, layer by layer
chunks.text: The more interesting view is inside the classifier. Every image gets pushed through ConvNeXt-Base twice — once as the original, once as the forward-backward reconstruction — and we compare activations at every one of its ~45 internal layers, from the earliest convolutional stem (depth 0) to the final classification head (depth ≈44). If the paper's hierarchical story is right, shallow layers (fine texture) should start diverging at small t, while only the deepest layers (semantic class) diverge at large t.

chunks.heading: Seeing it directly
chunks.text: Numbers aside, the clearest evidence is just looking at the images. Below, each row is one starting image; each column is the reconstruction after forward-backward diffusion at an increasing reversal timestep. At small t the reconstruction is nearly pixel-identical to the original. At larger t, fine texture is the first thing to change, followed eventually by pose, composition, and — at the largest t we tested — occasionally the object itself.

Fixed by making datasets its own inst

The actual forward-backward experiment script calls diffusion.psampleloopforwback and diffusion.ddimsampleloopforwback — methods that appear nowhere in gaussiandiffusion.py, and never have, across the entire git history. MPS doesn't

chunks.text: 4. torch.distributed collectives on an MPS tensor. The scripts use dist.allreduce/allgather (inherited from the original multi-GPU design) even for a single-process laptop run. chunks.text: This post's comparative framing was originally drafted by an AI research assistant under my general direction, synthesizing my own 2022 dissertation and Sclocchi et al. (2024). The mathematics has been independently re-derived and computed in R below, rather than simply reproduced from that draft. Two pieces of work on this blog turn out to share more mathematics than their subject headings suggest. My 2022 dissertation [@milne2022rg] uses the renormalization group (RG) to describe critical phenomena in thermodynamics and financial markets. An earlier post reproduces Sclocchi, Favero & Wyart's

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Both are, underneath, the same story: a discrete iterated map, a critical parameter, and an unstable fixed point that separates two very different fates for the system. This post makes that bridge concrete rather than just asserting it — implementing both maps in R, finding their fixed points numerically, and plotting the resulting cobweb diagrams side by side.

chunks.heading: Two hierarchies, one structure
chunks.text: Both frameworks simplify a high-dimensional system into a multi-scale tree. In statistical mechanics, a 2D spin lattice is grouped recursively into blocks, each decimated down to a single block-spin variable — Kadanoff's original coarse-graining move. In Sclocchi et al.'s Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), the same tree runs the other way: a class label at the root branches down through latent features to the pixels at the leaves. The parameters line up directly: In both, one parameter controls order versus disorder: K above a critical value Kc gives spontaneous magnetic alignment; f < 1 in the RHM
