chunks.heading: The diffusion side: belief propagation and the class transition
chunks.text: Sclocchi et al. solve the optimal denoising dynamics for the RHM with belief propagation, tracking the probability p of correctly reconstructing a feature at layer : p^=1 (perfect reconstruction) and p^=1/v (chance level) are the two trivial regimes. Whether p^=1 is attractive or repulsive depends on the product sf through F'(1) sf — and that's the whole ballgame: below the threshold, denoising can recover the class; above it, it can't. With s=2, m=3, v=10: the order phase (f=0.3) has fixed points at p (stable), pc (unstable), and p=1 (stable) — a genuine bifurcation. Push f up to 0.8 and p=1

chunks.heading: The diffusion side: belief propagation and the class transition
chunks.text: Two honesty notes. First, p=1/v=0.1 isn't an exact algebraic root of F for arbitrary parameters — I checked this numerically rather than assuming it, and it only holds exactly for special relationships between m, v, s, f. The stable floor above ( 0.098 / 0.076) sits close to 1/v but isn't pinned to it. Second, F'(1) sf is itself an approximation: the exact derivative carries a prefactor {m(v-1)}{mv-1}, which here is — so the true values are and rather than exactly 0.6 and 1.6. Both still land on the correct side of 1, which is all the theory actually needs.

chunks.heading: The diffusion side: belief propagation and the class transition
chunks.text: s, m, and v here were chosen to land close to the illustrative numbers in the original comparison, not pulled from Sclocchi et al.'s own experiments — treat them as a worked example of the mechanism, not a replication of their measured parameters.

chunks.heading: Same bifurcation, two dictionaries
chunks.text: Both maps are governed by the identical mechanism: a system crosses the basin boundary set by an unstable fixed point of a nonlinear discrete map, and the outcome on the other side is qualitatively different from where it started. A magnet losing its alignment, a market crashing, and a diffusion model's reconstructed class flipping to something else entirely are, in this sense, the same event described in three different vocabularies.

chunks.heading: Schröder's equation: the linearizing bridge
chunks.text: Both works lean on the same piece of machinery for handling these maps analytically: Schröder's functional equation [@curtright2011rg], where = '(x^) is the eigenvalue at a fixed point and is the (unknown) conjugating function. It linearizes the messy nonlinear dynamics of into simple scaling by near x^ — which is what lets you extend a discrete iteration into a continuous-time trajectory, x(t) = ^{-1}(^t (x)).

chunks.heading: A brief aside: the Johansen–Ledoit–Sornette crash model
chunks.text: In my dissertation, applying this to the Johansen-Ledoit-Sornette model of financial bubbles — where the scaling factor is complex rather than real — gives the Log-Periodic Power Law: with G periodic and x = |tc - t| the distance from the crash time tc [@johansen1998crashes]. The oscillations get faster (in x) as the crash approaches, which is the model's signature prediction of accelerating, log-periodic herding behaviour before a crash. Sclocchi et al. don't solve an analogue of this — but they make a structural observation that plays a similar bridging role.

chunks.heading: A brief aside: the Johansen–Ledoit–Sornette crash model
chunks.text: The convolutional U-Net used for denoising naturally approximates belief propagation: the encoder path acts as the upward BP pass (coarse-graining noisy pixels into abstract features), and the decoder path with its skip connections acts as the downward pass, mixing global class belief back down with local detail to reconstruct clean pixels.

chunks.heading: Where the analogy breaks: scale invariance
chunks.text: The two frameworks diverge on one point worth stating plainly rather than glossing over. In the RG picture, criticality brings true continuous scale invariance: the correlation length diverges, the lattice spacing becomes irrelevant, and the system is fractally self-similar — which is exactly why wildly different physical materials fall into the same universality class. Diffusion models don't have this. Scale invariance is broken during denoising: the macroscopic scale (the class label) undergoes a sharp, discontinuous transition at a critical noise level, while the microscopic scale (fine tex

chunks.heading: Where the analogy breaks: scale invariance
chunks.text: That's a time-scale separation reflecting the discrete, compositional structure of real data, not the continuous scale invariance of a system at a genuine critical point. The mathematics of the fixed point is shared; the physical picture it's describing isn't quite the same.

chunks.heading: Conclusion
chunks.text: Kadanoff's block-spin decimation and Sclocchi et al.'s belief propagation on the Random Hierarchy Model turn out to be the same functional-equation machinery pointed at two different problems — one asking how magnetic order emerges from a spin lattice, the other how a diffusion model recovers (or loses) a semantic class from noise. See the dissertation for the full RG derivation, and the earlier post for the diffusion side reproduced end to end on real images. Related: Mean-Field Theory and Annealed Disorder is a refresher on the annealed approximation this post's belief-propagation map relies

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Welcome! This blog is where I write up things I'm exploring in math, statistics, and machine learning — usually starting from a paper or an idea I want to understand better, and working through it in code until it's concrete. Expect a mix of interactive explainers, reproductions of results from papers I find interesting, and the occasional deep dive into a dataset or method. Posts will lean toward showing the work rather than just stating conclusions, so there's often code, data, and plots alongside the writing.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Put 23 people in a room and the chance that two of them share a birthday is better than 50%. It feels wrong, which is why it's called a paradox, but it's a true statement and the arithmetic is short.

chunks.heading: Count the complement
chunks.text: Assume 365 equally likely birthdays (ignore 29 February and seasonal effects). Computing "at least one match" directly is messy, so compute the opposite: no one shares a birthday. Person 1 can have any birthday. Person 2 must avoid 1 day, so has probability 364/365. Person 3 must avoid 2 days, so 363/365, and so on. For n people, The probability crosses 50% at n = 23 and passes 99% by n = 57.

chunks.heading: Why it feels wrong: pairs, not people
chunks.text: The intuition says "23 is small next to 365". But we aren't asking whether someone matches my birthday. We're asking whether any pair matches, and the number of pairs grows quadratically: Each pair matches with probability 1/365, so with 253 pairs a match is no longer surprising. (Pairs aren't independent, so this is only a heuristic, but it points at the right scaling.)

chunks.heading: An approximation
chunks.text: Setting this equal to 1/2 and solving for n gives which for d = 365 is about 22.5. So the threshold scales as {d} rather than d. That square-root law is what makes hash collisions arrive so much sooner than people expect: a 64-bit hash has d = 2^{64} values, yet collisions become likely after only about 2^{32} items.

chunks.heading: Monte Carlo check
chunks.text: Simulate it directly: draw n random birthdays many times and count how often a duplicate appears. The simulated points sit on the exact curve to within sampling noise (about 0.007 at 20,000 trials).

chunks.heading: Takeaways
chunks.text: - Count the complement: "no shared birthday" is a clean product. - The surprise comes from {n}{2} pairs, not n people. - Collision thresholds scale as {d}, a fact that shows up well beyond birthdays, in hashing and cryptographic collision attacks.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Every statistics course repeats that correlation is not causation. Almost none of them say what causation is, or how to get from data to a causal answer when you can't run an experiment. Judea Pearl spent forty years building the missing machinery: a language for causal assumptions (diagrams), an algebra for answering causal questions (the do-calculus), and a hierarchy that says which questions each kind of data can answer (the ladder of causation). This post is a tour of that machinery. It covers the person, the three rungs, the mathematics, working R checks of each idea, and why the work mat

chunks.heading: A note on sources
chunks.text: The biographical and historical details below are from memory of the standard sources (Pearl's own books, his Turing Award citation and the usual histories). Check specific dates, titles and attributions before quoting them. The mathematics and every number in the code outputs are computed here.

chunks.heading: Who is Judea Pearl?
chunks.text: Judea Pearl was born in Tel Aviv in 1936 and trained as an electrical engineer at the Technion, later taking graduate degrees in the United States, including a PhD from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn. After industrial research work on electronic devices he joined UCLA in 1970, where he built the Cognitive Systems Laboratory and has worked ever since. His career has two distinct halves, and the second grew out of the limits of the first. 1. Probabilistic reasoning for AI (1980s). At the time, AI reasoned with logic rules and ad-hoc "certainty factors".

chunks.heading: Who is Judea Pearl?
chunks.text: Pearl argued that uncertainty should be handled by probability theory, and made that practical by representing a joint distribution as a Bayesian network: a directed graph in which each variable depends only on its parents. His 1982 paper on message passing in trees and his 1988 book Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems introduced belief propagation, an efficient way to compute posteriors by passing local messages along the graph. 2. Causality (1990s onward). Pearl came to think that a Bayesian network, however good at prediction, says nothing reliable about what happens when you act

chunks.heading: Who is Judea Pearl?
chunks.text: His 1995 Biometrika paper "Causal diagrams for empirical research" introduced the do-calculus, and his book Causality (2000, second edition 2009) set out the full theory. The Book of Why (2018, written with Dana Mackenzie) is the popular version and the source of the "ladder of causation".

chunks.heading: Who is Judea Pearl?
chunks.text: He received the ACM Turing Award for 2011 "for fundamental contributions to artificial intelligence through the development of a calculus for probabilistic and causal reasoning". The citation names both halves. Pearl is also known beyond science. His son Daniel, a Wall Street Journal reporter, was kidnapped and murdered in Pakistan in 2002, and the family set up the Daniel Pearl Foundation in his memory.

chunks.heading: What came before
chunks.text: Pearl did not invent causal thinking from nothing. The pieces he unified were scattered across fields that barely spoke to each other. - Sewall Wright (1921) drew path diagrams for guinea-pig coat colours, the first causal graphs, but the method stayed inside genetics and econometrics. - R. A. Fisher gave the randomised experiment its modern form in the 1920s and 30s. Randomisation works because it deletes the arrows into treatment, which we'll see is exactly what Pearl's do() operator does to a diagram. - Jerzy Neyman (1923) and Donald Rubin (1970s) developed potential outcomes, the other maj

chunks.heading: What came before
chunks.text: - Trygve Haavelmo (1940s) argued that structural equations in economics describe how a system responds to intervention, not just how it is distributed. - Statisticians such as Simpson (1951) documented paradoxes, but statistics had no vocabulary to say which of the two conflicting answers was right. Pearl's contribution was to put these into one framework with a precise graphical language, and to prove which causal quantities can be computed from which data.

chunks.heading: The ladder of causation
chunks.text: Pearl sorts all causal reasoning into three levels, which he calls rungs. Each rung asks a qualitatively different question, and, crucially, data on a lower rung can never answer a higher-rung question without extra assumptions. Rung 1, seeing. Pure statistics lives here: conditional probabilities, regression, and today most of machine learning. Bayes' theorem, as in the prosecutor's fallacy, is a rung-1 tool. It tells you how to update beliefs on evidence, but not what would happen if you changed something. Rung 2, doing. Here we ask about the consequences of deliberate action. The key notati

chunks.heading: The ladder of causation
chunks.text: Rung 3, imagining. Counterfactuals concern a specific individual and a specific alternative history: "Would this patient have recovered had they not been treated?" The quantity P(yx x', y') reads "the probability that Y would have been y had X been x, given that we actually saw x' and y'". Responsibility, blame, regret and explanation all live here. A tidy way to remember the difference: the rooster's crow predicts sunrise (rung 1) but silencing the rooster doesn't stop the sun (rung 2), and "had the rooster not crowed, would the sun still have risen?" is a counterfactual (rung 3) with an obvi

chunks.heading: Same data, different worlds
chunks.text: Why can't rung-1 data reach rung 2? Because very different causal worlds can produce identical observational distributions. Here are two models with the same joint distribution of (X, Y). - Model A: X is a fair coin; Y depends on X: P(Y{=}1 X) = 0.3 + 0.4X. - Model B: a hidden coin U; X is just a copy of U; Y depends on U with the same formula, and X has no effect on Y. The observational columns are identical, and the interventional columns are not: in model A, forcing X moves Y by 0.4, and in model B it does nothing. No amount of rung-1 data separates them. You need to say which model you bel

chunks.heading: Causal diagrams and the three basic structures
chunks.text: A structural causal model (SCM) assigns each variable a function of its direct causes (its parents) plus independent noise: Drawing an arrow from each parent to its child gives a directed acyclic graph (DAG). The graph is the qualitative content of the model: it encodes which variables listen to which, and, just as importantly, which don't. Every DAG is built from three elementary patterns, and each carries a different statistical signature. - In a chain (X M Y) the association flows through M. Conditioning on M blocks it. - In a fork (X M Y) M is a common cause (a confounder), which creates a

chunks.heading: Causal diagrams and the three basic structures
chunks.text: The last is the surprising one, and it is the rule that Pearl's d-separation criterion generalises: a path is blocked by a set Z if it contains a non-collider in Z, or a collider that is neither in Z nor has a descendant in Z. The dsep function above implements it by the standard moralised-ancestral-graph test.

chunks.heading: Colliders in action
chunks.text: Suppose talent and looks are independent in the general population, but a casting director only hires people whose combination of the two is high enough. Among those hired, the two are negatively correlated: someone with modest talent must be good-looking to have got the job. This selection effect, also called Berkson's paradox, is a standard source of spurious findings ("why are the cleverest students so clumsy?") and a good reason not to "control for everything". It also has a cosmological cousin: Martin Rees's fine-tuning argument is a statement about the universes in which observers exist,

chunks.heading: Simpson's paradox, resolved
chunks.text: Here is the classic reversal, using the figures usually quoted for a 1980s comparison of two treatments for kidney stones: open surgery (A) and percutaneous nephrolithotomy (B). Treatment A does better for small stones, better for large stones, and yet B looks better overall. Whether the paradox is a paradox, or which table to trust, depends on the causal story. Doctors give the harder open surgery to the harder cases, so stone size Z influences both treatment X and recovery Y: Z is a confounder. Adjusting for stone size, weighting each treatment's within-size rates by how common each size is

chunks.heading: Simpson's paradox, resolved
chunks.text: The formula used is the backdoor adjustment: This answer is only right because the diagram says size is a confounder. If instead the "Z" were a post-treatment variable (say, a measured side effect of the treatment), adjusting for it would be the wrong move, and the aggregated table would be the right one. The same numbers can give opposite advice. The graph decides, and the data cannot.

chunks.heading: Interventions as graph surgery
chunks.text: Pearl's central idea is that an intervention is a local change to the model. Setting X to x replaces the equation for X with the constant x, which deletes every arrow into X and leaves all other equations alone. The result is the truncated factorisation: if the joint distribution factorises over the DAG as P(v) = P(vi {pa}i), then with the factors for the intervened variables dropped. This is exactly what randomisation does: it makes treatment independent of everything upstream.

chunks.heading: The backdoor criterion
chunks.text: When can we express P(y do(x)) using only observational quantities? The simplest sufficient condition is the backdoor criterion: a set Z satisfies it relative to (X, Y) if 1. no member of Z is a descendant of X, and 2. Z blocks every path from X to Y that starts with an arrow into X (the "back doors"). Then the adjustment formula above is valid. Checking condition 2 is a d-separation test on the graph with X's outgoing arrows removed, which is how backdoorok is written. Here it is on three graphs with different causes of trouble.

chunks.heading: The backdoor criterion
chunks.text: - Confounder: adjust for Z, as in the kidney-stone example. - M-bias: the empty set is valid. Z is not a confounder; it is a collider on the path X U1 Z U2 Y, which is already blocked. Adjusting for it would open the path and introduce bias. Habitually controlling for every pre-treatment variable is not safe. - Front-door: there is no valid set among the observed variables, since the only observed candidate M is a descendant of X. The backdoor route is closed to us. This is where the do-calculus earns its keep.

chunks.heading: The do-calculus
chunks.text: The backdoor criterion is a special case of something more general. Pearl's do-calculus consists of three rules for transforming expressions containing do(). Write G{{X}} for the graph with arrows into X deleted, and G{{Z}} for the graph with arrows out of Z deleted. For disjoint sets of variables X, Y, Z, W: Rule 2: exchange an action for an observation. [equation] Rule 3: insert or delete an action. [equation] where Z(W) is the set of Z-nodes that are not ancestors of any W-node in G{{X}}. Each rule says that when a certain d-separation holds in a surgically modified graph, two interventiona

chunks.heading: The do-calculus
chunks.text: The results that make this more than a curiosity are: - Soundness: every equality derived with the rules is true in every model compatible with the graph. - Completeness (Shpitser & Pearl, and independently Huang & Valtorta, 2006): if a causal effect can be identified from the graph and the observational distribution at all, then some sequence of do-calculus steps will derive it. An algorithm, the ID algorithm, finds one automatically, and returns "not identifiable" otherwise. So whether a causal question is answerable from your data is a decidable property of the diagram.

chunks.heading: The front-door formula
chunks.text: Now the harder case: U is never observed, so we can't adjust for it, but we have a mediator M that is shielded from U. A (hypothetical) example: genotype U affects both smoking X and cancer Y and cannot be measured; smoking acts on cancer only through tar deposits M. Three applications of the rules give The reasoning has three steps, each licensed by a rule. Here the graph conditions are checked by machine. Now the numerical test. Simulate a world with a genuine hidden confounder, so we know the true answer, and see whether the front-door formula recovers it from only the observed (X, M, Y).

chunks.heading: The front-door formula
chunks.text: The naive contrast overstates the effect, because people with high U are both more likely to have X = 1 and more likely to have Y = 1. The front-door formula, which never sees U, lands on the interventional truth.

chunks.heading: Rung 3: counterfactuals
chunks.text: Rungs 1 and 2 describe populations. Counterfactuals describe one unit. Pearl's recipe has three steps, given a fully specified SCM and an observed outcome: 1. Abduction: update the noise terms U to be consistent with what was observed. 2. Action: apply the intervention do(X = x') to the model. 3. Prediction: compute the outcome in the modified model, using the updated U. The result is the counterfactual Y{x'}(u). Counterfactuals are defined inside a model, as a mutilated model plus the unit's own unobserved background, rather than as events in other physical worlds. That is a useful contrast w

chunks.heading: Probability of necessity
chunks.text: A very practical rung-3 quantity is the probability of necessity, "given that the treated patient recovered, the chance they would not have recovered without treatment". It is what a court means by "but for" causation, and it is not identified by experiments alone. Tian and Pearl (2000) showed that experimental and observational data nevertheless bound it: We can test this because we can build a population in which each person's response type is known. There are four types: doomed (never recovers), immune (always recovers), causal (recovers only if treated) and preventive (recovers only if unt

chunks.heading: Probability of necessity
chunks.text: Doctors tend to treat the people most likely to benefit, so treatment is confounded. The true probability of necessity lies inside the bounds, as the theory requires, but the bounds are not tight: experiments and observations together say it is somewhere in an interval, and only extra assumptions (for example, no preventive types, called monotonicity) or knowledge of the mechanism can pin it down. That is the content of "rung 3 needs more than rung 2".

chunks.heading: Genesis: how Pearl shaped early modern AI
chunks.text: Before the late 1980s, the dominant AI approach to uncertainty was to attach ad-hoc "certainty factors" to rules, as in the medical expert system MYCIN, or to avoid numbers altogether. Probability was dismissed as intractable: a joint distribution over n binary variables has 2^n entries. Pearl's insight was that real domains have structure, since most variables are directly relevant to only a few others, and that a DAG captures that structure and makes inference local. Belief propagation computes exact marginals on trees by passing messages between neighbours, in time linear in the number of v

chunks.heading: Genesis: how Pearl shaped early modern AI
chunks.text: The same machinery spread through the field: - Probabilistic graphical models, developed by Lauritzen and Spiegelhalter, Jordan, Koller and Friedman and many others, built a whole toolkit (junction trees, variational inference, structure learning) on Bayesian networks. - Hidden Markov models and Kalman filters, the workhorses of speech recognition and tracking, turned out to be special cases of belief propagation on chains. - Error-correcting codes: the decoders for turbo and LDPC codes, used in mobile networks and satellite links, were recognised in the late 1990s as loopy belief propagation

chunks.heading: Genesis: how Pearl shaped early modern AI
chunks.text: Pearl's message-passing idea is inside the phone in your pocket. - Statistical physics: belief propagation has deep ties to mean-field theory and the Bethe approximation. Fixed points of belief-propagation maps and mean-field theory with annealed disorder are discussed elsewhere on this blog, and they are the same mathematics. The 1980s revolution made reasoning under uncertainty a respectable engineering discipline, and set the stage for the data-driven AI that followed.

chunks.heading: Ongoing: what modern AI is missing
chunks.text: Pearl's later complaint is that the field took the first half of his work and mostly ignored the second. In a 2018 essay (Theoretical impediments to machine learning with seven sparks from the causal revolution) he characterised deep learning as, in effect, sophisticated curve fitting: powerful, but confined to rung 1. The issues are concrete. - Distribution shift and robustness. A model that learns P(y x) is correct only while the data-generating process stays put. Causal mechanisms are the parts that tend to stay stable under change, which is the motivation for invariant risk minimisation (A

chunks.heading: Ongoing: what modern AI is missing
chunks.text: - Decisions, not predictions. Recommendation, pricing and treatment systems are used to intervene. Evaluating a new policy from logs of an old one is a rung-2 question, handled by off-policy evaluation and counterfactual reasoning in advertising and reinforcement learning (Bottou et al. and others). - Fairness. "Would this loan decision have been different had the applicant been of another group, all else causally equal?" is a counterfactual, and counterfactual fairness (Kusner et al.) formalises it. Purely associational fairness metrics can be satisfied by models that are plainly discriminato

chunks.heading: Ongoing: what modern AI is missing
chunks.text: - Explanation. Counterfactual explanations ("you would have been approved with an income £3,000 higher") are rung-3 statements. Regulators increasingly want them. - Large language models. Models trained to predict text have absorbed enormous amounts of causal talk, and can often answer causal questions correctly, but they can also fail in fluent and confident ways. Benchmarks such as CLadder and Corr2Cause were built to separate genuine causal reasoning from pattern recall. Whether next-token prediction can climb the ladder, or only mimic having climbed it, is an open and live debate, and Pear

chunks.heading: Ongoing: what modern AI is missing
chunks.text: - Agents. An AI agent acts, and every action is an intervention on a system whose logs were generated by other behaviour. Judging whether an agent's intervention caused an outcome, rather than coincided with it, is a rung-2 and rung-3 problem. The instrumentation ideas in Instrumenting Agent Cybernetics are about observing agent behaviour, and the do-calculus is the natural language for asking what those observations imply.

chunks.heading: Caveats and critics
chunks.text: Pearl's framework is not universally embraced, and honest accounts note the disagreements. - Identification results depend on the diagram being right. The calculus tells you what follows from your assumptions, but cannot validate them from observational data. Sensitivity analysis and domain knowledge remain essential. - The potential-outcomes school (Rubin, Imbens and others) reaches many of the same results by different means, and some statisticians prefer it for its focus on estimation. The two frameworks are formally equivalent in the cases they both cover, and the long-running debate has b

chunks.heading: Takeaways
chunks.text: - Pearl has two legacies: Bayesian networks and belief propagation, which gave AI a workable theory of uncertainty in the 1980s, and causal inference, which gave science a formal language for intervention and counterfactuals. - The ladder of causation (seeing, doing, imagining) organises questions by what knowledge they require. Data at one rung cannot answer a question at a higher rung without causal assumptions. - A causal diagram is the assumption set. d-separation reads independence off it, graph surgery models an intervention, and the backdoor and front-door formulas are corollaries of th

chunks.heading: Takeaways
chunks.text: - The do-calculus is complete: whether a causal effect is identifiable from observational data is a decidable property of the graph. - Counterfactuals need more than experiments, but experiments and observations together can bound them, as with the probability of necessity. - For AI, the lesson is that prediction is not the same as understanding what happens when you act. Robustness, policy evaluation, fairness, explanation and agent oversight are all causal questions, which is why Pearl's frameworks keep reappearing in current research.

chunks.heading: Further reading
chunks.text: - Judea Pearl and Dana Mackenzie, The Book of Why (2018). The accessible introduction and source of the ladder. - Judea Pearl, Causality: Models, Reasoning and Inference (2nd ed., 2009). The full theory. - Judea Pearl, Madelyn Glymour and Nicholas Jewell, Causal Inference in Statistics: A Primer (2016). A short textbook. - Judea Pearl, "Causal diagrams for empirical research", Biometrika (1995). The origin of the do-calculus. - Ilya Shpitser and Judea Pearl, "Identification of joint interventional distributions in recursive semi-Markovian causal models" (2006). Completeness. - Bernhard Schölko

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: A forensic expert tells the court: "The DNA profile matches the defendant, and only one person in a million would match by chance." The prosecutor concludes: "So there is only a one-in-a-million chance the defendant is innocent." The conclusion does not follow. It swaps a conditional probability for its converse, and the error has contributed to real miscarriages of justice.

chunks.heading: Two different questions
chunks.text: Let E be the evidence (a DNA match) and I the event that the defendant is innocent. The expert can legitimately report the chance of a match if the defendant is innocent. The court needs a different quantity, the chance the defendant is innocent given the match. These are not equal in general, any more than "most cricketers are men" means "most men are cricketers".

chunks.heading: Bayes' theorem supplies the missing piece
chunks.text: where G is guilt. The missing ingredient is the prior P(I): how likely was this person to be the source before the match was known? Suppose the crime happened in a city of N = 2{,}000{,}000 possible suspects, and the defendant was found by trawling a database, with no other evidence. A sensible prior is that each person is equally likely to be the source, so P(G) = 1/N. A true source always matches, so P(E G) = 1. The probability of innocence is about 67%, not one in a million.

chunks.heading: Natural frequencies
chunks.text: The same answer is easier to see by counting people. Among 2,000,000 people: - 1 is the true source, and matches. - The other 1,999,999 are innocent, and about 1{,}999{,}999 10^{-6} 2 of them match by chance. So roughly 3 people match, and only 1 of them is guilty. Picking one matching person at random, the chance they are innocent is about 2/3.

chunks.heading: How much the prior matters
chunks.text: The match probability alone doesn't fix the answer. It depends on how many people could plausibly have done it. A one-in-a-million match is strong evidence when the pool is a few hundred people, and weak when it is millions. Strong evidence only becomes decisive once the prior is also taken into account.

chunks.heading: Simulation check
chunks.text: Simulate many "crimes" in a city of N people: pick the true source, test everyone, and look at the people who match. Then ask how often a randomly chosen matching person is innocent. Pooling all matching people across the simulated crimes reproduces the Bayes answer of roughly two-thirds, and is nowhere near 10^{-6}. The last line is a different quantity: it averages the innocent fraction crime by crime. It comes out lower (about 0.57) because crimes with no innocent matcher count as a full 0, and averaging a ratio is not the ratio of averages. The Bayes calculation, and the question "of every

chunks.heading: Takeaways
chunks.text: - P(E I) and P(I E) are different quantities. Equating them is the prosecutor's fallacy. - The prior (how many people could have done it) is needed to get from one to the other. - Natural frequencies, such as "about 2 innocent people would also match", make the correct reasoning hard to miss. - The mirror image is the defence attorney's fallacy: arguing that because several people would match, the match is worthless. It is still evidence; it just must be weighed against the prior.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Bending light around a black hole: geodesics, the photon sphere and the exact deflection of light; 2. Ray tracing a black hole: cameras, celestial spheres, Einstein rings and multiple images; 3. The Kerr black hole: spin, frame dragging, the Carter constant and the D-shaped shadow; 4. Light from the disk: orbits, temperature, redshift and Doppler beaming.

chunks.heading: About the sources
chunks.text: The account of how the film's images were made, and the parameters used to match them, come from the paper the Double Negative team and Thorne published afterwards: James, von Tunzelmann, Franklin and Thorne (2015), Gravitational lensing by spinning black holes in astrophysics, and in the movie Interstellar. Thorne's book The Science of Interstellar (2014) tells the same story for a general reader. The star field and the disk's texture here are synthetic, so these are recreations of the film's physics, not copies of its frames. Every number in the code outputs is computed when the page is buil

chunks.heading: Kip Thorne and the Double Negative Gravitational Renderer
chunks.text: Kip Thorne is a theoretical physicist at Caltech who has spent his career on black holes, gravitational waves and the strange corners of general relativity. He co-wrote Gravitation, the standard graduate text, and co-founded LIGO, which detected gravitational waves from colliding black holes in 2015. For that he shared the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics with Rainer Weiss and Barry Barish. Interstellar grew out of a film treatment he developed with the producer Lynda Obst, and he served as the film's scientific adviser and an executive producer. According to the 2015 paper, work on the black hole

chunks.heading: Kip Thorne and the Double Negative Gravitational Renderer
chunks.text: Thorne wrote a step-by-step prescription for mapping light from the sky, or from a disk, onto a camera near a spinning hole, and checked it in Mathematica. A Double Negative team including Oliver James, Eugénie von Tunzelmann and the visual-effects supervisor Paul Franklin turned it into a production renderer, the Double Negative Gravitational Renderer (DNGR):

chunks.heading: Kip Thorne and the Double Negative Gravitational Renderer
chunks.text: - about 40,000 lines of C++, running on Double Negative's render farm of 1,633 blade servers; - 23 million pixels per IMAX frame, each traced as a ray bundle, a narrow beam whose cross-section is evolved through curved spacetime, so that stars stay sharp and smooth without flickering; - from 30 minutes to several hours per frame on 10 CPU cores; - the camera's motion, relativistic aberration, Doppler shifts and gravitational redshift all built in. Then came the film-making decisions, and they matter for what follows: - Spin.

chunks.heading: Kip Thorne and the Double Negative Gravitational Renderer
chunks.text: Gargantua's story needs an almost maximally spinning hole: that is what lets an hour on Miller's planet cost seven years on Earth. At that spin the shadow is flattened on one side, the disk's images pile up along the flat edge, and the disk looks off-centre. Nolan and Franklin judged that too confusing for a mass audience, so the images use spin a = 0.6 (in units of the hole's mass) instead. - Doppler shifts. Gas in the disk orbits at a good fraction of the speed of light.

chunks.heading: Kip Thorne and the Double Negative Gravitational Renderer
chunks.text: A real observer would see the approaching side blue-shifted and blazing and the receding side red-shifted and dim. The film left these shifts out. - The disk. It is an "anaemic" artist's disk, not a real quasar disk, which would fry anyone nearby with X-rays. It is thin, it is not accreting, and it shines as a blackbody at a uniform 4500 K. - Lens flare. Audiences expect images filmed through a real camera, so the final images were convolved with the measured point-spread function of an IMAX lens, which gives the soft "veiling flare" glow. The recreation follows the same recipe, with the same

chunks.heading: The mathematics in five steps
chunks.text: Everything rests on one idea. Light follows null geodesics, the straightest possible paths through curved spacetime with zero interval. Rendering means following those paths backwards, from the camera out to wherever the light came from. 1. The spacetime. A spinning black hole of mass M and angular momentum J = aM is described by the Kerr metric. In Boyer–Lindquist coordinates, with G = c = M = 1, Here is the slowing of clocks, the angular velocity at which space itself is dragged round, and , , simple functions of r and (part 3).

chunks.heading: The mathematics in five steps
chunks.text: 2. Three conserved quantities. A light ray in this spacetime carries three constants: its energy, its angular momentum about the spin axis, b, and Carter's constant, q. Carter discovered q in 1968 from a hidden symmetry that lets the equations of motion separate (part 3). Together they fix a ray's path completely.

chunks.heading: The mathematics in five steps
chunks.text: 3. The ray equations. DNGR integrates Hamilton's equations for the Hamiltonian H = 12 g^{}p p: with R(r) and () built from b and q. Five coupled ODEs per pixel. 4. The camera. Each pixel's direction is converted, by relativistic aberration, from the camera's frame to that of a local "zero-angular-momentum" observer swept round by frame dragging, and from there into the ray's initial momenta (part 2, part 3). 5. Shading. A ray that escapes shows the point of the sky it reaches. Lensing conserves surface brightness, by Liouville's theorem, so that point keeps its true brightness (part 2). A ray

chunks.heading: The mathematics in five steps
chunks.text: The ray tracer behind this post integrates those equations with an adaptive Runge–Kutta method, compiled with numba, and checks itself against everything known exactly: the exact deflection angle for a non-spinning hole, Bardeen's formula for the edge of a spinning hole's shadow, the conservation of Carter's constant (which the integrator never uses), and the camera speeds quoted in the DNGR paper. The details, and the checks, are in the explainers.

chunks.heading: Step 1: a black hole in front of the stars
chunks.text: Start with no disk at all: a non-spinning black hole and the night sky behind it, seen from a ship in orbit 30\,M from the hole. This is the classic image of gravitational lensing, the one Alain Riazuelo's film clip made famous and that opens the DNGR paper's discussion. The hole bends every ray that passes it, by an angle that grows without limit as the ray grazes the photon sphere at r = 3M. Rays that pass inside the critical impact parameter b = 33\,M fall in, which makes the shadow two and a half times wider than the horizon itself.

chunks.heading: Step 1: a black hole in front of the stars
chunks.text: Light from directly behind the hole arrives from every direction round the Einstein ring. Inside the ring sits a second image of the whole sky, and inside that a third, each about e^{} 23 times thinner than the last (part 1).

chunks.heading: Step 2: spin
chunks.text: Now let the hole spin. Frame dragging carries light round with the hole: rays travelling with the rotation can skim closer before escaping, and rays travelling against it are captured further out. The shadow loses its circular symmetry. This is the shape Nolan and Franklin turned down. At the film's a = 0.6 the shadow is still nearly round and almost centred. At a = 0.999 it is a D flattened on the approaching side, which is the first thing a viewer would notice about a fast-spinning black hole (part 3).

chunks.heading: Step 3: Gargantua as the film showed it
chunks.text: Add the disk: a thin sheet of gas in the equatorial plane, orbiting on circular geodesics from the innermost stable orbit (3.83\,M for a = 0.6) out to about 20\,M, glowing like a 4500 K blackbody and seen from the film's camera position. The disk is a flat ring, yet the image wraps it over and under the hole. Light leaving the top face of the far side of the disk passes over the hole and is bent down towards the camera, so the far side appears arched above the shadow.

chunks.heading: Step 3: Gargantua as the film showed it
chunks.text: Light from the underside of the far side passes beneath the hole and is bent up, forming the ring below the shadow. A third, thin image of the top face hugs the shadow's edge. The difference spin makes is clearest with the disk in place. Here the same disk surrounds a hole at the film's spin and at nearly the story's spin (compare Figures 14 and 15a of the DNGR paper):

chunks.heading: Step 4: switching on the physics the film left out
chunks.text: The gas does not sit still. At the inner edge of the disk it orbits at more than half the speed of light, so its light is Doppler shifted: up in frequency on the approaching side and down on the receding side. Everywhere, it is also gravitationally redshifted as it climbs out of the hole's well. Both are captured by one factor per ray, where u^t and describe the orbiting gas and b is the ray's angular momentum (part 4). The shift changes the colour, and through Liouville's theorem (I/^3 is the same for every observer) it changes the brightness too. A blackbody at temperature T, seen through a

chunks.heading: Step 4: switching on the physics the film left out
chunks.text: The 4500 K gas appears anywhere from {python} f"{4500glo:.0f}" K to {python} f"{4500ghi:.0f}" K. The DNGR paper quotes shift factors of "order 1.5 and 0.4" for its version of this disk, and the range here is {python} f"{glo:.2f}" to {python} f"{ghi:.2f}". The paper also shows the effect in two steps, colour first and then brightness. Here are the same two steps: The true image is lopsided. The approaching side is white-hot and the receding side dims to a dull red-brown, up to {python} f"{1/glo4:.0f}" times fainter in total light and far fainter still to the eye.

chunks.heading: Step 4: switching on the physics the film left out
chunks.text: The DNGR paper calls the fully realistic disk "exceedingly lopsided, with the hole's shadow barely discernible", and it was never a candidate for the film. Nature does not share Hollywood's concerns. The asymmetry is real, and it is why the Event Horizon Telescope's 2019 image of the black hole in M87 is a ring brighter on one side. Here is the film's version beside the physical one:

chunks.heading: Gargantua in motion
chunks.text: The disk is not a still picture. Its gas orbits, the inner edge faster than the outer, so any pattern in it is sheared into a tighter and tighter spiral. With the camera held still the ray map never changes: it is traced once, and each frame rotates the gas underneath it, every ring at its own orbital angular velocity (r). There is one subtlety. Light from different parts of the image has travelled for different times. The image of the disk curled under the shadow is light that went round the back of the hole, and it left the gas long before the light from the near side. The tracer records eac

chunks.heading: Gargantua in motion
chunks.text: Each 15-second clip compresses about {python} f"{spantM/3600:.0f}" hours of Gargantua's time: the inner edge of the disk goes round almost twice, the outer edge less than a fifth of a turn. First as the film showed it: and then with the Doppler and gravitational shifts. Now the gas brightens as it swings round towards the camera on the left and fades as it recedes on the right: The video's texture adds some clumpier structure to the gas so that the rotation is easy to follow. The ray map is the same 5.8 million rays for every frame, and the clips are rendered by animate.py in the gargantua pro

chunks.heading: The soundtrack
chunks.text: The music is computed from the disk too. Each note is a ring of gas, and its pitch is the ring's orbital frequency. Those frequencies are a few millionths of a hertz, far below hearing, so every one of them is raised by the same 24 octaves. That is a factor of 2^{24} 17 million, and it keeps every ratio between them, so the chord you hear is the chord the rings make. The rings are chosen to be in resonance with the outer edge, orbiting 1, 1½, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 times as fast.

chunks.heading: The soundtrack
chunks.text: That gives the open fifths and octaves of an organ chord, a nod to the church organ in Hans Zimmer's score. The outer edge sounds first and the inner rings join one by one, every 1.5 seconds. Each note swells and fades once per turn of its ring in the clip. The voice is three slightly detuned pipes per note, with organ-like overtones and a synthetic stone-hall reverb. It is all generated by soundtrack.py, with no recorded or licensed audio.

chunks.heading: How long it takes
chunks.text: Computing power has moved on since 2014, and a still image at blog resolution is far less demanding than a 23-million-pixel IMAX frame traced as ray bundles. Each ray takes on the order of a hundred adaptive Runge–Kutta steps. Once a ray map is traced, shading it with a different disk model or a different set of frequency shifts takes a second or two, which is how the film, colour-shift and full versions above all come from one trace.

chunks.heading: What this leaves out
chunks.text: A few things that DNGR did, and this recreation does not: - Ray bundles. DNGR evolved the cross-section of a narrow beam around each pixel's ray using the equation of geodesic deviation, which gives exact magnifications and smooth, flicker-free motion. Here, the same information comes from differences between neighbouring rays: stars are placed by mapping triangles of the image grid onto the sky (part 2), and extended light is filtered with a mip-map. - The disk. The film used a thin disk, a 17-million-voxel volumetric disk and procedurally textured close-ups.

chunks.heading: What this leaves out
chunks.text: Here it is an infinitely thin, opaque disk with a simple streak texture. - The lens and the film stock. DNGR convolved images with an IMAX lens's measured point-spread function and computed colours with the sensitivity curves of motion-picture film. Here a generic glare and the human eye's colour response (CIE 1931) stand in. - Motion. In the film the camera moves, so stars stream round the critical curves and the images are motion-blurred. These are stills.

chunks.heading: Thorne's other image
chunks.text: The DNGR paper ends by noting that the same code produced Interstellar's wormhole, described in a companion paper (James, von Tunzelmann, Franklin and Thorne 2015, American Journal of Physics). The paper's own assessment is that its work on the disk "retreads largely known ground", which goes back to Jean-Pierre Luminet's 1979 image of a disk round a non-spinning hole, computed and then drawn by hand. Its lensing of a star field by a camera close to a fast-spinning hole, with the caustics and critical curves that structure it, was new. A Hollywood film paid for research in general relativity,

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: > "A monstrous tripod, higher than many houses, striding over the young pine trees, and smashing them aside in its career; a walking engine of glittering metal ... Can you imagine a milking stool tilted and bowled violently along the ground?" > > H. G. Wells, The War of the Worlds (1898), Book I, chapter X Wells gives us a three-legged walking machine and almost nothing about how it walks. This post takes him at his word and builds one. The machine is a 257-tonne, 30-metre tripod simulated in MuJoCo, the physics engine that now underpins a large part of robot-learning research. It walks into a

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: - what MuJoCo is, and why Google DeepMind bought it and gave it away; - the leg kinematics, statics and stability of a three-legged machine, worked through with the model; - why Wells's "bowled milking stool" cannot simply roll, and the planned-fall gait that works instead; - the other end of the story: how the cylinders would have to be fired from Mars, the transfer orbit to Earth, and what arriving at 12 km/s would do to the Martians inside. The video below is the simulation itself, seen from eye height in the village, with a soundtrack synthesised from the simulated motors, footfalls and fi

chunks.heading: About the model and the sources
chunks.text: The simulation code lives in the martian-tripod project alongside this blog. Every number in this post's code outputs comes from running it, or from the orbital calculations below. Wells gives few engineering details, so the machine's dimensions and masses are choices, not quotations. The history of MuJoCo is written from memory of the published record, so check specific dates before quoting them.

chunks.heading: Where the Martians came down
chunks.text: Seven of the ten cylinders land in the novel, all within about 25 miles of London. The interactive atlas below follows them from the sand pits on Horsell Common to the great pit on Primrose Hill. It also traces the Martian advance, the narrator's route through Surrey and London, and his brother's flight to the Essex coast. Use the day buttons or Play to watch the invasion unfold, and click any marker for the passage it comes from.

chunks.heading: MuJoCo: the physics engine of robot learning
chunks.text: MuJoCo (Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact) was written by Emanuel Todorov, with Tom Erez and Yuval Tassa, at the University of Washington. It was introduced in the 2012 paper "MuJoCo: A physics engine for model-based control". As the title says, it was built for control: for computing what an articulated body will do, quickly and accurately, so that an optimiser could plan its movements.

chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text: Game physics engines usually simulate each rigid body separately and hold them together with joint constraints. MuJoCo instead works in generalised coordinates, the joint angles themselves, and writes the dynamics of the whole mechanism as where q and v are joint positions and velocities, M is the mass matrix, c collects gravity, Coriolis and centrifugal terms, the motor torques, and f the contact and constraint forces acting through their Jacobian J. The distinctive part is contact. MuJoCo treats contacts as soft constraints and finds the contact forces by solving a small convex optimisation

chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text: The method is fast, stable at large timesteps, and well-defined in both directions. Given a motion, it can recover the forces that produced it, and that inverse dynamics is what model-based controllers need. Models are written in an XML format, MJCF. The tripod's model file is generated from a single Python parameter file, so changing a leg length changes everything consistently.

chunks.heading: From research tool to AI infrastructure
chunks.text: MuJoCo's speed made it the default simulator for a new kind of AI. - Deep reinforcement learning (2015 onward). Learning to control a body by trial and error needs millions of simulated episodes. The continuous-control benchmarks that became standard (HalfCheetah, Hopper, Walker, Ant, Humanoid in OpenAI Gym, and later the DeepMind Control Suite) were all MuJoCo models. Algorithms such as TRPO, PPO, DDPG and SAC were developed and compared on them. - Sim-to-real robotics. OpenAI's Dactyl hand learned to manipulate a cube in simulation before doing it on a real robot hand.

chunks.heading: From research tool to AI infrastructure
chunks.text: DeepMind trained small humanoid robots to play football in MuJoCo and transferred the policies to hardware. - DeepMind's acquisition (2021). DeepMind, where Tassa and others now worked, bought MuJoCo in October 2021 and made it free. In 2022 it was released as open source under the Apache 2.0 licence. That removed the licence cost that had kept it out of many labs and classrooms. - Scaling up. MuJoCo 3 added MJX, a re-implementation in JAX that runs thousands of simulations in parallel on GPUs and TPUs. The point is the same as with large language models: learning is limited by how much experi

chunks.heading: From research tool to AI infrastructure
chunks.text: In short, MuJoCo is to robot learning roughly what large text datasets are to language models: the source of experience. The control methods in this post are classical rather than learned, but they lean on the same features. These are an exact, fast forward model, cheap inverse dynamics and Jacobians, ray casting (used for the Heat-Ray) and easy access to every internal quantity.

chunks.heading: The machine
chunks.text: The model follows Wells where he is specific and makes engineering choices where he is not.

chunks.heading: Leg kinematics
chunks.text: Each leg hangs from the underside of the hood at azimuth ai \{0^, 120^, 240^\}, on a circle of radius rh = 2.6 m, dh = 2 m below the hood's centre. It has three joints: a yaw that swings the leg's plane round, then a hip pitch qh and knee qk that work in that plane like a two-link arm.

chunks.heading: Explainer series
chunks.text: This section and the gait planning below are covered in more depth in a four-part explainer series: forward kinematics, inverse kinematics, statics and the Jacobian and planning the falling walk.

chunks.heading: Forward kinematics
chunks.text: Within the leg plane, measure the thigh and shin by their elevation angles 1 = -qh and 2 = -(qh + qk). The foot, relative to the hip, is at where {m}i = (rh ai,\ rh ai,\ -dh) is the hip mount.

chunks.heading: Inverse kinematics
chunks.text: Going the other way, to find joint angles that put the foot at a given point, is what every gait needs. Transform the target into the hip's frame to get (x, y, z). Then the yaw is = {atan2}(y, x), which leaves a planar problem with horizontal reach = {x^2 + y^2} and height z. The law of cosines gives the knee bend: with 2 = 1 + . There are two solutions, . The model takes the knee-up one, with knees above the line from hip to foot. That is how a spider or a harvestman stands, and it is the silhouette everyone draws for Wells's machines. A solution exists only if the foot lies in the annulus |L

chunks.heading: Inverse kinematics
chunks.text: In the walking stance the thigh is almost level and the shin drops nearly vertically, like a harvestman's leg. Rearing up to look round takes the foot to about 90% of full reach. That is why the machine has to stop to do it: from there it cannot take a full stride.

chunks.heading: Statics: what the motors must hold
chunks.text: A leg pushing on the ground with force {f} at the foot needs joint torques where J is the foot's Jacobian, the matrix that maps joint velocities to foot velocity. This is the principle of virtual work: power in at the joints equals power out at the foot, { q} = f{ p}. For a vertical foot force Fz, the hip-pitch torque is just Fz times the foot's horizontal distance from the hip, less the moment of the leg's own weight: Here is that estimate against what MuJoCo's balance controller actually commands while the machine stands still.

chunks.heading: Statics: what the motors must hold
chunks.text: The hand calculation and the simulation agree. The hip carries most of the load because the foot is almost 20 m out from it. The knee, sitting nearly above the foot, carries much less. That is the advantage of the spider stance: the shin stands almost vertical, so the knee works little, and the hip motor does most of the work.

chunks.heading: Can a tripod roll? The milking-stool problem
chunks.text: Wells's image, a milking stool "tilted and bowled violently along the ground", suggests the machine rolls over its legs like a wheel without a rim. That is a classic model in walking research, the rimless wheel (McGeer, 1990): N rigid spokes of length L around a hub of mass M and radius of gyration kL. Between footfalls the wheel pivots over the stance spoke. When the next spoke strikes the ground, the collision is instantaneous, so angular momentum about the new contact point is conserved. Two spokes are 2 = 2/N apart, which gives For a three-spoke wheel, 2 = 120^ = -12.

chunks.heading: Can a tripod roll? The milking-stool problem
chunks.text: Unless k^2 > 12, the ratio is negative, which would need the trailing foot to pull on the ground. It can't, so the footfall stops the roll dead. The milking stool only bowls along if most of its inertia is out in its legs. The tripod's isn't, as MuJoCo's mass properties show. So the legs must carry the body over every step. The project's rimlesswheel.py checks the impact law against MuJoCo contact simulations: the six-spoke wheel's steady rolling speed down a 15° slope matches theory to about 1%, and a three-spoke wheel stops at the first footfall.

chunks.heading: Balance: the support triangle and the hinge
chunks.text: A body standing on point feet is statically balanced when its centre of mass lies above the support polygon, the convex hull of the feet. For a tripod that is a triangle. With all three feet down the machine is stable, but it cannot step: lifting any foot shrinks the support polygon to the line between the other two. On two feet the machine is a hinge. Nothing the motors do can produce a moment about the line through two point feet, so across that line the body simply falls.

chunks.heading: Balance: the support triangle and the hinge
chunks.text: Treat it as an inverted pendulum with the centre of mass at height h. If y is the horizontal distance of the centre of mass from the hinge line, The fall is slow because the machine is tall, but it cannot be stopped from two feet. The swinging leg must land in time to catch it. The tumble is therefore part of the gait itself: Wells's bowled milking stool, in three dimensions.

chunks.heading: Walking by planning the fall
chunks.text: The project's first gait waited out the topple. It moved the centre of mass to just inside the edge of the next two-foot support, lifted a leg, let the body fall onto it, and settled. That works, but slowly: in the project's tests, about 1.1 mph, with the hood tilting by up to 17°. The faster gait plans the fall instead, using the standard model from humanoid robotics: the linear inverted pendulum with a zero-moment point (ZMP). Hold the centre of mass at constant height h. Then its horizontal position c obeys where z is the ZMP, the point on the ground through which the net ground force acts.

chunks.heading: Walking by planning the fall
chunks.text: The ZMP is what the legs control, and it must stay inside the support polygon. With three feet down, it can go anywhere in the triangle. With one leg swinging, it is confined to the line between the other two, which is the hinge again, seen from the planner's side.

chunks.heading: Walking by planning the fall
chunks.text: Over a timestep t with z held fixed, the pendulum's motion is exact: Given the footstep rhythm, the planner chooses z0, , z{N-1} over a 14-second horizon to minimise a quadratic cost: The terms keep the walking speed, keep up with the footstep schedule, smooth the ZMP and centre it in the support ({ p}k is the centroid of the planted feet). The constraints are the pendulum dynamics and linear inequalities keeping each zk inside its support triangle or on its hinge line. It is a quadratic programme, solved with OSQP, and re-solved from the measured state at every change of support and every 0.4

chunks.heading: Walking by planning the fall
chunks.text: Re-planning from the measured state is what makes this model-predictive control. A whole-body controller then turns the plan into joint torques. It computes the ground force and moment that keep the centre of mass and hood on plan, and shares them among the planted feet by least squares, never pulling on the ground and staying within friction. It maps each foot's share to joint torques through J^, the statics formula from earlier.

chunks.heading: Walking by planning the fall
chunks.text: The centre of mass never stops. It swings from side to side as each two-foot hinge appears in a different direction, which is the 3-D version of the bowled stool. The hood stays within a few degrees of level, and the machine walks at about 5.5 mph, five times the speed of the wait-and-topple gait with a sixth of its tilt. How fast could it go? Animals of very different sizes walk in dynamically similar ways at the same Froude number {Fr} = v^2/(g), where is leg length.

chunks.heading: Walking by planning the fall
chunks.text: People switch from walking to running near {Fr} 0.5. By that measure the simulated machine is strolling, at a tenth of a person's dynamic pace. Its speed is limited by the 40 MN·m motors and by the planner, not by geometry. Faster rhythms manage 6–7 mph for a dozen steps and then fall, as the swing legs saturate. A machine that strode at Wells's evident pace would need much stronger joints, or a planner that also chooses where to put its feet.

chunks.heading: The road from Mars
chunks.text: The fighting-machines are the end of a much longer journey. Wells describes it in his first chapter: astronomers see "a huge outbreak of incandescent gas upon the planet", then another, "and so for ten nights, a flame each night". The Martians are firing a vast gun, one shot a night, and each shot is a cylinder about thirty yards across that will land in Surrey. How hard is that?

chunks.heading: Launching from the surface
chunks.text: To leave Mars and still be moving at speed v relative to it once far away, energy conservation gives the speed needed at the surface: A gun has no burn time: all of that speed must be given inside the barrel. For a barrel of length L and constant acceleration a, v^2 = 2aL, so the acceleration the passengers feel is The atmosphere then slows the cylinder on the way out. For a body with ballistic coefficient = m/(CD A) crossing an exponential atmosphere of surface density 0 and scale height H at angle , the speed falls by a factor \!(-0 H / (2)).

chunks.heading: Launching from the surface
chunks.text: Mars helps here too: its column of air, 0 H, is about 40 times smaller than Earth's. This is why the gun is on Mars and not on Earth. Jules Verne's moon gun would lose a large part of its speed to the air, while a Martian gun gives up only a few per cent.

chunks.heading: Choosing the moment: porkchops and oppositions
chunks.text: Which v? That depends on when the gun fires and how long the trip takes. Model Mars and Earth on circular, coplanar orbits (1.524 AU and 1 AU). Then fix the departure time and the flight time. The cylinder's path between Mars's position at departure and Earth's position at arrival is the solution of Lambert's problem: the Keplerian orbit through two points in a given time. It is solved here with the universal-variable method. Plotting the required speeds over a grid of departure dates and flight times gives the mission designer's porkchop plot.

chunks.heading: Choosing the moment: porkchops and oppositions
chunks.text: The cheapest shot is the Hohmann transfer, half an ellipse touching both orbits. It takes eight and a half months and must be fired about five months before opposition, while Earth is still well behind Mars, so that Earth arrives at the meeting point at the same time as the cylinder. Wells has his astronomers see the flashes as Mars approaches opposition, which is the right season. Firing at opposition, when the planets are closest, is not cheapest: Earth is already pulling ahead, and catching it quickly costs much more speed.

chunks.heading: Choosing the moment: porkchops and oppositions
chunks.text: Even the gentlest shot needs a muzzle speed of almost 6 km/s. Accelerating to that at a survivable 10 g would need a barrel well over a hundred kilometres long. A barrel of a kilometre or so, closer to anything one might call a gun, means more than a thousand g. Wells's Martians are, in his description, little more than great heads with hands. Perhaps a body built like that, raised in Mars's 0.38 g, packs well for a violent ride.

chunks.heading: Ten nights, ten shots
chunks.text: Why one shot a night? A gun built into the ground turns with the planet. Mars's day (the sol) lasts 24 h 37 min, almost the same as Earth's, so the gun points along its firing line once per sol. Each cylinder follows nearly the same path, so they arrive about a day apart, as they do in the novel: the first lands in the early hours of a Friday, the second around Friday midnight, the third on Saturday night. Near opposition Mars is highest in the sky around midnight, so watchers on Earth would see each flash at nearly the same hour, drifting about 40 minutes later each night: Wells's "a flame ea

chunks.heading: Arriving: entry and impact
chunks.text: The cylinder reaches Earth's atmosphere at the entry speed in the table, at least 11.6 km/s. It is a ballistic body with no wings or parachute in Wells, so its descent follows the equations of planar atmospheric flight: with the angle below horizontal and (h) = 0 e^{-h/H}. For a steep, fast entry the classic Allen–Eggers result gives the peak deceleration in closed form, independent of the body's mass, so the passengers' worst moment depends only on how fast and how steeply they come in. The impact speed, by contrast, depends strongly on mass. The cylinder's mass is not given, so the calculati

chunks.heading: Arriving: entry and impact
chunks.text: A heavy cylinder barely notices the air. It would reach Horsell Common at several kilometres per second and release the energy of a small nuclear weapon, leaving a crater rather than Wells's "enormous hole" in a sand pit, with a cylinder still intact enough to unscrew. A light cylinder is slowed to a few hundred metres per second, which is survivable for a strong hull and fits the novel's sandy pit and the "still so hot" metal much better. Either way, the occupants ride through a peak deceleration of well over a hundred g, set by the entry speed and angle, not by the hull. A shallower entry or

chunks.heading: Takeaways
chunks.text: - MuJoCo grew from a 2012 research engine for model-based control into the standard simulator for robot learning. Its fast, convex contact model and generalised-coordinate dynamics make it suited to both classical control and reinforcement learning, and DeepMind's 2021 purchase and open-sourcing made it free to everyone. - A tripod's leg is a two-link arm on a yaw joint. Inverse kinematics is the law of cosines; the knee-up spider stance puts the load on the hips; and statics is = J^ f, which the simulation confirms by hand.

chunks.heading: Takeaways
chunks.text: - A three-legged machine cannot roll passively. The rimless-wheel impact law, ^+/^- = (k^2 + 2)/(1 + k^2), is negative for a tripod unless most of its mass is in its legs. - Walking on three legs means repeatedly falling about a hinge. Planning that fall with a linear inverted pendulum and a model-predictive ZMP planner gives a steady 5.5 mph with the hood within a few degrees of level. - The cylinders are the hard part. A gun on Mars works, because Mars has little air. The cheapest shot leaves about five months before opposition, needs almost 6 km/s, a barrel of tens or hundreds of kilometres
