chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: On 16 July 1969 at 13:32 UTC a Saturn V lifted off from Launch Complex 39A. Eight days later the command module Columbia splashed down in the Pacific with three men who had been to the Moon. This series rebuilds that flight, numerically, from the records NASA published in 1969 and 1970, and uses it as a tour of orbital mechanics. 1. Launch to translunar injection (this post): the ascent, the parking orbit, and the burn that leaves Earth. 2. Translunar coast and lunar orbit insertion: free return, midcourse corrections, and braking into lunar orbit. 3. Descent and landing: Eagle separates from

chunks.heading: How the reconstruction works
chunks.text: No continuous telemetry for the whole mission survives in usable form. What does survive are tables: the spacecraft's position and velocity at key moments ("state vectors"), the times of every burn, and the orbits that resulted. These were produced after the flight by NASA, Boeing and TRW from radar tracking and onboard data. So the reconstruction works from anchors. Each documented state is taken as true. Between anchors, the trajectory is filled in by one of three methods: - Interpolation, where the tables are dense enough (the ascent).

chunks.heading: How the reconstruction works
chunks.text: - Propagation, integrating the equations of motion forward with a modern force model: Earth's gravity including its equatorial bulge, plus the Moon and the Sun, using JPL's DE421 ephemeris for where they were in July 1969. - Fitting, where a burn is known only by its start, end and result. A simple rocket model is solved for the steering that best joins the two anchors. Wherever the model arrives at a documented anchor, the difference between the two is reported. Those residuals are some of the most informative numbers in the post. The display marks every value by where it came from:

chunks.heading: The first six hours
chunks.text: Press play, or jump to an event. Playback speeds up automatically through the long, quiet stretches and slows down for the burns. There are four panels. The ground track follows Apollo 11 over the rotating Earth. The inertial view looks down on the orbit from above its plane, in a frame that does not rotate, which is where the orbital mechanics is easiest to see. The 3D view is a computer-generated model of the Saturn V, built to scale and flown along the reconstructed trajectory, with staging, tower jettison and the transposition and docking.

chunks.heading: The first six hours
chunks.text: The last panel scrolls the crew's and Mission Control's words with the clock. Turn the sound on and choose Real time to hear NASA's recordings wherever they exist for that moment; the launch film plays in the same panel around liftoff. The rest of the post walks through what is happening in each phase, and why.

chunks.heading: Launching from a spinning Earth
chunks.text: Before the engines light, the vehicle is already moving. Kennedy Space Center sits at 28.5° N, and Earth's rotation carries it east at The 1969 ascent table lists exactly this at liftoff: an Earth-fixed velocity of 1.5 ft/s (the vehicle has barely moved) but a space-fixed velocity of 1,340.7 ft/s, or 408.6 m/s. That is about 5% of the speed needed for orbit, free, provided the rocket flies east. The launch site also limits the orbit. An orbit's plane passes through Earth's centre, so the orbit must reach at least the latitude of the place it started from.

chunks.heading: Launching from a spinning Earth
chunks.text: For a launch from latitude on heading A (measured east of north), spherical trigonometry gives the inclination: Apollo 11's parking orbit had i = 32.521^. Solving for the inertial heading at liftoff gives A = 32.521^ / 28.447^, so A 73.6^. The Saturn V rolled onto a heading north of due east, trading a little of Earth's free speed for the orbital plane needed to reach the Moon on that day.

chunks.heading: The gravity turn
chunks.text: The ascent is a compromise between two losses. Climbing vertically wastes thrust holding the rocket up against gravity, so the vehicle should turn horizontal quickly. Turning while still in the thick lower atmosphere puts large side loads on a vehicle 110 m tall, so the vehicle should stay pointed along its velocity until the air thins. The Saturn V pitched over gently and then let gravity bend the trajectory, which is why it is called a gravity turn. The flight-path angle tells the story. It climbs to about 29° at maximum dynamic pressure, 83 seconds after liftoff, and is then flattened by th

chunks.heading: The gravity turn
chunks.text: The green dots are the eleven documented rows of the ascent table; the lines between them are interpolated. The gap between the two speed curves at liftoff is Earth's rotation. It stays at roughly 0.4 km/s all the way to orbit.

chunks.heading: The parking orbit
chunks.text: At 11 minutes 49 seconds the third stage shut down with Apollo 11 moving at 25,567.9 ft/s (7.793 km/s), level with the horizon, 103 nautical miles up. Everything about the orbit follows from that single state vector. The vis-viva equation links speed v to distance r from Earth's centre and the orbit's semi-major axis a: From a, the period is P = 2{a^3/}. The eccentricity vector, e = v h/ - { r} with h = r v, gives the shape, and h gives the plane. Running the documented insertion state through these formulas reproduces NASA's published orbit almost exactly: There is a puzzle hidden in that tab

chunks.heading: The parking orbit
chunks.text: The orbit was inserted at an altitude of 103.2 n mi, yet its published apogee, the highest point, is only 100.4 n mi. The explanation is that the two numbers use different references. The insertion altitude is measured above the ellipsoid, the slightly squashed shape of the real Earth, which at 32.5° N is about 6 km below the equatorial radius. The apogee and perigee are measured above a sphere of equatorial radius. With that understood, the numbers agree to within 0.1 n mi.

chunks.heading: Venting and the orbital paradox
chunks.text: The parking orbit lasted two and a half hours, a little over one and a half revolutions, while the crew and Mission Control checked the spacecraft. Propagating the insertion state forward through that time, with Earth's oblateness, the Moon and the Sun, gives this speed at the moment the third stage reignited: The model is 36 ft/s (11 m/s) fast. That is too large to be rounding. It is the sort of gap a small, steady push would make, and the S-IVB third stage was pushing. In orbit its liquid hydrogen boiled off continuously and had to be vented. The vent was arranged to push the stage gently fo

chunks.heading: Venting and the orbital paradox
chunks.text: Here orbital mechanics turns against intuition. Pushing forward adds energy, which raises the far side of the orbit. Half a revolution later, the spacecraft is higher and therefore moving more slowly. Over one and a half revolutions, a steady forward push leaves the vehicle slower and later than it would otherwise be. Solving for the constant along-track acceleration that reproduces the documented speed gives: On a stack of around 140 tonnes, 1 mm/s² is a thrust of about 140 newtons, or roughly 30 pounds-force. That is a plausible size for hydrogen venting, though the 1969 tables used here do

chunks.heading: Venting and the orbital paradox
chunks.text: It has a testable consequence: by the time of ignition it raises the orbit by about 15 km at that point, which a documented ignition altitude would confirm or rule out. The rest of the reconstruction includes this acceleration in the parking orbit.

chunks.heading: Translunar injection
chunks.text: At 2 hours 44 minutes 16 seconds, over the central Pacific on the way towards Hawaii, the S-IVB's J-2 engine restarted and burned for 346.83 seconds. When it stopped, Apollo 11 had left the parking orbit and was on its way to the Moon.

chunks.heading: Why burn low and fast
chunks.text: The specific orbital energy, kinetic plus potential per kilogram, is In the parking orbit -30.4\ {km}^2/{s}^2. To reach the Moon's distance it must rise to about -0.7. A burn that changes speed by v changes the energy by so the same v buys more energy the faster the vehicle is already moving. This is the Oberth effect, and it is why the burn was made in low orbit, at 7.8 km/s, rather than after climbing away from Earth. The documented state 10 seconds after cutoff (the formal "translunar injection" point) gives the new orbit: That is an ellipse with eccentricity 0.977 and a semi-major axis of

chunks.heading: Reconstructing the burn
chunks.text: The tables give the burn's start and end, the propagated state at ignition, and the documented state just after it. They do not say how the engine was steered. To fill that in, the burn is modelled as a constant-thrust rocket, so its acceleration rises as propellant is used, with the thrust direction pitched and yawed off the velocity vector by angles that change linearly with time. That gives five unknowns: a0 and an offset and a rate for each of pitch and yaw. They are solved by least squares so that the trajectory lands on the documented TLI state.

chunks.heading: Reconstructing the burn
chunks.text: - The acceleration rises from 0.65 g to 1.4 g as the S-IVB empties. The crew felt the burn build steadily for almost six minutes. - Gravity losses are about 140 m/s. The engine's ideal velocity change is around 3,183 m/s, but the speed gained is 3,044 m/s. As the burn went on the vehicle climbed, and its flight-path angle rose from 0° to about 7°. Once the path tilts upwards, part of gravity pulls back along the direction of travel, and the engine has to make that up.

chunks.heading: Reconstructing the burn
chunks.text: - The fit misses the documented state by 36 km and 5 m/s. Most of the miss is along the track, equivalent to arriving about 3 seconds late. That is the accumulated error of propagating two and a half hours from insertion with a simplified venting model. The reconstruction spreads the correction across the burn, then restarts exactly from the documented TLI state.

chunks.heading: Free return, and why it still needed correcting
chunks.text: Apollo 11 left Earth on a free-return trajectory: a path that, with no further burns, swings around the far side of the Moon and falls back to Earth. If the main engine had failed, the crew would still have come home. The reconstruction can test that directly. Take the documented TLI state, include the small "evasive" burn the crew made at 4 hours 40 minutes to move away from the spent S-IVB (19.7 ft/s, its direction taken from the maneuver PAD read up to the crew), and propagate with no further burns.

chunks.heading: Free return, and why it still needed correcting
chunks.text: One more anchor keeps the path honest: at 26 hours 45 minutes, when the real midcourse correction was made, the trajectory is snapped onto the state NASA documented for that moment. Then it is left alone. Select Earth–Moon above to see the path; it is the dashed yellow curve.

chunks.heading: Free return, and why it still needed correcting
chunks.text: The uncorrected path does loop around the Moon and come back, but it passes about 220 n mi above the lunar surface, against the 86.7 n mi at which Columbia actually fired its engine to enter lunar orbit. Returning to Earth, it would have struck the atmosphere at about 55°, far too steeply, where the safe entry corridor is a band of only a degree or two around 6.5°. This shows how sensitive a lunar trajectory is. Re-running the propagation with the injection speed raised by just 1 m/s, one part in 11,000, moves the closest approach by about 675 km and the arrival by 17 minutes.

chunks.heading: Free return, and why it still needed correcting
chunks.text: The miss is real: no rocket stage is perfectly accurate, which is why Apollo carried a schedule of midcourse corrections. The reconstruction is good enough to see this. Propagated from the documented TLI state with the evasive burn, it stays within 3 n mi and 3 ft/s of every state NASA tabulated up to 4 hours 40 minutes; by 26 hours it has drifted 84 n mi, which is why it is re-anchored there. Only one correction proved necessary on the way out, a 3-second burn of the service propulsion engine at 26 hours 45 minutes.

chunks.heading: Free return, and why it still needed correcting
chunks.text: Part 2 reconstructs that burn and the arrival at the Moon. The dashed red lines mark the radii of Earth and the Moon. The uncorrected trajectory dips towards the Moon at about 75 hours and plunges back into Earth at about 147 hours.

chunks.heading: Method and sources
chunks.text: For how the coordinate frames, views, synchronisation and data sources fit together across the series, see the explainer Frames of Reference in the Apollo 11 Reconstruction. The reconstruction is written in Python with numpy and is driven from a single file of documented anchors, each tagged with its source. The force model is Earth's central gravity plus the J2 oblateness term, with the Moon and Sun as third bodies. Their positions come from JPL's DE421 ephemeris, rotated into the mean equator and equinox of 16 July 1969, which is the frame Apollo's tables use.

chunks.heading: Method and sources
chunks.text: The integrator is an adaptive Dormand–Prince 5(4) method with a relative tolerance of 10⁻¹¹. - R. W. Orloff and S. Garber, Apollo by the Numbers: A Statistical Reference, NASA SP-2000-4029, Apollo 11 ascent, Earth-orbit and translunar tables, via the Apollo Flight Journal edition. - Boeing, Apollo/Saturn V Postflight Trajectory, AS-506 (D5-15560-6, October 1969), for the TLI state vector. The geocentric distance, latitude and longitude here are as transcribed by Grant Hutchison in Converting Apollo State Vectors To Orbits, whose companion post is a good guide to these documents. - TRW, Apollo

chunks.heading: Method and sources
chunks.text: One correction was made to the source data. In the scanned ascent table, the longitude at S-IC centre-engine cutoff reads −81.1517°, which would put the rocket 50 km west of the pad after 25 n mi of travel east. It has been taken as −80.1517°. Next: Part 2, translunar coast and lunar orbit insertion.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: This is the second of four posts that rebuild the flight of Apollo 11 from the numbers NASA published in 1969 and 1970. 1. Launch to translunar injection: the ascent, the parking orbit, and the burn that leaves Earth. 2. Translunar coast and lunar orbit (this post): three days of coasting, one midcourse correction, and the two burns that put Columbia and Eagle into orbit around the Moon. 3. Descent and landing: Eagle separates from Columbia and flies the powered descent to Tranquility Base. 4. Rendezvous, return and entry: ascent, rendezvous with Columbia, the burn home, and splashdown.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Part 1 left the spacecraft at 2 hours 50 minutes, moving away from Earth at 10.8 km/s. This part follows it for the next four days, to 100 hours, when Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin are about to undock Eagle. Along the way it covers how the spacecraft was tracked, why one small burn on day two mattered so much, where the Moon's gravity takes over from Earth's, why every burn at the Moon was made out of radio contact, and why the orbit around the Moon would not stay the shape it was put in.

chunks.heading: A correction to Part 1
chunks.text: Building this part turned up something missing from Part 1. About two hours after TLI, once Eagle had been pulled clear of the spent S-IVB stage, the crew fired the service propulsion system (SPS) engine for 2.9 seconds. This "evasive" burn of 19.7 ft/s moved Columbia and Eagle safely away from the stage, which was about to vent its leftover propellant to send itself past the Moon. Part 1's free-return test did not include that burn, so its uncorrected path was off. Part 1 has been updated: with the evasive burn included, the reconstruction stays within 3 n mi and 4 ft/s of every documented st

chunks.heading: How this part is built
chunks.text: As in Part 1, the reconstruction works from anchors, states documented in the 1969 tables, and fills the gaps between them with a force model. Two things are new. - The Moon's own shape. Near the Moon, the model adds the two largest terms of the Moon's gravity field beyond a simple sphere: its flattening (J2) and its elongation towards Earth (C{22}). Positions on the Moon use the IAU's model of the Moon's orientation, so the ground track can be drawn in lunar latitude and longitude. - Burns that last minutes.

chunks.heading: How this part is built
chunks.text: Lunar orbit insertion took almost six minutes. The engine is modelled as a constant-thrust rocket with an exhaust velocity of 3.10 km/s, steered in the local-horizontal frame that the crew's maneuver PADs use. The steering is solved for, by least squares, so that the trajectory meets the documented states at ignition and cutoff. The display marks every value by where it came from:

chunks.heading: Four days, from Earth to lunar orbit
chunks.text: Press play, or jump to an event. Playback runs quickly through the long coast and slows down for the burns and around the Moon. The first panel shows the whole trip, either in a frame that turns with the Moon (the clearest way to see the path) or in a fixed one, and can close in on the Moon. The second is the Moon itself, with the ground track, the landing site, the side in darkness, and the side hidden from Earth, where there is no radio. The third is a computer-generated view of Columbia and Eagle, docked, flown along the reconstructed trajectory, rolling slowly in "barbecue" mode during the

chunks.heading: Four days, from Earth to lunar orbit
chunks.text: The last panel scrolls the voice transcripts with the clock. Turn the sound on and choose Real time to hear NASA's recordings wherever they exist for that moment. The rest of the post explains what is going on, roughly in the order it happened.

chunks.heading: Tracking a spacecraft from Earth
chunks.text: For the three days between TLI and the Moon, nobody aboard was steering. Columbia and Eagle were falling, along a path set by the TLI burn and by the gravity of Earth, the Moon and the Sun. Mission Control knew where they were by tracking them: the 85-foot dishes of the Manned Space Flight Network in Goldstone, Madrid and Honeysuckle Creek measured the range to the spacecraft from the round-trip time of a radio signal, and the range rate from its Doppler shift. Fitting a trajectory to hours of those measurements gave a state vector good to a fraction of a mile.

chunks.heading: Tracking a spacecraft from Earth
chunks.text: The flight controllers shared the results. Every so often the Public Affairs Officer (PAO) read out the spacecraft's distance and speed to the press. Those calls are in the transcript, and they make a good test of the reconstruction, because none of them was used to build it. The distances turn out to be heights above the surface, not distances from the centre, and once the Moon is close they switch to being measured from the Moon.

chunks.heading: Tracking a spacecraft from Earth
chunks.text: The dots are the speeds the PAO announced; the lines are the reconstruction. Earth's gravity slows the spacecraft from 35,500 ft/s at TLI to under 3,000 ft/s two and a half days later. Then the Moon's pull wins and the speed relative to the Moon climbs again. The differences between the PAO's distances and the model's are below. On the final approach to the Moon the speeds agree within a few ft/s and the heights within about 20 to 45 n mi, roughly a minute of travel. Further out they mostly differ by tens of miles, which is what a short delay between when a number was computed and when it was

chunks.heading: Tracking a spacecraft from Earth
chunks.text: Three calls are off by 450 to 650 n mi. For those, the distance and speed disagree with the model in opposite senses, so a late reading cannot explain them; they are more likely slips in the reading or the transcription. The reconstruction itself is checked against the states NASA tabulated for the start of the coast. Propagated from the documented TLI state, with the evasive burn included, it lands on each of them within about 3 n mi and 4 ft/s:

chunks.heading: The one midcourse correction
chunks.text: The flight plan allowed for four midcourse corrections on the way out. Only one was needed. At 26 hours 44 minutes 58 seconds the SPS fired for 3.13 seconds and changed the velocity by 20.9 ft/s, about 6 m/s, at a moment when the spacecraft was moving at 5,025 ft/s relative to Earth. Small as it was, it mattered. By 26 hours the reconstruction, propagated from TLI, has drifted 84 n mi from where NASA's tables put the spacecraft. That is not an error in the physics; a trajectory to the Moon is so sensitive that tiny differences at the start grow into large ones.

chunks.heading: The one midcourse correction
chunks.text: So at MCC-2 the reconstruction is re-anchored on the documented state and starts again. The burn itself is known from the maneuver PAD that Bruce McCandless, the CapCom, read up to the crew an hour before: the velocity change in the local-vertical frame, mostly downwards, towards Earth, and partly forwards. Applying the PAD's direction scaled to the achieved 20.9 ft/s does not bring the spacecraft to the right place:

chunks.heading: The one midcourse correction
chunks.text: Applied as recorded, the burn would bring the spacecraft past the Moon at 177 n mi rather than the documented 86.7 n mi; with no burn at all, it would pass at 326 n mi. The fitted burn that does arrive at the right height, at the right speed and with loss of signal at the right moment is 19.0 ft/s, about 2 ft/s smaller than the documented one and in a slightly different direction. That 2 ft/s is a measure of how sensitive the trajectory is, more than of anything wrong with the burn.

chunks.heading: The one midcourse correction
chunks.text: At this point each foot per second moves the arrival by tens of nautical miles. The documented state used as the anchor is given to the nearest tenth of a nautical mile in height and the nearest hundredth of a degree in direction, and a hundredth of a degree in the direction of travel, 200,000 km from Earth, is already a few tens of kilometres. The fit absorbs that rounding. What the comparison does show is why Apollo did not rely on a single correction: the navigation teams tracked the result of each burn and planned the next, and on Apollo 11 the other scheduled corrections were not needed.

chunks.heading: Where the Moon takes over
chunks.text: Halfway to the Moon by distance is not halfway by gravity. The Moon is 81 times less massive than Earth, so the point where their pulls balance lies about 90% of the way there. For working out trajectories, though, the balance point is not the most useful boundary. What matters is where it becomes more accurate to treat the Moon as the main attractor and Earth as a disturbance than the other way round. Laplace worked out the radius of that sphere of influence: where a is the Earth–Moon distance and m/M the mass ratio.

chunks.heading: Where the Moon takes over
chunks.text: For the Moon that is about 66,000 km. Inside it, the motion is well described by a two-body orbit around the Moon; outside, by one around Earth. Joining the two at the boundary is the method of patched conics, which Apollo's planners used for first estimates before refining with numerical integration, as this reconstruction does throughout.

chunks.heading: Where the Moon takes over
chunks.text: NASA logged the crossing at 61 hours 39 minutes 55 seconds: The documented crossing, 34,765 n mi from the Moon's centre, sits a little inside the Laplace radius for that moment, 36,886 n mi. The formula is an approximation, and NASA's software used its own definition of the boundary. The speeds at the crossing are the clearer story. Relative to Earth, the spacecraft had slowed to 2,990 ft/s. Relative to the Moon it was moving faster, 3,775 ft/s, because the Moon itself travels at about 3,350 ft/s in its orbit, across the spacecraft's path. From here, the Moon accelerated it all the way in.

chunks.heading: Behind the Moon
chunks.text: Every burn at the Moon was made out of radio contact. That was not chosen; it is geometry. To slow down into lunar orbit, the spacecraft has to burn at its closest point to the Moon, and a free-return trajectory passes closest behind the Moon, as seen from Earth. So the critical burn happened with the Moon between the crew and Mission Control, and the controllers learned whether it had worked only when the signal came back. The loss and acquisition of signal (LOS and AOS) times are well documented, from PADs read to the crew and from PAO announcements. In the model they come from pure geometry

chunks.heading: Behind the Moon
chunks.text: The last row is the most striking. The PAD gave the crew two AOS times: one if the burn went as planned, and one if the engine did not fire at all. Without a burn the spacecraft would come out from behind the Moon sooner, at 76:05:30, still on the free-return path towards Earth. The reconstruction, which simply follows the approach trajectory around the Moon with no burn, gives 76:05:30.4. Mission Control could tell at the first moment of contact which trajectory Apollo 11 was on, from the clock alone. The signal returned at 76:15:29; the burn had happened. The later times drift slowly through

chunks.heading: Lunar orbit insertion
chunks.text: At 75 hours 49 minutes 50 seconds, 86.7 n mi above the far side, Columbia's engine fired for 357.5 seconds, nearly six minutes, to slow the stack by 2,917 ft/s.

chunks.heading: Arriving fast
chunks.text: The spacecraft arrived at 8,250 ft/s relative to the Moon. Escape speed at that height is so the spacecraft was on a hyperbola: left alone, it would have whipped round the Moon and left with about 1.1 km/s to spare, which is what the free-return design intended. To be captured, it had to shed at least 800 ft/s. To reach the planned orbit, it shed 2,917. As with TLI, the Oberth effect favours burning where the spacecraft is moving fastest, at the closest point to the Moon. Changing speed by v there changes the orbital energy by v\, v, so the same braking does the most good.

chunks.heading: A six-minute burn
chunks.text: Six minutes is long. During the burn the spacecraft travelled about 750 km, more than 20° of the way round the Moon. A burn that long cannot be treated as an instant change of velocity, so it is modelled as a finite, constant-thrust burn. The fit solves for the steering that joins the documented state at ignition to the documented cutoff conditions: Two features of the fitted steering stand out. First, the thrust at ignition points 15.7° away from the PAD direction. The PAD's velocity change is an impulsive equivalent: the single kick at one instant that would have the same result.

chunks.heading: A six-minute burn
chunks.text: A real burn that sweeps through 20° of arc has to start pointing off that direction and end pointing off it the other way. Second, the fit settles on a steady pitch of 0.075° per second relative to the local horizontal. That is almost exactly the rate at which the local horizontal itself turns as the spacecraft moves round the Moon, about v/r = 2.5/1900 radians per second, or 0.076° per second. In other words the thrust stayed close to fixed in space, as the guidance would hold it, while the Moon's surface turned beneath.

chunks.heading: A six-minute burn
chunks.text: The burn also changed the plane of the orbit. The PAD had a sideways component of 394 ft/s, which in the reconstruction turns the plane by about 5°. The approach path had been chosen for a safe free return; the orbit had to pass over the landing site two days later. The height keeps falling through the burn: the spacecraft reaches its closest point to the Moon during the braking, not before it. The result was an orbit of about 170 by 60 n mi, with a period of 2 hours 8.6 minutes.

chunks.heading: LOI-2
chunks.text: Two revolutions later, at 80 hours 11 minutes 36 seconds, a second burn of 16.9 seconds lowered the far point of the orbit. This one was made at the low point, behind the Moon again, and was nearly impulsive, so it is easier to fit. The orbit after LOI-2 was 66.1 by 54.5 n mi, not circular. That was deliberate, and the last row of the table shows the reconstruction agreeing with its purpose: two and a half days later, at 102 hours 45 minutes, the plane of the orbit passes within 0.03 n mi of Tranquility Base. The orbit's shape was chosen so that the Moon's gravity would pull it round to nearly

chunks.heading: Mascons
chunks.text: In 1968, Paul Muller and William Sjogren at JPL analysed the tracking of the Lunar Orbiter spacecraft and found that the Moon's gravity was lumpy. Under the large circular maria, the dark plains on the near side, there are concentrations of mass, mascons, that pull orbiting spacecraft down as they pass over and speed them up. Their effect on a low orbit is large: over a day they can change its height by miles. The force model in this reconstruction has only the two largest, smoothest terms of the lunar gravity field.

chunks.heading: Mascons
chunks.text: Those cannot reproduce the mascons, and the comparison shows it: The green dots are the documented orbits, from NASA's tables and PAO announcements. The real orbit's high point fell from 66.1 to 63.7 n mi and its low point rose from 54.5 to 56.0 n mi in the 20 hours before undocking, closing towards the circle the planners wanted. The model's orbit (red and blue) wobbles by a few tenths of a mile each revolution and otherwise stays where LOI-2 left it, as does the orbit around a perfectly round Moon (grey). The gap between the green dots and the coloured lines is the mascons.

chunks.heading: Mascons
chunks.text: By undocking the model is 5 n mi low and 18 ft/s fast. For that reason Part 3 does not continue this propagation; it starts from NASA's documented state at the start of the powered descent and works backwards and forwards from there. The missing physics is known; modelling it would take a gravity field with many more terms, of the kind built later from Lunar Prospector and GRAIL tracking.

chunks.heading: The view from lunar orbit
chunks.text: Apollo 11's orbit was retrograde: it went round the Moon from east to west, at an inclination of about 1° to the lunar equator. Seen from Earth the spacecraft crossed the near side from right to left, passed over the eastern maria, Smythii, Fecunditatis and Tranquillitatis, and disappeared behind the western limb into the radio shadow. Watch the Moon panel through a revolution to see the track cross the landing site. On the second revolution the crew pointed a television camera out of the window and flew the approach to the landing site for viewers on Earth, calling out the landmarks Eagle wou

chunks.heading: If the engine had not fired
chunks.text: The free-return trajectory was the safety net for LOI. If the SPS had failed to fire, Apollo 11 would have swung round the Moon and come back. The reconstruction can follow that path too: take the arrival state at LOI-1 ignition and propagate with no burn. Select Rotating with the Moon above to see it as the purple dashed curve. The spacecraft would have reached Earth's atmosphere at about 145 hours, six days after launch. The yellow dashed curve is the path with no midcourse correction, passing the Moon higher and coming back on a different line. In the frame that turns with the Moon, both fo

chunks.heading: Method and sources
chunks.text: For how the coordinate frames, views, synchronisation and data sources fit together across the series, see the explainer Frames of Reference in the Apollo 11 Reconstruction. The reconstruction is written in Python with numpy and is driven from a single file of documented anchors, each tagged with its source. The force model is Earth's central gravity plus J2, the Moon and the Sun as third bodies from JPL's DE421 ephemeris, and, within 20,000 km of the Moon, the Moon's J2 and C22 terms (J2 = 2.03310^{-4}, C{22} = 2.23810^{-5}), oriented by the IAU 2009 lunar rotation model.

chunks.heading: Method and sources
chunks.text: Everything is expressed in the mean equator and equinox of 16 July 1969, the frame of the Apollo tables. The integrator is Dormand–Prince 5(4) with a relative tolerance of 10⁻¹¹. Heights above the Moon are measured from a sphere of radius 1,738.09 km, the reference radius of the 1969 tables. Burns are fitted with a damped least-squares (Levenberg–Marquardt) solver, with the PAD values as weak priors.

chunks.heading: Method and sources
chunks.text: 1. From the documented TLI state, coast with the documented evasive burn to midcourse correction 2. 2. Re-anchor on the documented state at MCC-2 ignition and fit the 3-second burn so the trajectory arrives with the documented height and speed at LOI-1 ignition, the documented loss of signal, and the documented closest approach. 3. Fit LOI-1 and LOI-2 as finite burns to the documented ignition and cutoff conditions, with the landing site's distance from the orbit plane at landing as one more target. 4. Propagate to 100 hours with no further changes. Every other number in the post, including th

chunks.heading: Method and sources
chunks.text: - R. W. Orloff and S. Garber, Apollo by the Numbers, NASA SP-2000-4029, Apollo 11 translunar and lunar orbit tables, via the Apollo Flight Journal edition. - TRW, Apollo Mission 11 Trajectory Reconstruction and Postflight Analysis (1970). - The Apollo 11 Flight Journal, for the maneuver PADs, the LOS and AOS times, and the narrative of the coast and lunar orbit. - NASA's Apollo 11 Technical Air-to-Ground Voice Transcription and Onboard Voice Transcription, via Spacelog, for the transcript and the PAO calls. - NASA's mission audio highlights reels for Day 2, Day 3 and Day 4 at the Internet Arch

chunks.heading: Method and sources
chunks.text: Each reel is an edited selection; segments are pinned to mission time by matching the reel's captions to the transcript, and are accurate to a few seconds. - P. M. Muller and W. L. Sjogren, "Mascons: lunar mass concentrations", Science 161 (1968), 680–684. The maria in the Moon panel and the 3D view are drawn as circles at their approximate positions and sizes, to give a sense of place, not as a map.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: This is the third of four posts that rebuild the flight of Apollo 11 from the numbers NASA published in 1969 and 1970. 1. Launch to translunar injection: the ascent, the parking orbit, and the burn that leaves Earth. 2. Translunar coast and lunar orbit: three days of coasting, one midcourse correction, and the burns that put Columbia and Eagle into lunar orbit. 3. Descent and landing (this post): Eagle undocks, drops to 50,000 feet, and flies twelve and a half minutes of powered descent to Tranquility Base.

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: 4. Rendezvous, return and entry: ascent, rendezvous with Columbia, the burn home, and splashdown. Part 2 ended at 100 hours, with the two spacecraft still docked in a 63 by 56 nautical mile orbit. This part covers the next three hours: undocking, the separation of Columbia and Eagle, the burn behind the Moon that lowered Eagle's orbit, and the powered descent itself. The descent is the most heavily documented part of the flight, and also the part where the 1969 tables are thinnest, because almost all of it happened under closed-loop guidance. So this part rebuilds the guidance as well as the t

chunks.heading: How this part is built
chunks.text: As before, the reconstruction works from anchors: documented states, burn times and results. What is new is the powered descent, which is reconstructed in three pieces. - The braking phase is simulated with the LM's own guidance law. The computer in Eagle steered with a quadratic guidance law, described by its designer Allan Klumpp, aimed at a target state stored in its memory. The targets for Apollo 11 are in the published listing of the Luminary 99 software's pad loads. The reconstruction flies that law, with the descent engine's documented throttle schedule, from the documented PDI state.

chunks.heading: How this part is built
chunks.text: - The approach phase uses the same law, with the approach targets. It is checked against Aldrin's altitude callouts and against the angles he read off the landing point designator. - The last two minutes are fitted to the callouts. Armstrong took over at about 400 feet. From there the path is flown by a controller like the LM's rate-of-descent mode, steered to follow the altitudes, descent rates and forward speeds Aldrin called out, and to end at the landing site at contact light. A handful of quantities that no surviving table gives are solved for, and the post says which ones as it goes. Eve

chunks.heading: Undocking to touchdown
chunks.text: Press play, or jump to an event. Playback slows down through the descent and runs at close to real time for the last few minutes. The first panel is the descent seen from the side, height against distance to the landing site. The second is a map of the approach, with Eagle's and Columbia's ground tracks. The third is a computer-generated view of Eagle, flown along the reconstruction over a model of the terrain near Tranquility Base; try Aldrin's window for the crew's view. The last panel shows Eagle's computer display as the reconstruction has it, with the program alarms, alongside the voice t

chunks.heading: Undocking to touchdown
chunks.text: Turn the sound on and choose Real time to hear NASA's recording of the landing, and to see the 16 mm film shot through Aldrin's window. The radio buttons above the panels switch the side view between the whole powered descent, the last eight thousand feet, and the last two minutes; and the map between the 300-mile approach and the few thousand feet around the landing site.

chunks.heading: Undocking and separation
chunks.text: At 100 hours 12 minutes, behind the Moon, Eagle undocked. When the signal came back six minutes later Armstrong reported "The Eagle has wings." For the next twenty minutes the two spacecraft flew in formation while Armstrong turned Eagle round in front of Columbia's window so that Collins could look over its landing gear. Then, at 100:39:53, Collins fired Columbia's thrusters for 9 seconds, a gentle push of 2.7 ft/s straight down, towards the Moon. A push towards the Moon does not make a spacecraft drop away. A radial burn changes the shape of the orbit but not its size, so the period is the s

chunks.heading: Undocking and separation
chunks.text: Relative to Eagle, Columbia traces a closed loop once per revolution, about 0.5 n mi below and then above, and up to 2 n mi behind, and returns to where it started an orbit later. It is a small, safe separation that keeps the two spacecraft in sight of each other without either one having to plan around the other, which is why it was chosen.

chunks.heading: Undocking and separation
chunks.text: The reconstruction does not start at undocking. It starts at PDI, an hour later, and is traced backwards through the descent orbit insertion burn to here. These checks, then, test the whole chain: The separation burn and the orbit after it match NASA's tables to within about a mile. The undocking state is further out, 7.5 n mi in height and 33 ft/s in speed. The tables give only height and speed, not position along the orbit, and an orbit 63 by 56 n mi passes through 62.9 n mi twice each revolution. The 1969 orbit's low point had been dragged around by the mascons (Part 2), and this reconstruc

chunks.heading: Descent orbit insertion
chunks.text: On the next pass behind the Moon, at 101:36:14, Eagle's descent engine fired for 30 seconds, at 10% thrust and then 40%, and slowed it by 76.4 ft/s. That is less than 1.5% of its orbital speed, but it was enough to drop the far side of its orbit from about 60 nautical miles to about 8. Half an orbit later, at its lowest point, Eagle would be 50,000 feet above the surface, about 260 miles east of the landing site. This is the same trick as the transfer orbits in Parts 1 and 2, in miniature: a small burn on one side of an orbit moves the opposite side a long way. To lower perilune by r from a ne

chunks.heading: Descent orbit insertion
chunks.text: The height of the low point is the number that mattered, and it is the one that is hardest to pin down. The tables give 57.8 n mi at DOI cutoff; the onboard computer worked out an orbit of 57.2 by 9.1 n mi, against 8.5 predicted, all measured from the landing site's radius. The reconstruction's descent orbit, traced back from the documented PDI state, is 59.8 by 7.9 n mi. A mile at perilune was well within what the guidance could absorb: Bennett's 1970 analysis notes that an overburn of only 12 ft/s, 3 seconds, would have put Eagle on a path that hit the Moon. Its two-stage throttle schedule w

chunks.heading: Powered descent initiation
chunks.text: At 102:33:05 Eagle's descent engine lit again, at 10% thrust, to settle the propellant and let the engine's gimbal centre on the centre of mass. Twenty-six seconds later the computer commanded full thrust. Eagle was 47,000 feet above the landing site, moving at 5,560 ft/s, and 264 nautical miles from where it would land. Here the reconstruction does its main piece of solving. NASA's tables give the time, height and speed at PDI. They do not give where along the orbit Eagle was, or the exact slope of its path.

chunks.heading: Powered descent initiation
chunks.text: Those two numbers, together with one illegible guidance target, are found so that the simulated descent, flown by the LM's own guidance law, reproduces three documented events: the throttle coming down 386 seconds after ignition, Eagle reaching 7,129 feet at 102:41:32, when the computer switched to the approach phase, and, traced backwards, the 57.8 n mi height at DOI cutoff.

chunks.heading: Powered descent initiation
chunks.text: The fitted flight-path angle is a quarter of a degree, close to the zero expected at the low point of the descent orbit, and the range is close to Bennett's "about 260 n mi". The 47,444 ft height is above the landing site; the crew's estimate from timing landmarks was 52,000 ft, and the computer's own figure differed from the landing radar's by 2,900 ft when the radar locked on, the "DELTA-H" Aldrin called at 102:38:04.

chunks.heading: The braking phase
chunks.text: Eagle's computer did not follow a stored trajectory. Every two seconds it worked out an acceleration command from where it was and where it wanted to be. Klumpp's guidance law makes the commanded acceleration a quadratic in the time-to-go T (negative, counting up to zero at the target): in a frame centred on the landing site with x up, z downrange and y across. The targets rT, vT, aT are not the landing site; they are a point some way beyond the end of the phase, chosen on the ground so that the path arrives at "high gate" in the right attitude and at the right height for the crew to see the l

chunks.heading: The braking phase
chunks.text: which makes the time-to-go consistent with the target jerk j{Tz}. The descent engine provides the thrust: the guidance's command minus gravity. Here the design meets the hardware. The descent engine could not be throttled between 65% and about 92% of its rated 10,500 lbf without damaging its injector, so for most of the braking phase it ran at a fixed 92.5%, and the guidance used only the direction of its command. As the vehicle lightened, the thrust it asked for fell, and when it fell below 57%, the computer took over the throttle.

chunks.heading: The braking phase
chunks.text: On Apollo 11 that "throttle recovery" came at 386 seconds, against 384 planned. Simulated with the Luminary 99 targets, the braking phase passes through high gate at 7,131 ft, with time-to-go to its target point 56 s (the targets were set about 60 s beyond high gate), and arrives 133 ft/s down where the mission report gives 125.

chunks.heading: The braking phase
chunks.text: There is an independent check in NASA's audio. Through the braking phase the Public Affairs Officer read out Eagle's altitude and speed for the press, and the highlights reel catches three of those calls in a stretch whose timing is fixed by the crew's words around them: One feature of the reconstruction is not checked by anything. In the first two minutes after PDI the simulated LM climbs by about 3,700 ft before it starts down, because the guidance holds the thrust slightly above the horizontal while the speed is still high. With the PDI state placed exactly at the low point of the orbit it

chunks.heading: The alarms
chunks.text: Four minutes into the burn, as Eagle yawed to put its windows up and its landing radar towards the surface, the crew turned to the computer display and saw a program alarm: 1202. It recurred at 102:39:02, and three more, 1201 and 1202, came in the approach phase. Both codes meant that the computer had more work queued than it had time to do and had restarted, dropping the lower-priority jobs and keeping the guidance running. The cause, found after the flight, was the rendezvous radar's interface sending a stream of spurious counts that took up roughly an eighth of the computer's time. The guid

chunks.heading: The approach phase
chunks.text: At 102:41:32 the computer switched to the approach program, P64, with a new set of targets close to the landing site, and pitched Eagle nearly upright, so that for the first time the crew could see where they were going. The display now showed a landing point designator angle: Armstrong could look through a scale etched on his window, at that angle, and see where the computer was taking him. Aldrin read the angle out three times. The reconstruction can compute it from the geometry, as the angle of the line of sight to the computer's aim point below Eagle's horizontal plane: These are independe

chunks.heading: The approach phase
chunks.text: They also confirm the geometry of what happened next. The point the guidance was flying to was not the planned landing site. A small error in Eagle's velocity at PDI, from undocking and venting that the navigation had not counted, had left the computer about 21,000 ft uprange of where it thought it was, and it was steering for a point about four miles beyond the planned site. The crew had noticed early, from landmarks passing "a little long". What the designator showed Armstrong was a crater the size of a football stadium, West crater, with a field of boulders around it.

chunks.heading: Armstrong flies the last two minutes
chunks.text: At about 102:43:20, 410 feet up and moving forward at 50 to 60 ft/s, Armstrong switched to the rate-of-descent mode, P66. The computer still controlled the throttle, holding whatever descent rate Armstrong set with a switch; he flew the attitude, and so the horizontal speed, by hand. He kept going, over West crater and its boulder field, looking for a clear place. That last part of the path is reconstructed from what Aldrin called out, nearly every few seconds: height, descent rate, and forward speed. The model is flown by a controller with the same structure as P66, a 1.5-second time constant

chunks.heading: Armstrong flies the last two minutes
chunks.text: The calls fit together well, with one exception. Added up, the forward speeds Aldrin read cover only about 2,600 ft, while the automatic approach left Eagle about 3,500 ft from where it landed when Armstrong took over. To close the gap, the reconstruction's forward speed starts at the automatic speed and comes down to the calls over about a minute; it runs 5 to 15 ft/s above them through P66. The calls were the computer's estimate of velocity, updated by the landing radar, and the timing of a spoken number is uncertain by a second or two, so a difference of this size is within what the record

chunks.heading: Armstrong flies the last two minutes
chunks.text: The purple dashed line in the charts and the side view is where the computer would have taken Eagle without him. It reaches its target, 111 ft above the aim point, about 55 seconds before the actual contact light, 1,100 ft short of where Eagle landed, at the western edge of West crater and its boulders.

chunks.heading: Sixty seconds
chunks.text: On the ground, the descent engine's propellant was watched second by second. When a low-level sensor in the tanks tripped, a clock started: when it ran out, the crew would have 20 seconds to land or abort. Charlie Duke called "60 seconds" at 102:45:02 and "30 seconds" at 102:45:31. Contact light came at 102:45:40. The reconstruction's descent uses 6,949 ft/s, 173 ft/s (2.6%) more than the 6,775.6 ft/s NASA's tables give, and lands with 650 lb of usable propellant, about 73 seconds of hover. Bennett's post-flight analysis puts the margin at touchdown at 40 to 50 seconds.

chunks.heading: Sixty seconds
chunks.text: Both differences point the same way: the reconstruction flies a little less efficiently than Eagle did, most of it in the braking phase, where the fitted path is about 4,900 ft further from the site and 75 ft/s faster at high gate than Bennett's nominal. The propellant figures also depend on the engine's efficiency, here taken as a specific impulse of 303 s; an engine about 2% less efficient, 296 s, would bring the margin down to Bennett's figure. The low-level warning had in fact come early: propellant sloshing in the tanks uncovered the sensor, and post-flight analysis found Eagle had more l

chunks.heading: Tranquility Base
chunks.text: "Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed." Eagle had come down about four miles from the planned target, which is what a 21,000 ft error at PDI would do, plus Armstrong's 1,100 ft. Where those 21,000 ft came from, and how Apollo 12 avoided them, is the subject of a separate post: Vent, Bent, Descent, Lament. The Sun was 10.6° above the eastern horizon in the reconstruction, low enough for every boulder to throw a long shadow, which was why the landing time was set when it was. Collins, in Columbia, was 64 n mi up and about 230 n mi to the west, already moving on round the Moon. On

chunks.text: For how the coordinate frames, views, synchronisation and data sources fit together across the series, see the explainer Frames of Reference in the Apollo 11 Reconstruction. The trajectory before PDI is the force model of Parts 1 and 2: the Moon with its J2 and C{22} terms, Earth and the Sun as third bodies, integrated with a Dormand–Prince 5(4) method. For the descent, the LM is simulated with the guidance computed every 2 seconds and held between updates, as the computer did, with a 2.2 s lead time; the engine is a constant-thrust rocket with an exhaust velocity of 2.97 km/s, and the vehicle

chunks.heading: Method and sources
chunks.text: 1. The LM's orbital plane is Columbia's, from Part 2's reconstruction. The guidance's aim point is placed 1,100 ft uprange and 400 ft across from where Eagle landed (mission report, Bennett). 2. The PDI state takes the documented time, height and speed. Its position along the orbit, its flight-path angle and the braking-phase downrange velocity target (unreadable in the scanned pad load) are solved for by least squares against the throttle-down time, the height at P64, and the DOI cutoff height. 3. The braking and approach phases are flown by Klumpp's guidance law with the Luminary 99 targets.

Launch to translunar injection: the ascent, the parking orbit, and the burn that leaves Earth. 2. Descent and landing: Eagle undocks, drops to 50,000 feet, and flies twelve and a half minutes of powered descent to Tranquility Base. 4. Rendezvous, return and entry (this post): ascent, rendezvous with Columbia, the burn home, and sp

chunks.heading: Introduction
chunks.text: Part 3 ended with Eagle on the surface. Twenty-one and a half hours later, at 124:22:01, its ascent engine fired and the top half of the lander left the bottom half behind. This part covers the 71 hours from there to the Pacific: seven minutes of powered ascent, three and a half hours of rendezvous, Columbia's burn out of lunar orbit, the coast home, and the entry.

chunks.heading: How this part is built
chunks.text: The method is the same as before: documented anchors, physics between them, and a small number of quantities solved for so that the physics passes through the anchors. Everything else NASA published is a check. What is new here is that three of the four phases are steered, by guidance or by the crew, so the reconstruction has to fly them, not just coast between them. - The ascent is flown with a constant-thrust engine and a linear-tangent steering law, the textbook optimal law for climbing to orbit over a flat, airless planet.

chunks.heading: How this part is built
chunks.text: Its two constants, Eagle's mass and the engine's exhaust velocity are fitted to the insertion state Aldrin read off his display. - The rendezvous is flown burn by burn: each of the first two burns is solved so that the orbit after it matches the one NASA's tables give, and the third, the one that sets up the intercept, is solved so that Eagle reaches Columbia. - Columbia's orbit is fitted to the times Mission Control gave for losing and regaining its signal behind the Moon, and to the heights and speeds in the tables. - Transearth injection is fitted to arrive at the documented entry point, an

chunks.heading: Liftoff to splashdown
chunks.text: Press play, or jump to an event. Playback speeds up through the long coasts and slows down for the burns, the docking and the entry. The first panel follows the phase: the ascent seen from the side; the rendezvous as Columbia's crew saw it, with Eagle's position plotted relative to Columbia; the coast home in a frame that turns with the Moon; and the entry as height against time. The second panel is a map: the Moon's near side while the spacecraft are in lunar orbit, Earth as seen from Columbia on the way home, and the Pacific for the entry.

chunks.heading: Liftoff to splashdown
chunks.text: The third is a computer-generated view; try Columbia's window during the rendezvous, and Wide to pull back. The last panel has the computer's display as the reconstruction has it, the voice transcript, and NASA's audio and film where they exist; turn the sound on and pick Real time to hear them. The radio buttons above the panels pin the first panel to one phase; Follow the flight lets it change with the timeline.

chunks.heading: Liftoff
chunks.text: Eagle's ascent stage carried one engine, with no throttle and no gimbal: 3,500 lbf, on or off. Everything about the ascent came from pointing it. For ten seconds after liftoff the computer held Eagle vertical, to clear the descent stage and the ground, then pitched it over sharply, and for the next seven minutes tipped it steadily further towards the horizontal until it was in orbit. The pitch programme the reconstruction uses is the linear-tangent law, where is the thrust's elevation above the local horizontal. Over a flat surface with constant gravity and no air, this is the law that reaches

chunks.heading: Liftoff
chunks.text: Two steering constants, the liftoff mass and the engine's exhaust velocity are solved for. The four conditions they have to meet are the height, climb rate and speed at engine cutoff, which Aldrin read off the display at 124:29:21 ("5537.3, 32.8 feet per second, 60,666"), and the ascent's total delta-v from NASA's tables. The fitted liftoff mass is 10,800 lb, and the fitted exhaust velocity corresponds to a specific impulse of 307 s, close to the ascent engine's rating; the propellant this burns is within 1% of Bennett's 4,934 lb.

chunks.heading: Liftoff
chunks.text: None of that was imposed. The orbit Eagle reached, about 48 by 9 n mi, matches the tables and the onboard estimates. So does one number nobody planned for. Twenty-nine minutes after insertion Collins told Eagle its out-of-plane rate was minus 1 ft/s. The reconstruction's Eagle lifts off from Tranquility Base, which by then had been carried almost two miles out of Columbia's orbital plane by the Moon's rotation, and it flies straight down the plane's direction without steering sideways. It arrives with an out-of-plane rate of −0.95 ft/s, and the crew decided not to correct it.

chunks.heading: Liftoff
chunks.text: During the burn Aldrin called out speeds, climb rates and heights, and towards the end the velocity still to gain: The climb rates and the end-of-burn calls follow the reconstruction closely. The first two altitude calls are 300 to 800 ft below it, and the horizontal speed called at 124:24:32, 1,500 ft/s, is 180 ft/s ahead of it. The transcript's times are good to a second or two, and a 1,500 ft/s horizontal speed is what the reconstruction reaches 16 s later, so this is either a timing slip or a sign that the real ascent pitched over faster in its first minutes than a single linear-tangent la

chunks.heading: Which radius?
chunks.text: Fitting the ascent turned up something about NASA's tables. Lunar heights in Apollo by the Numbers are given in nautical miles above "the Moon", and Parts 2 and 3 measured them from the 1,738.09 km reference sphere that the TRW reconstruction uses. For the rendezvous rows that does not work. Each row gives a height and a speed, and the orbit afterwards; Kepler's laws fix the speed from the height and the orbit's size, so the rows can test their own reference radius: Measured from the 1,738.09 km sphere, the speeds come out 4 to 6 ft/s too low, every time.

chunks.heading: Which radius?
chunks.text: Measured from the landing site's radius, 1,735.48 km, they agree to a fraction of a foot per second, and the radius that fits best is within 0.3 km of the landing site's. The rendezvous was planned and flown from the LM's computer, which measured height from the landing site, and the tables keep that convention. This part uses it throughout. Parts 2 and 3 are not changed: their tables (LOI and DOI, from the CSM's side) fit the reference sphere as well or better.

chunks.heading: The rendezvous
chunks.text: Columbia was 60 n mi up and about 250 n mi ahead of Eagle along the orbit. Eagle did not chase it. A spacecraft that speeds up climbs into a higher, slower orbit and falls behind; to catch something ahead of you in orbit, you go lower, not faster. Eagle's 9 by 48 n mi orbit had a shorter period than Columbia's, and it gained on Columbia by about 9° per hour just by being lower. Apollo 11 used the coelliptic rendezvous, designed for Gemini and flown on every lunar landing until Apollo 14.

chunks.heading: The rendezvous
chunks.text: It has three burns, each with a single purpose: 1. CSI, concentric sequence initiation, half an orbit after insertion at the high point of Eagle's orbit, raises the low point so that Eagle's orbit is nearly circular. 2. CDH, constant delta height, half an orbit later, makes Eagle's orbit coelliptic with Columbia's: the same shape, a constant 15 n mi below. Seen from Columbia, Eagle now slides forward along a straight line underneath it. 3. TPI, terminal phase initiation, starts the intercept when the line of sight to Columbia reaches a set elevation above the horizon. From there Eagle travels

chunks.heading: The rendezvous
chunks.text: The reason for the indirection is that each burn is small and each error is easy to see and fix, and the final approach always looks the same to the crew: Columbia rising against the stars at a fixed angle, the same every time, which they had flown hundreds of times in the simulator.

chunks.heading: Relative motion
chunks.text: The left panel's rendezvous view is the classic picture: Columbia fixed at the origin, Eagle plotted as height and distance relative to it. In that frame the motion follows the Clohessy–Wiltshire equations. For a target in a circular orbit with mean motion n, small offsets x (ahead) and z (above) obey A spacecraft a constant height h below drifts forward at x = {3}{2} n\, h; with h = 15 n mi and Columbia's two-hour orbit that is about 1.2 n mi a minute, so the 60 n mi between them after CDH closed to the 27 n mi of TPI in 46 minutes. The loops before CSI are Eagle's eccentric orbit seen from a

chunks.heading: The burns
chunks.text: CSI and CDH are each solved so that the orbit after the burn is the one NASA's tables give. The crew read their burn solutions to the ground, and those are checks: The CDH solution agrees with the one the crew read out to within 2 ft/s in each component, and the height difference it leaves, 15.8 n mi, is close to the 15.5 n mi Eagle's backup guidance computer gave. TPI is solved differently, as the burn that puts Eagle on Columbia at the end of the braking, 42 minutes later, and it comes out at 20.3 ft/s against the 25.3 flown. Its components depend on exactly where Columbia was along its orbi

chunks.heading: Braking and docking
chunks.text: TPI puts Eagle on a collision course; the closing speed has to come off by hand. From 127:37 Armstrong braked in steps, keeping the line-of-sight rate to Columbia small and the closing rate in proportion to the range, a gate of so many feet per second at each mile. The reconstruction's path here follows the range and rate calls in the transcript, along the line of sight of the intercept: Without braking, the intercept would have arrived with a closing speed of about 30 ft/s. At 127:52 Eagle was stationkeeping about 100 ft from Columbia, and Collins flew the last few feet.

chunks.heading: Braking and docking
chunks.text: The docking was the one rough moment of the rendezvous: as the latches closed, the two spacecraft yawed against each other by 15° or so, "a funny one", Collins said afterwards, before the latches caught. Armstrong and Aldrin came back through the tunnel with the rock boxes. At 130:09 Eagle was let go, and half an hour later Columbia moved 2.2 ft/s away from it.

chunks.heading: Columbia's orbit
chunks.text: No table gives where Columbia was along its orbit during these hours, only its height and speed at a few events. But Mission Control's calls to the crew are full of times: "about a minute to LOS", "see you over the hill at 131:48", each one an occultation by the Moon that the ground predicted from tracking. Columbia's orbit is fitted to eight of these, to the tables' heights and speeds, to the orbit after the final separation, to the TPI burn the crew read out, and to the range and rate the Public Affairs Officer gave a few minutes before TPI.

chunks.heading: Columbia's orbit
chunks.text: The signal times fit to within about 45 seconds, which is the resolution of "about a minute to LOS". The heights are within about a mile, except at TEI ignition, where the reconstruction is 3.3 n mi high: as in Part 3, the reconstruction's lunar gravity has only its two largest terms, and the low point of the real orbit wandered with the mascons.

chunks.heading: Transearth injection
chunks.text: At 135:23:42, behind the Moon on its 31st orbit, Columbia's service propulsion engine fired for two and a half minutes and added 3,279 ft/s. It turned a 54 by 63 n mi orbit into a hyperbola relative to the Moon, and a long, falling ellipse relative to Earth that met the atmosphere 59½ hours later. The energy of the escape is set by the burn's size: v^2 = v^2 - 2{Moon}/r, a speed at infinity of about 4,000 ft/s relative to the Moon. Its direction is set by where around the orbit the burn happens, and its timing and aim at Earth by both.

chunks.heading: Transearth injection
chunks.text: The reconstruction keeps the documented ignition time and takes the burn's direction from the pre-burn PAD (3,201.1 ft/s forward, 681.8 sideways, 265.0 up), then solves for small corrections to its pitch and yaw and for its size so that, with the one midcourse correction actually flown, the trajectory crosses 400,000 ft at the documented time, latitude, longitude and angle. The sideways component in the PAD is real: the trajectory home had to leave the Moon's equatorial orbit at an angle to reach the right latitude on Earth.

chunks.heading: Transearth injection
chunks.text: The fitted burn is 3,284.6 ft/s, 5.6 ft/s more than the tables and 1 more than the PAD; the flight dynamics officer's preliminary figure, read out by the PAO, was 3,283.5. The fit trades a slightly hotter burn against the start state: the reconstruction's Columbia begins TEI 3.3 n mi high, and leaves at 61.6 n mi against 58.1. From there to entry everything lines up. The state 15 hours later at MCC-5 is within 8 n mi out of 169,000 and a quarter of a foot per second, and the state at CM/SM separation 44 hours after that within 5 n mi and 13 ft/s, all as checks.

chunks.heading: Transearth injection
chunks.text: The entry speed and heading, which the fit did not use, agree to 0.2 ft/s and 0.02°. MCC-5, 4.8 ft/s at 150:30, was the only correction on the way home; MCC-6 and MCC-7 were cancelled. On the way the crew gave two television broadcasts. In the evening one, at 177:32, each of them spoke about what the flight meant; it is in the Day 8 audio.

chunks.heading: Entry
chunks.text: At 195:03:06 the command module, separated from its service module a quarter of an hour earlier, reached 400,000 ft, 3° south of the equator, 1,500 n mi from its target, moving at 36,194 ft/s and descending at 6.5°. The angle is the whole problem of lunar entry. Steeper than about 7.5° and the deceleration exceeds what the crew and structure were built for; shallower than about 5.5° and the command module does not lose enough speed on its first pass to stay in, and skips back out on a long ellipse.

chunks.heading: Entry
chunks.text: The corridor is two degrees wide at the end of a trajectory 240,000 miles long, and MCC-5's 4.8 ft/s was what kept it centred. The command module was not a ballistic capsule. Its centre of mass was offset from its axis, so it flew at an angle of attack of about 20° and produced lift, about 0.28 of its drag. By rolling, the computer pointed that lift up, down, or sideways, and so controlled how deep the command module flew and how far. The reconstruction flies it as a point mass with drag D = 12 v^2 CD A and lift L = 0.282\,D, in the US Standard Atmosphere 1976 turning with Earth, with the 12,1

chunks.heading: Entry
chunks.text: where is the bank angle and { u} is the local vertical with its component along the velocity removed. The bank angle is held at zero (lift up) for the first 70 seconds and rolled to the −15° the display showed, as the 1970 entry analysis describes. After that it is described by its cosine, the share of lift pointing up, at eleven times, plus the time of the first reversal of its sideways component; the later reversals are at the times the analysis gives. These are solved so that the speed at the start of the final phase, the load factor at the bottom of the loft, the second load-factor peak, t

chunks.heading: Entry
chunks.text: The first peak, 6.55 g at 82 s, comes from the entry angle and the lift-up start alone, before any fitted parameter has acted; the entry analysis gives 6.73 g from the accelerometers, the mission report "about 6.5". The lowest point of that first dip, 183,100 ft, compares with 182,109. After it the computer lofted the command module, rolling to keep a little lift upward, to stretch the range: Apollo 11's landing point had been moved 215 n mi further downrange the day before, away from a line of thunderstorms, and the extra distance had to come from somewhere.

chunks.heading: Entry
chunks.text: The reconstruction climbs back to about 220,000 ft before the final phase brings it down for the second peak. The fitted bank history is a reconstruction of what the guidance would have had to command, not a record of it; several different histories could meet the same handful of numbers. Its broad shape is what the entry analysis describes: lift up into the first pulse, a roll towards lift down as the deceleration built, mostly lift up through the loft, and in the final phase bank angles near 90° with the sideways lift reversed at the three documented times (dotted lines) to keep the crossran

chunks.heading: Splashdown
chunks.text: The drogue parachutes opened at about 24,000 ft, 9 minutes after entry interface, and the three mains at about 10,000 ft. The reconstruction treats both as drag only, with no wind (there was a surface wind of about 18 knots), and solves for the two ballistic coefficients that put the mains out at 10,000 ft and the command module in the water at the mission report's 195:18:35. The main-parachute descent comes out at 32 ft/s at the water, which is what three 83-foot canopies were designed to give.

chunks.heading: Splashdown
chunks.text: Once the transcript's clock is aligned to the mission report's splashdown time, Armstrong's last three altitude calls on the way down agree with the reconstruction to within about 250 ft; the first, 3,750 ft, is 840 ft below it, which suggests the drogue phase was a little slower than this simple drag model. Columbia came down upside down, in the "stable 2" position, and righted itself when the flotation bags inflated. The Hornet's swimmers were there within ten minutes; the crew, in biological isolation garments, were on the carrier an hour after splashdown, 8 days, 3 hours and 18 minutes aft

chunks.heading: What the reconstruction shows
chunks.text: Across the four parts, the reconstruction has flown Apollo 11 from the launch pad to the Pacific through 195 hours, re-anchoring at each phase but otherwise letting physics carry it. A few points hold across the whole flight: - NASA's 1969–70 numbers are self-consistent to a degree that is easy to take for granted. Burn sizes, times, states and orbits from different documents, produced by different groups, agree with each other through Newtonian physics to a few feet per second, often less. - The weakest link is the Moon's gravity.

chunks.heading: What the reconstruction shows
chunks.text: The model's lunar field has its two largest terms. Over a few hours that is good to a mile or two; over a day it is not, and every lunar part needed a fresh anchor for where along the orbit the spacecraft were. - The record that pins things best is often the least formal one. Signal-loss times read out by Mission Control, Aldrin's altitude and speed calls, the Public Affairs Officer's range figure before TPI, and the crew's readbacks of their burn solutions are the checks that constrain this part most tightly.

chunks.heading: What the reconstruction shows
chunks.text: - Where the reconstruction does not fit, it says so. The descent used 2.6% more delta-v than Eagle did; the TPI burn differs in its components; the entry's bank history is one of several that would do. Those are the places the 1969 record does not fully determine.

chunks.heading: Method and sources
chunks.text: For how the coordinate frames, views, synchronisation and data sources fit together across the series, see the explainer Frames of Reference in the Apollo 11 Reconstruction. The force model is the one used throughout: Earth with J2, the Moon with J2 and C{22}, the Sun, integrated with a Dormand–Prince 5(4) method in the geocentric mean-of-1969 frame, with the Moon and Sun from JPL's DE421. The entry uses Earth with J2 and the atmosphere only, integrated with fourth-order Runge–Kutta at half-second steps. 1. Columbia's state at 131:00 (position along the orbit, height, speed, flight-path angle)

chunks.text: The plane comes from Part 3's orbit carried forward. 2. The ascent: two steering constants, the liftoff mass and the exhaust velocity, fitted to the DSKY insertion state, the tables' speed and the ascent delta-v. Thrust 3,500 lbf (Bennett), 10 s vertical rise. 3. CSI and CDH: forward and radial components fitted to the documented orbits after each (CDH's sideways component from the crew's readback); finite burns on the LM's RCS. TPI: three components solved for an intercept at the end of TPF. Braking follows the range calls.

chunks.heading: Method and sources
chunks.text: 4. TEI: pitch, yaw and size, from the PAD direction, fitted to the entry-interface time, place and angle, and to the TEI cutoff state; MCC-5 as flown (PAD vector, ABTN time). 5. Entry: bank profile fitted as described above; drogues and mains as drag, two ballistic coefficients fitted.

V. Bennett, Apollo Lunar Descent and Ascent Trajectories, NASA TM X-58040 (1970): ascent engine, vertical rise, propellant. - NASA's Apollo 11 air-to-ground and onboard voice trans
